How to use this guide

2 diagrams · 2 min read

An optical link is a chain of conversions: bits become electrical symbols, symbols become light, light becomes current, current becomes bits again. Every topic in this guide exists to keep errors low at each hop for the least power and cost. Sections 1–5 are the physics and signal-processing core, 6–11 the product landscape built on it, 12–15 the operator's toolkit, and 16–26 deeper topics, from new fiber types and silicon photonics to long-haul coherent transmission.

Scope. Vendor-neutral and standards-first (IEEE 802.3, OIF, the MSAs), Ethernet-centric. The depth target is correct mental models: where a formula appears, it makes an intuition precise rather than asking to be derived.

Three questions that decode any optic

  1. Lanes. How many electrical lanes face the host, how many optical lanes face the fiber, and at what rate each? A 400G QSFP-DD DR4 has 8 × 50G electrical and 4 × 100G optical lanes, so a gearbox must sit between them.
  2. Encoding. How does each lane carry bits: NRZ (1 bit per symbol), PAM4 (2 bits per symbol), or coherent QAM on two polarizations (8 or more bits per symbol)?
  3. Recovery. What cleans the signal up, and where: host SerDes equalization, a module DSP, FEC on the host, FEC inside the module, or several of these?

Four relationships used everywhere

  • Bit rate = symbol rate (baud) × bits per symbol × polarizations.
  • Port speed = lanes × lane rate.
  • Reach ends for one of two reasons: too little light arrives (loss), or the light arrives but the symbols have smeared into each other (distortion and noise).
  • Lost margin shows up first as rising corrected FEC errors, long before a link drops. Healthy-but-degrading and broken look very different in the counters.

A retimed link is equalized in three separate segments, but its Reed-Solomon FEC runs end to end, so errors from all three share one budget.

Companion lab. Optics Bench, an interactive lab that accompanies the guide, turns five of these ideas into instruments: NRZ and PAM4 eyes side by side at the same bit rate, coherent constellations against OSNR, a link-budget calculator with the PMD figures from section 6, a PMD-name and lane-rate decoder, and Mach-Zehnder vs ring modulators (section 25).

Pros and cons for AI networks. Sections where an AI fabric faces a real technology choice close with an “AI networks: pros and cons” callout, and section 9 opens with a map of all of them by network tier.

A learning path

The sections can be read in order, but an expert's knowledge is layered rather than sequential: every operational question rests on a product fact, every product fact on an electrical or optical constraint, and every constraint on a few numbers from physics. The ladder below groups the guide into six such layers, with the sections to read and a test for each. Read bottom to top the first time; afterwards, enter at the rung where your question lives and climb down until the explanation holds.

Each rung's test is a question that the sections on that rung answer with numbers rather than adjectives; the mastery checks in section 30 draw on all six.

Section 1 · Foundations

Physics foundations

3 diagrams · 11 min read
In this sectionFiber: multimode vs single-modeWavelength windowsImpairments in plain termsFiber in numbers: attenuation, dispersion and nonlinearityLasers and modulatorsDetectorsReceivers and noise: what a sensitivity figure is made of

Two things end every optical link: too little light arrives (loss), or light arrives but the symbols have smeared together (dispersion, bandwidth limits, noise). Every choice of fiber, wavelength, laser and detector trades between those two limits.

Fiber: multimode vs single-mode

Multimode (MMF) Single-mode (SMF)
Core diameter 50 µm ~9 µm
Grades OM3, OM4, OM5 OS2 (ITU-T G.652.D)
Wavelengths 850 nm (OM5 is specified from 846 to 953 nm for SWDM) O-band ~1310 nm, C-band ~1550 nm
Light source VCSEL DFB, EML, silicon photonics, tunable lasers
What limits reach Modal dispersion: many light paths arrive at different times Attenuation, then chromatic dispersion as baud rises
Reach at 100G per lane ~50–100 m 500 m–10 km IM-DD; 80 km+ coherent
Cost profile Cheapest optics, costlier cable, short reach Costlier optics (falling fast), cheap cable, any reach

Multimode reach shrinks with every speed step, while single-mode parallel optics (DR) have become cheap. That is why new data-center builds increasingly run single-mode almost everywhere.

Wavelength windows

  • O-band (1260–1360 nm). Chromatic dispersion in standard SMF is near zero around 1310 nm, so intensity-modulated pulses stay sharp. Nearly all IM-DD single-mode optics (DR, FR, LR) live here.
  • CWDM vs LAN-WDM inside the O-band. CWDM spaces four lanes 20 nm apart (1271, 1291, 1311, 1331 nm), which keeps lasers cheap. LAN-WDM packs lanes much closer to 1310 nm, so the outer lanes see less dispersion; it is used where 10 km reach matters.
  • C-band (1530–1565 nm). Lowest loss (~0.2 dB/km) and the band where erbium-doped fiber amplifiers (EDFAs) work, so DWDM and coherent live here. Dispersion is large (~17 ps/nm/km), which a coherent DSP removes electronically.
  • 850 nm (MMF). VCSEL territory; SWDM spreads lanes across 850–940 nm on OM5.

Grey single-mode optics sit where dispersion vanishes; coherent sits where loss is lowest and amplifiers work, and lets its DSP handle the dispersion.

Impairments in plain terms

Impairment What happens Who it hurts most Countermeasure
Attenuation Power decays with distance (~0.3–0.5 dB/km O-band, ~0.2 dB/km C-band) and at every connector and splice Everyone Shorter spans, clean connectors, amplifiers in C-band
Chromatic dispersion (CD) Wavelengths within a pulse travel at different speeds, so symbols spread into their neighbors IM-DD at high baud, away from 1310 nm Stay near 1310 nm; coherent DSP compensation
Modal dispersion Light paths in MMF arrive at different times MMF only Better grade (OM4/OM5), shorter reach
Polarization mode dispersion (PMD) The two polarizations drift apart in time, randomly Long spans at high baud Coherent adaptive equalizer
Reflections and MPI Light bounces between connectors and interferes with itself PAM4 (closely spaced levels) Clean or angled (APC) connectors, fewer mated pairs
Nonlinearity At high launch power the fiber itself distorts the signal Amplified long-haul Optimal launch power
Noise Receiver thermal/shot noise; amplifier ASE noise Everyone; ASE in amplified coherent Sensitive receivers (APD), OSNR planning

Fiber in numbers: attenuation, dispersion and nonlinearity

The table above says what each impairment does. An expert also carries the numbers, because the numbers decide which family of optic lives where.

Attenuation. Three mechanisms shape the loss curve: Rayleigh scattering from the glass's frozen-in density fluctuations, which falls as 1/λ⁴ and dominates below 1500 nm; the hydroxyl absorption peak at 1383 nm, which G.652.D "low water peak" fiber suppresses so that the E-band is usable; and infrared absorption by the silica lattice, which climbs steeply past 1600 nm and sets the far edge of the L-band. Typical G.652.D fiber is about 0.33 dB/km at 1310 nm and 0.18–0.20 dB/km at 1550 nm (ITU-T G.652.D itself allows 0.4 and 0.3 dB/km; vendor cable specifications are typically 0.34–0.38 and 0.20–0.25); multimode at 850 nm is 2.3–3.0 dB/km (TIA-568.3 specifies 3.0 dB/km for OM3, OM4 and OM5 alike; ISO/IEC 11801 allows 3.5). That is why the C-band owns long haul, and why multimode reach is measured in tens of meters once baud is high.

Chromatic dispersion. For G.652 fiber ITU-T gives the dispersion coefficient as

D(λ) = (S0 / 4) · (λ − λ04 / λ3)

with the zero-dispersion wavelength λ₀ anywhere between 1300 and 1324 nm and the slope S₀ at most 0.092 ps/(nm²·km). The numbers that follow: about −4 ps/(nm·km) at the 1271 nm CWDM lane, +2 at 1331 nm and +17 at 1550 nm; over 10 km the outer CWDM lanes accumulate 40–50 ps/nm at the lane centers and nearly 60 at the lane edge on worst-case fiber, and 80 km at 1550 nm accumulates about 1,360 ps/nm. Two consequences matter for IM-DD. First, a 53 GBd PAM4 signal occupies about 0.3 nm of spectrum at 1310 nm, so 50 ps/nm smears each symbol by roughly 15 ps against an 18.8 ps unit interval: that is why IEEE held 100G-per-lane CWDM4 to 6 km (400GBASE-LR4-6, and reached 10 km at 100G per lane only with the single-wavelength 100GBASE-LR1; the 100G Lambda MSA's 400G-LR4-10 keeps the same CWDM lanes and gets to 10 km by budgeting the full −59 to +33 ps/nm and relaxing TDECQ to 3.9 dB), and why 800GBASE-LR4, at 200G per lane with an 8.8 ps symbol (113.4375 GBd with the inner FEC) and a spectrum about 0.65 nm wide, moved to LAN-WDM lanes huddled around λ₀. Second, because a photodiode detects power, dispersion turns the two sidebands of an intensity-modulated signal against each other and carves notches into the channel response, the first at

fnull = √( c / (2 · D · L · λ2) )

At 1310 nm and 40 ps/nm the first null sits at 47 GHz, close to the 53 GHz Nyquist frequency of a 200G-per-lane signal; at 1550 nm after 80 km it sits at 6.8 GHz. That one formula is why no high-baud IM-DD optic runs at 1550 nm beyond a few kilometers, and why coherent detection, which recovers the optical field and undoes dispersion digitally, takes over there.

Polarization mode dispersion. G.652.D specifies a link design value of 0.2 ps/√km and modern cable typically measures 0.1 or better, so a 1,000 km route accumulates about 3 ps: irrelevant for data-center IM-DD, tracked easily by a coherent DSP, and a real limit only on old fiber (0.5–2 ps/√km) at 10G NRZ beyond a few tens of kilometers.

Mode field, cutoff and bandwidth. G.652.D's mode field diameter is 8.6–9.2 µm (±0.4) at 1310 nm and about 10.4 µm at 1550 nm; a mode-field mismatch at a splice or connector is a loss, which is why G.657.A2 bend-insensitive fiber keeps the same MFD so that it splices to G.652.D without penalty. The cable cutoff wavelength is at most 1260 nm: below it the fiber carries a second mode, which is why the O-band, and the 1271 nm CWDM lane's lower edge, start there. Multimode fiber's equivalent figure is effective modal bandwidth, 2,000 MHz·km for OM3 and 4,700 MHz·km for OM4 and OM5 at 850 nm (OM5 adds 2,470 at 953 nm), and that bandwidth-distance product is what caps 100G-per-lane VCSEL links at tens of meters.

Nonlinearity. The Kerr effect makes the refractive index rise with intensity, n = n₀ + n₂·I, with n₂ about 2.6 × 10⁻²⁰ m²/W and an effective area of about 80 µm² in G.652 (110–130 µm² in terrestrial G.654.E large-effective-area fiber and up to about 150 µm² in G.654.B and G.654.D submarine fiber, which is why those routes use them). The nonlinear phase a channel picks up scales with launch power × effective length ÷ effective area, and it shows up as self-phase modulation on one channel and as cross-phase modulation and four-wave mixing between WDM channels. Two scattering effects have thresholds: stimulated Brillouin scattering reflects a narrow-linewidth continuous-wave laser back toward its source once it exceeds roughly +5 to +10 dBm on a long span, which is why coherent transmitters and external laser sources dither or broaden their lines; stimulated Raman scattering moves power from shorter to longer wavelengths across the C+L band, a few dB of tilt at high total power, which line systems pre-compensate. None of this touches a 500 m DR link at +1 dBm per fiber; all of it governs section 26.

The two curves between them explain the product map: VCSELs at 850 nm accept 2–3 dB/km because the link is 100 m; grey single-mode optics sit at 1310 nm because dispersion vanishes there and a photodiode cannot undo it; coherent sits at 1550 nm because loss is lowest and EDFAs work there, and its DSP removes the 17 ps/(nm·km).

Sources: G.652 attribute tables, 802.3cu dispersion by lane, 400G-LR4-10 MSA, OM3 and OM4 attenuation, G.654.E white paper.

Lasers and modulators

There are two ways to put data on light: swing the laser's drive current directly, or leave the laser on and modulate its output with a separate device. Direct modulation is cheaper; external modulation is cleaner and faster. Section 25 shows how the silicon photonic versions are built.

Source Modulation Where it is used Trade-off
VCSEL (850 nm) Direct SR/VR multimode Cheapest, lowest power; MMF only
DML (directly modulated DFB) Direct 10G/25G-lane LR, 100G CWDM4 Cheap, but chirp limits speed and reach
EML (DFB + electro-absorption modulator) External, integrated 100G and 200G-lane DR/FR/LR Low chirp, high bandwidth; one laser per lane
Silicon photonics (CW laser + Mach-Zehnder or ring modulator) External, on silicon DR4/DR8 parallel, co-packaged optics One laser can feed several lanes; scales like a chip
Thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) External Mach-Zehnder Emerging for 200G/lane and up, coherent Very high bandwidth, low drive voltage
Tunable laser (ITLA) Feeds a coherent IQ modulator Coherent DWDM Narrow linewidth, tunable across the C-band

Chirp is the wavelength wobble a laser shows when its current swings. Combined with dispersion it smears pulses, which is why directly modulated lasers run out of road at high baud and long reach.

Detectors

  • PIN photodiode + TIA. The standard IM-DD receiver: the photodiode turns photons into current, the transimpedance amplifier turns current into voltage.
  • APD (avalanche photodiode). Internal gain buys several dB of sensitivity for ER-class grey optics, at higher cost and temperature sensitivity.
  • Square-law detection. A photodiode measures power only; phase and polarization are invisible to it. So IM-DD can equalize the intersymbol interference that dispersion causes (an FFE or MLSE in the DSP does exactly that), but it cannot invert dispersion itself: beyond a few tens of ps/nm, double-sideband intensity modulation plus dispersion produces nulls in the detected spectrum that no equalizer can restore, which is why IM-DD reach is dispersion-capped. A coherent receiver adds a local laser so that mixing converts phase into measurable intensity, and its DSP can then undo dispersion exactly.

Receivers and noise: what a sensitivity figure is made of

A receiver's sensitivity is not one number from one source. It is the quantum limit of light plus a stack of penalties, and knowing which penalty dominates tells you what a better receiver could buy.

Responsivity. A photodiode converts light to current at R = ηqλ/hc, which caps at 1.06 A/W at 1310 nm and 1.25 A/W at 1550 nm for perfect quantum efficiency; germanium and InGaAs PINs reach 0.8–1.0 A/W, and GaAs at 850 nm about 0.5. One microwatt of light is therefore about one microamp of current, and a −10 dBm signal about 100 µA: small, which is why the transimpedance amplifier (TIA) that follows is the component that decides the noise.

Three noises, three regimes.

  • Thermal (circuit) noise from the TIA is fixed by its bandwidth and design, typically 10–15 pA/√Hz input-referred, which over the roughly 30 GHz bandwidth of a 53 GBd linear TIA is about 2 µA rms. A PIN receiver is thermal-limited: signal current grows with power P but the noise does not, so electrical SNR grows as P², and 1 dB of optical power is worth 2 dB of SNR. Every DR, FR and SR module lives here.
  • Shot noise is the light's own granularity, with variance 2qIB, so it grows as √P. A receiver reaches the shot-noise regime only when something lifts the signal above the circuit noise: avalanche gain in an APD, an optical preamplifier (SOA or EDFA), or coherent mixing with a strong local oscillator. There SNR grows as P, 1 dB optical is 1 dB electrical, and sensitivity can approach the physics.
  • Intensity noise that rides in with the light (laser RIN, amplifier ASE, multipath interference from reflections) scales with P itself, so more power does not help: it sets an error floor that only a quieter source, a higher OSNR or fewer reflections can lower.

The ladder from the quantum limit to a real module. Ideal on-off keying with a photon-counting receiver needs about 10 photons per bit for a BER of 10⁻⁹; at 106.25 Gb/s and 1310 nm (photon energy 1.52 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) that is 0.16 µW, or −38 dBm. Shot noise with a Gaussian decision in an NRZ receiver already costs a few dB (about −35 dBm). The TIA's thermal noise adds 20 dB and more, the single biggest step. PAM4 costs a further 4.8 dB of optical power (9.5 dB of electrical SNR), because its three eyes are each a third of the height; the FEC-era BER target of 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ gives about 2.5 dB of that back. Finite extinction ratio, receiver bandwidth, residual ISI and reflections take another 3–4 dB. The result is a specified sensitivity of about −4.4 dBm OMA outer for a clean signal in 400GBASE-DR4 (−4.6 for FR4, −6.8 for LR4-6): some 33 dB above the quantum limit, almost all of it electronics. The standard then lets the receiver give back 2.0–2.5 dB for a transmitter at the TDECQ limit (the sensitivity row relaxes 1 dB per dB of stressed eye closure above a 0.9–1.4 dB floor), which is where the stressed sensitivity figures of −1.9, −2.6 and −4.8 dBm come from.

Three practical readings follow. An APD or SOA-preamplified receiver buys back 5–10 dB, which is how ER-class grey optics reach 40 km. Coherent detection with a strong local oscillator reaches the shot-noise regime, which, with the DSP's dispersion compensation, is most of why coherent wins beyond tens of kilometers. And because a PIN receiver's SNR scales with P², the first dB of lost margin on a grey link costs twice what it seems: a connector that eats 1 dB of light has taken 2 dB of electrical SNR from the slicer.

Sources: 400GBASE-DR4 receiver rows, FR4 and LR4-6 rows, PAM4 modulation penalty, quantum and shot-noise limits, 53 GBd linear TIA noise.

Section 2 · Foundations

Signaling and modulation

1 diagram · 4 min read
In this sectionBaud is not bit rateNRZ vs PAM4Lane rates in practiceAfter PAM4: the 400G-per-lane questionThe coherent modulation family

PAM4 carries 2 bits per symbol instead of NRZ's 1, halving the symbol rate for a given bit rate, but each eye is one-third as tall, costing about 9.5 dB of SNR. The industry took that trade at 50G per lane because doubling the baud instead would have pushed lasers, drivers and copper channels past their bandwidth.

Baud is not bit rate

  • Symbol rate (baud, GBd) is how many times per second the signal changes state. Bit rate = baud × bits per symbol.
  • Bandwidth follows baud, not bits. The frequency that matters is Nyquist = baud ÷ 2. A 100G PAM4 lane at 53.125 GBd needs about 26.6 GHz of bandwidth; the same 100G as NRZ would need about 53 GHz.
  • So adding bits per symbol buys bit rate without buying bandwidth. The price is SNR, and the receipt is the FEC and DSP that every PAM4 link now carries.

NRZ vs PAM4

NRZ (PAM2) PAM4
Levels 2 4
Bits per symbol 1 2
Eyes 1 3, stacked
Eye height at the same swing Full One-third
SNR penalty vs NRZ — ~9.5 dB (20·log₁₀ 3)
FEC RS(528,514) mandatory on SR, LR, ER, SR4, CR4, KR4 and CWDM4; negotiated on short copper and backplane (CR-S, KR-S); none on LR4 and ER4 Mandatory
Linearity demand Low: drivers can simply switch High: levels must stay evenly spaced
Typical lane rates 10G, 25G 50G, 100G, 200G

The intuition for 9.5 dB: the same peak-to-peak swing is now split into three gaps. Noise that used to be harmless now pushes a symbol across a decision threshold.

Gray coding (right) means neighboring levels differ in one bit, so the most common PAM4 error costs one bit, not two. The Optics Bench lab shows the same eyes with real noise and bandwidth limits.

PAM4-specific concepts

  • Gray coding. Levels map to 00, 01, 11, 10, so the most likely error (landing on an adjacent level) corrupts one bit, not two.
  • Level linearity (R_LM, level separation mismatch ratio: at least 0.95 in most PAM4 PMDs). Nonlinear drivers or TIAs squeeze the outer or inner eyes. A PAM4 link can fail on linearity with plenty of optical power.
  • TDECQ (transmitter and dispersion eye closure, quaternary). The PAM4 transmitter quality metric, in dB, lower is better. It asks how much noise the transmitter's signal could still tolerate after a reference equalizer, compared with an ideal transmitter. It replaced eye masks because a raw PAM4 eye is often closed before equalization yet perfectly usable after it.
  • OMA vs average power. Optical modulation amplitude is the power difference between the outer levels; receivers care about OMA. DOM reports average power, so a module can show healthy Rx power while its OMA, and therefore its eye, is poor.
  • MPI sensitivity. Reflections that re-enter the signal path beat against it and add noise that scales with signal amplitude, worst on the outer levels; with eyes one-third the height, PAM4 tolerates far less reflection than NRZ, which is why PAM4 PMDs tabulate the maximum discrete reflectance against the number of connectors (for 400GBASE-DR4-2: −25 dB for one, −41 dB for ten).

Lane rates in practice

Nominal lane Modulation Symbol rate Line rate FEC that fills the overhead
10G NRZ 10.3125 GBd 10.3125 Gb/s 64b/66b coding only
25G NRZ 25.78125 GBd 25.78125 Gb/s RS(528,514) on most PMDs; none on 100G LR4/ER4
50G PAM4 26.5625 GBd 53.125 Gb/s RS(544,514)
100G PAM4 53.125 GBd 106.25 Gb/s RS(544,514)
200G electrical, and 500 m optical PAM4 106.25 GBd 212.5 Gb/s RS(544,514)
200G optical, 2 km and longer PAM4 113.4375 GBd 226.875 Gb/s RS(544,514) + inner Hamming(128,120)

The step from 106.25 to 113.4375 GBd on 2 km-plus 200G lanes is the overhead of an extra FEC layer added inside the module (section 5). The odd-looking numbers all come from the same recipe: 100 Gb/s of payload, 256b/257b transcoding, RS(544,514) overhead, then PAM4 halves the baud.

After PAM4: the 400G-per-lane question

IEEE 802.3 chartered a 400 Gb/s per lane study group in March 2026; its PAR was approved on 25 September 2026 and the P802.3dv Task Force now covers 400G, 800G and 1.6T over electrical links and single-mode fiber up to 500 m, with submission for approval projected for September 2029 (study group page). The leading candidates are PAM4 at roughly 224 GBd and PAM6 at roughly 174 GBd (comparison). It is the NRZ-to-PAM4 trade again: more levels lower the baud and ease component bandwidth, but squeeze the eyes further and cost more SNR.

The coherent modulation family

A coherent receiver measures the optical field, not just its power, so it can use four dimensions: in-phase and quadrature amplitude on each of two polarizations. Each step to a denser constellation buys bits per symbol but needs more OSNR, so reach falls.

Format Bits per symbol, per polarization Dual-polarization total Typical use
DP-QPSK 2 4 100G long haul; low-rate modes of multi-rate pluggables
DP-8QAM 3 6 Intermediate rates (300G modes)
DP-16QAM 4 8 400ZR (~60 GBd), 800ZR (~120 GBd)
DP-64QAM, shaped Up to 6 Up to 12 High-capacity metro transponders

Probabilistic constellation shaping (PCS) sends inner constellation points more often than outer ones. That moves performance closer to the Shannon limit and lets one transceiver trade capacity against reach in fine steps instead of jumping between formats.

Worked example: DP-16QAM carries 8 bits per symbol. At about 60 GBd that is roughly 480 Gb/s gross, which carries 400GbE plus FEC and framing overhead. That is 400ZR.

Section 3 · Foundations

Electrical interface and SerDes

2 diagrams · 6 min read
In this sectionWhat a SerDes isThe host channel and equalizationAUI naming: reading the electrical interfaceGearboxes and retimersSerDes generations at a glanceCopper and link trainingElectrical channel specs: why a host link can fail with good opticsCompliance points: who owns which test point

The host SerDes lane rate is the clock of the whole industry. Each doubling (25G, 50G, 100G, 200G) brought a new switch-silicon generation, a new form-factor family and a new set of optics, because the module must present exactly the lanes the host drives.

What a SerDes is

A SerDes (serializer/deserializer) is the high-speed I/O block on a switch ASIC, NIC or GPU that turns wide parallel data into a few very fast serial lanes. Switch capacity is simply SerDes count × lane rate: 512 lanes × 100G = 51.2 Tb/s; 512 × 200G = 102.4 Tb/s. 102.4 Tb/s silicon with 512 × 200G SerDes has been shipping in production volume since March 2026 (announcement).

The host channel and equalization

Between the SerDes and the module sit package traces, PCB traces, the cage connector and the module's edge fingers. Copper attenuates high frequencies far more than low ones, so the signal arriving at the module is smeared. SerDes and DSPs fight back with equalizers:

  • FFE (feed-forward equalizer) at the transmitter. Pre-distorts the signal so the channel's smearing cancels it.
  • CTLE (continuous-time linear equalizer) at the receiver. Boosts the high frequencies the channel attenuated.
  • DFE (decision-feedback equalizer). Subtracts the echo of symbols already decided; powerful, but an early wrong decision propagates.
  • ADC + DSP receivers. At 100G and 200G per lane, receivers digitize the signal and equalize numerically, which is why "SerDes" and "DSP" increasingly blur together.

At 200G per lane the host channel is so lossy that designs add retimers, route signals over flyover twinax cables above the board instead of through it, or move the optics next to the chip (co-packaged optics, section 10).

AUI naming: reading the electrical interface

IEEE calls the electrical interface between host and module an AUI (attachment unit interface). C2M means chip-to-module, the host-to-pluggable link; C2C means chip-to-chip. The OIF publishes matching electrical specs called CEI (for example CEI-112G-VSR for 100G-lane host-to-module links).

AUI Lanes × rate Port speed Lane modulation
CAUI-4 4 × 25G 100G NRZ
100GAUI-2 2 × 50G 100G PAM4
100GAUI-1 1 × 100G 100G PAM4
200GAUI-4 4 × 50G 200G PAM4
400GAUI-8 8 × 50G 400G PAM4
400GAUI-4 4 × 100G 400G PAM4
800GAUI-8 8 × 100G 800G PAM4
200GAUI-1 / 400GAUI-2 / 800GAUI-4 1 / 2 / 4 × 200G 200G / 400G / 800G PAM4
1.6TAUI-8 8 × 200G 1.6T PAM4

Gearboxes and retimers

  • Retimer. Same number of lanes in and out at the same rate; it recovers the clock and data and re-launches a clean signal. Example: a 400G QSFP112 DR4 module, 4 × 100G electrical to 4 × 100G optical.
  • Gearbox. Changes lane count and rate. Example: a 400G QSFP-DD DR4 module on a 50G-lane host, 8 × 50G electrical to 4 × 100G optical.
  • Why it matters. Gearboxes add power and latency, and they are the reason one "400G DR4" can behave differently in two hosts. When electrical and optical lane rates match, the module can be simpler, and linear designs without any DSP become possible.

The optical side is identical in both rows; only the host lane rate, and therefore the work the module DSP does, changes.

SerDes generations at a glance

Host lane rate Typical switch capacity Signature ports Era
10G NRZ 0.64–1.28 Tb/s 10G SFP+, 40G QSFP+ ~2010–2014
25G NRZ 3.2–6.4 Tb/s 25G SFP28, 100G QSFP28 ~2015–2018
50G PAM4 12.8–25.6 Tb/s 200G QSFP56, 400G QSFP-DD/OSFP ~2018–2021
100G PAM4 25.6–51.2 Tb/s 400G QSFP112, 800G QSFP-DD800/OSFP ~2021–2025
200G PAM4 51.2–102.4 Tb/s 800G and 1.6T OSFP / QSFP-DD1600 2025 onward

Copper and link training

Passive DAC cables have no electronics, so the host SerDes must equalize the whole copper path. That is why copper links use auto-negotiation and link training: the two SerDes exchange settings to tune their equalizers to the specific cable. Optical modules terminate the electrical channel inside the module, so the optical link itself does not train. Confusing the two is a common cause of copper link failures.

Electrical channel specs: why a host link can fail with good optics

IEEE judges a host electrical channel with three numbers, and a port that fails them eats the same FEC budget a dirty connector would.

  • Insertion loss at Nyquist. Channel attenuation at baud ÷ 2: 26.56 GHz for 100G lanes, 53.125 GHz for 200G lanes. For 100G lanes, 802.3ck recommends at most 28 dB for a backplane (KR1) and 20 dB for chip-to-chip (802.3ck values). At 200G, 802.3dj's 200GBASE-CR1 cable budget is 40 dB die to die at 53.125 GHz (11.5 dB per host plus 17 dB of cable assembly) (proposal).
  • COM (channel operating margin). A simulation that runs a reference transmitter and receiver, with reference equalization, over the measured channel and reports how far the signal stands above noise, residual ISI and crosstalk, in dB. 802.3ck requires at least 3 dB for KR1 and chip-to-chip channels.
  • ERL (effective return loss). Reflections weighted by how much they would still hurt after equalization; 802.3ck sets a channel minimum of 9.7 dB.

The operational lesson. If the same optic is clean in one port and errored in another, suspect the host channel: a long trace to a far cage, a worn connector, or a marginal flyover cable. That is why 200G systems add retimers or flyover cables, and why section 5 says host FEC counters alone cannot convict an optic.

Compliance points: who owns which test point

Every electrical and optical number in a PMD or AUI clause is tied to a test point (TP), and each test point is a contract boundary. Knowing them tells you which party a failing measurement convicts.

Point Where it is What is specified there Who must comply
TP0, TP5 Host ASIC transmitter and receiver pins Reference points used in channel models (COM); not measured in production Host designer
TP1a Host output at the module connector (AUI-C2M) Eye height and vertical eye closure (VEC) after a reference CTLE, effective return loss, transition time Host
TP2 Optical output after a 2–5 m patch cord OMA outer, average power, extinction ratio, TDECQ, RIN, wavelength, SMSR Module transmitter
TP3 Optical input Sensitivity and stressed sensitivity in OMA outer (with the SECQ of the stressed signal), maximum receive power and OMA, damage threshold, aggressor OMA Module receiver
TP4 Module electrical output into the host Eye height and VEC at the module connector (near end) and after one reference host channel (far end) Module
TP4a Host input after its own trace What the host receiver must accept Host

Why it matters in a retimed module. The DSP breaks the link into three independently specified segments: host to module (TP1a to TP4a in one direction), fiber (TP2 to TP3) and module to host (TP4 to TP4a). The host never sees the optical eye and the fiber never sees the host trace, so a module can be optically perfect and still fail in a port whose channel exceeds the AUI-C2M budget of the previous subsection, and a port can be electrically perfect while the far transmitter's TDECQ is out of specification. Linear (LPO) modules remove that isolation: there is no TP2 a linear module can pass on its own, so host and module are qualified as a pair, and the host's equalizer is what makes the optical eye.

Measurement notes. The TP2 patch cord is short, so a transmitter is measured without fiber penalties; dispersion is accounted for on the receiver side, which is why stressed receiver sensitivity at TP3 includes a dispersion-equivalent impairment. TDECQ at TP2 is measured through a reference receiver filter and equalizer (section 22), so an optic with a pleasant-looking eye on a wideband scope can still fail, and one with a visibly closed eye can pass because the reference equalizer reopens it. AUI-C2M at 100G per lane and below has no link training: the host sets the module's input equalization and output emphasis through CMIS and nothing adapts on its own except what the DSP does internally. 802.3dj adds in-band training for its 200G-per-lane interfaces, and OIF's CMIS out-of-band link training (CMIS-LT, approved in 2026) adds a management-channel way to tune each lane in each direction for any module type, with linear optics as the main driver.

Sources: AUI-C2M test points, TP4 near-end and far-end limits, CMIS-LT white paper, 802.3dj in-band training.

Section 4 · Foundations

DSPs and signal conditioning

7 diagrams · 12 min read
In this sectionInside a PAM4 DSPRetimed vs LRO vs LPO vs CPOAI networks: pros and consFRO and mix-and-match: linear at one end, retimed at the otherInside a coherent DSPPower and process

A module DSP is a small mixed-signal computer that recovers clean symbols from a distorted signal and re-launches them, and it is the single largest power consumer in a pluggable. That is why the industry's next-generation designs either remove it (LPO), keep half of it (LRO), or move the optics next to the host so the host's SerDes can do the work (CPO).

Inside a PAM4 DSP

A retimed IM-DD module has two independent signal paths, each with its own equalizer:

  1. Host-side receiver. Takes the electrical lanes from the host: CTLE, ADC, FFE, clock and data recovery (CDR). Output: clean symbols.
  2. Lane mapping. Retimer (lanes in = lanes out) or gearbox (8 × 50G to 4 × 100G, for example).
  3. Line-side transmitter. DAC plus pre-emphasis and pre-distortion that compensate the laser and driver's limited bandwidth and nonlinearity.
  4. Line-side receiver. After the photodiode and TIA: ADC, FFE, often DFE or MLSE (maximum-likelihood sequence estimation, which decides on sequences of symbols rather than one at a time and copes with heavy smearing), then CDR.
  5. Host-side transmitter. Re-launches clean electrical lanes toward the host.
  6. Optional inner FEC. At 200G per lane on 2 km-plus links, the DSP adds and removes an inner FEC layer (section 5).
  7. Telemetry. Per-lane SNR, pre-FEC BER estimates and histograms, exposed to the host through CMIS (section 12).

The key property: a retimed module splits the end-to-end link into three separately equalized segments (host to module, module to module over fiber, module to host). Each segment only needs to meet its own budget, so any compliant host interoperates with any compliant module.

Retimed vs LRO vs LPO vs CPO

Moving down the rows, the module DSP shrinks and then disappears; its work moves to the host SerDes, or, with CPO, mostly becomes unnecessary because the electrical path is millimeters long.

Architecture DSP location Power (800G, vendor figures) Interoperability Reach today Diagnostics
FRO, fully retimed (DSP) In the module, both directions ~14–18 W Plug-and-play against standards 500 m to 10 km+ Full per-segment telemetry
LRO / RTLR (half-retimed) In the module, transmit path only; receive path linear ~30% below retimed Host receiver must handle the far module's linear output Short reach Partial
LPO (linear pluggable) None in the module; linear driver and TIA only ~7–8.5 W Validated per host-and-module pairing 500 m DR; 500 m FR4 variant Limited; host SerDes sees one long channel
CPO (co-packaged) None; optical engine sits beside the switch ASIC Lowest per bit Integrated system, not pluggable 500 m to 2 km class Platform-dependent

Power figures are vendor-reported, not independent measurements (LPO module, LRO demo).

  • LPO. Without a DSP, the host SerDes must equalize the entire path: host trace, module driver, laser, fiber, photodiode, TIA, far-end trace. The gains are power, latency and cost. The costs are tighter host requirements, interoperability that must be tested per pairing, and less visibility into which segment is degrading. The LPO MSA released a 100G-per-lane DR specification in March 2025 and a 400G-FR4-LPO (500 m) specification in September 2025 (March 2025, September 2025).
  • LRO. Keeps a DSP on the transmit side, where cleaning up the laser drive matters most, and leaves the receive side linear. It roughly halves the DSP's work while keeping the optical signal standards-clean. The OIF formalized the idea as RTLR (retimed transmitter, linear receiver) in a 112G implementation agreement published in late 2025 (announcement).
  • The 200G-per-lane problem. Linear designs get harder as baud rises, because the host channel loss and the optics' bandwidth limits both grow. Expect retimed modules to remain the default at 200G per lane, with linear variants confined to the shortest, best-controlled links.

AI networks: pros and cons

A non-blocking AI back-end fabric needs four to six transceivers for every GPU-facing port (section 9), so module power multiplies into megawatts, and every watt saved in the optics is a watt available for GPUs. That arithmetic is the whole case for linear optics; the case against it is operational.

At OFC 2026, 1.6T modules were in volume production and at least one supplier showed retimed, half-retimed and linear versions of the same module, so this is now a design choice rather than a roadmap question.

Option Pros in an AI fabric Cons in an AI fabric Best fit
Retimed (full DSP) Plug-and-play against IEEE PMDs, so any compliant host meets any compliant module; reaches 2 km and beyond with inner FEC; per-segment telemetry shows whether the host, the fiber or the far end is degrading Highest power (about 20–26 W at 1.6T) and the most heat in the cage; the DSP adds latency and cost to every port Mixed-vendor fabrics, links over 500 m, and anywhere fast fault isolation matters more than watts
LRO (half-retimed) About 30% less power than retimed (about 11–15 W at 1.6T); the transmit side stays standards-clean, so qualification is easier than for LPO The receive side relies on the host SerDes; diagnostics are partial; fewer suppliers, and the OIF agreement covers only 112G lanes so far Short leaf-to-spine links where power matters but per-pair LPO qualification costs too much
LPO (linear) Lowest module power (under 10 W at 1.6T), latency and cost; fewer active parts to fail The host SerDes must equalize the whole link, so every host-and-module pair needs qualification; margins shrink at 200G per lane; no DSP telemetry to separate a dirty connector from an aging laser or a weak host lane Single-vendor or tightly controlled clusters with links of 500 m or less, where power and latency dominate

Bottom line. LPO trades watts for operational risk. It pays off where one team controls the host, the module and the fiber plant, and it costs more than it saves where vendors are mixed, links are long, or troubleshooting speed is what keeps training jobs running. Compare system power, not module power: linear modules work only with host SerDes built to drive them.

Sources: OFC 2026 module status, LPO MSA interoperability and its diagnostic concerns; power figures as in the table above.

FRO and mix-and-match: linear at one end, retimed at the other

FRO (fully retimed optics) is the name now used for the conventional module with a DSP in both directions, set beside LRO and LPO. The two ends of a link are bought and qualified separately, so they need not match. A fabric can put linear optics where the watts pile up, on switch faceplates, and keep FRO at the accelerator, where plug-and-play and diagnostics matter most.

  • FRO. A DSP on transmit and on receive. The module meets the IEEE optical spec on its own, whatever host it sits in.
  • LRO, also called TRO (transmit-retimed). A DSP on transmit only. The light it sends stays standards-clean; the host SerDes recovers what arrives.
  • LPO. No DSP. The module is analog, and the host SerDes equalizes in both directions.

Judge each direction, not the link. Each direction is its own path from one host's transmitter to the other host's receiver, cut into shorter segments wherever a DSP sits. What decides the difficulty is how much of that path a single equalizer must cover.

A mixed LPO-to-FRO link uses the two in-between cells, one per direction; LPO at both ends uses the bottom-right cell twice.

The result: LPO facing FRO has no linear-to-linear direction. Its host receives clean light through one linear receiver, exactly the LRO case, and its own transmit signal is cleaned up by the far DSP rather than a far host SerDes. That makes it easier than LPO at both ends, but the linear transmit direction has no spec at any lane rate, and its margin depends on the switch SerDes and trace. That is why the LPO MSA calls LPO-to-retimed an engineered link outside its specs, with support on its roadmap and no date. At ECOC 2025, multi-vendor 800G links mixed linear and retimed optics, and OIF showed retimed, half-retimed and unretimed optics working together; neither names an LPO-to-FRO link.

Each direction's linear segment ends at one equalizer: the FRO's DSP going out, the switch SerDes coming back.

Every pairing at a glance. Pairings with no linear-to-linear direction need the least qualification. At 100G per lane, LPO at both ends is the only LPO pairing a spec covers, and an LPO end facing FRO or LRO is an engineered link. At 200G per lane, only FRO at both ends is fully specified so far.

The two cells pairing LPO with FRO are the only engineered links with no hard direction.

Linear at the switch, FRO on the accelerator. This mix suits AI back-ends, for four reasons:

  • The heat sits on the switch. A 64-port 1.6T switch carries about 1.5 kW of FRO optics on its faceplate, against about 0.8 kW with LRO or under 0.6 kW with LPO. An accelerator port carries one module beside an accelerator drawing around a kilowatt or more.
  • Accelerator SerDes stay on a standard channel. FRO keeps the accelerator or NIC SerDes on an ordinary host-to-module link, so no linear qualification for each accelerator, NIC or server generation. LPO needs "capable ASICs and well-designed transmission lines", in the LPO MSA's words.
  • Diagnostics stay at the expensive end. The FRO's DSP reports host-side and media-side SNR at the end where a flap stalls a training job, so the accelerator's host link is measured apart from the fiber path.
  • Switch-to-switch links can go fully linear. Where leaf and spine share one platform and links stay at 500 m or less, LPO at both ends is the case the LPO MSA covers at 100G per lane; at 200G per lane, use LRO at both ends.

Keeping FRO at the accelerator gives up one module's saving in four; with LRO on the switch ports as well, the mix keeps about half the all-linear saving (30 of 56 W).

The reverse mix, linear at the accelerator and FRO at the switch, fits when the accelerator vendor qualifies its own ports for linear and the switch side is mixed or has long traces. With switch-to-switch links linear either way, both mixes draw the same watts; linear at the switch wins on faceplate heat and on how few host types need qualifying.

At 200G per lane. Linear transmit is the hard half at 224G, because optical nonlinearity grows and host SerDes swing is limited, so a retimed transmitter is the usual fix (dense NPO, section 10). Expect LRO, not LPO, on switch ports facing FRO on accelerators. Transmit-only 3 nm DSPs with 802.3dj-compliant optical outputs are offered for 1.6T TRO and LRO modules. OIF launched CEI-224G-Linear and EEI-224G-RTLR projects in 2024, and no published agreement for either turned up as of October 2026; the LPO MSA lists 200G as a roadmap item.

Each end is its own decision, and the accelerator comes first because it has the most host types to qualify for linear.

In operations.

  • Qualify the trio. For LPO facing FRO, qualify switch port, LPO module and FRO module together, because the FRO's DSP must recover that host's linear transmit signal. Check each vendor's support list: at least one switch vendor's 800G LPO guidance requires LPO at both ends.
  • Read telemetry per direction. Going out, the FRO's media-side SNR measures the whole linear segment, switch SerDes to FRO front end, apart from the accelerator's host link. Coming back, the switch SerDes reports the FRO's signal as received. With LPO at both ends, each direction is measured only end to end.
  • Swap like for like. Replacing either end with another type turns a qualified pairing into a new one. The host must recognize the module type to load linear or retimed SerDes settings, so record each link's pairing, not just each port's optic.
  • Keep mixes to 500 m-class PMDs. FEC still runs end to end in the host (section 5). But 2 km-plus 200G PMDs add an inner FEC inside the module DSP, and a linear receiver has nothing to decode it with.

AI networks: pros and cons

Mix Pros in an AI fabric Cons in an AI fabric Best fit
FRO at both ends Plug-and-play against IEEE PMDs; full telemetry in both directions; any reach, including inner-FEC links Highest optics power and faceplate heat Mixed vendors, links over 500 m, fast fault isolation
Linear between switches only At 100G per lane, LPO at both ends is the case the LPO MSA covers; one platform at each end makes qualification a one-time job Access links to accelerators stay at full power One switch vendor, many server types
Linear at the switch, FRO on the accelerator About three-quarters of the all-linear saving; accelerator ends stay plug-and-play and observable An engineered link for each switch, LPO and FRO trio until specs cover it; not every switch supports LPO facing a retimed end; no 200G LPO spec yet AI back-ends with one switch platform and several accelerator generations
LRO at the switch, FRO on the accelerator IEEE-compliant transmit at both ends; the practical form at 1.6T today About half the all-linear saving; linear receive is specified only at 112G so far 200G-lane fabrics
Linear at every end Lowest power and latency Every host and module pair qualified, accelerators included; the least telemetry Systems sold and validated as one unit

Bottom line. Choose optics per end and judge them per direction. LPO facing FRO has no linear-to-linear direction, so it is easier than LPO at both ends, but its linear transmit direction has no spec and stays an engineered link. Linear switch ports with FRO accelerators keep three-quarters of the all-linear saving where LPO is specified, at 100G per lane (800G). At 1.6T the realistic mix today is LRO at the switch, which keeps about half.

Sources: FRO, LRO and LPO at the Ethernet Alliance, October 2026, FRO, LRO and LPO defined, LPO MSA FAQ on retimed far ends and host needs, LPO MSA 100G-per-lane specification, OIF 112G RTLR, and retimed, half-retimed and unretimed optics at ECOC 2025, mixed linear and retimed 800G links, ECOC 2025, OIF CEI-224G-Linear launch, 2024, OIF EEI-224G-RTLR launch, 2024, transmit-only DSP for TRO and LRO, LPO at both ends in one vendor's guidance, book-ended and engineered links, 802.3dj inner FEC applies to 2 km-plus PMDs. Module power uses the vendor-listed 1.6T ranges above.

Inside a coherent DSP

A coherent DSP does far more work, because it reconstructs the full optical field.

  1. Four ADCs digitize the in-phase and quadrature components of both polarizations.
  2. Chromatic dispersion compensation. A large static filter undoes the fiber's dispersion, which is why coherent links need no dispersion-compensating fiber.
  3. Polarization demultiplexing and PMD compensation. An adaptive 2 × 2 equalizer tracks the polarization state as it wanders and separates the two data streams.
  4. Carrier recovery. Removes the frequency offset and phase noise between the transmit laser and the receiver's local laser.
  5. Symbol decision and soft-decision FEC decoding.
  6. Transmit side. FEC encoding, constellation mapping, pulse shaping (which keeps the channel spectrally narrow so it fits its DWDM slot), and DACs driving the IQ modulator.

Coherent DSPs report the link's physics directly: estimated CD in ps/nm, differential group delay, OSNR or electrical SNR, frequency offset and pre-FEC BER. Those values make coherent links unusually easy to diagnose once you know where to look.

Power and process

DSP power falls with each CMOS node (7 nm, 5 nm, now 3 nm). Even so, a 1.6T DSP-based module lists at roughly 20–26 W (vendor figures). Multiplied across tens of thousands of ports in an AI cluster, that is megawatts, which is the economic force behind LPO, LRO and CPO.

Section 5 · Foundations

Forward error correction

5 diagrams · 12 min read
In this sectionHow Reed-Solomon FEC thinksThe insight that matters operationally: FEC is end to endReading FEC counters200G per lane: concatenated FECCoherent FECBER in depth: from SNR to lost framesAI networks: pros and cons

Every PAM4 Ethernet link is designed to run with errors: the optical PMD may deliver a raw bit error ratio of about 2.4 × 10⁻⁴, and RS(544,514) FEC corrects it to effectively error-free. Mastery means reading how far a link sits from that threshold, not whether it currently has errors.

How Reed-Solomon FEC thinks

  • The transmitter groups data into codewords of 10-bit symbols and appends parity symbols. The receiver can repair a limited number of bad symbols per codeword.
  • RS(528,514), "KR4". 14 parity symbols, corrects up to 7 symbols per codeword. Used with 25G NRZ lanes (100G SR4, CWDM4, CR4). The CWDM4 MSA, for example, requires a pre-FEC BER of 5 × 10⁻⁵ with this code (spec).
  • RS(544,514), "KP4". 30 parity symbols, corrects up to 15 symbols per codeword. Mandatory on every PAM4 Ethernet lane (50G, 100G, 200G). IEEE optical specs are written to a BER of 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ at the PMD (802.3bs analysis).
  • Symbols, not bits. One corrupted symbol costs the same whether 1 or 10 of its bits flipped, so RS codes handle short bursts well. Long bursts, such as those error-propagating DFEs can produce, are what break them, which is why codeword symbols are spread round-robin across PCS lanes and, from 802.3bs on, two codewords (four at 200G per lane in 802.3dj) are symbol-interleaved.
  • Latency. RS(544,514) processing adds on the order of 100 ns (802.3dj presentation), one reason AI scale-up fabrics care which FEC is used.

The insight that matters operationally: FEC is end to end

In a retimed IM-DD module the DSP does not decode the KP4 code. The near-end host encodes, the far-end host decodes, and every error made anywhere in between lands in the same codewords: the near host's electrical channel, the optical link, and the far host's electrical channel. The FEC-input budget, about 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ for random errors, is shared: 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ is the optical sub-link's allocation, and each electrical segment gets a small slice of about 10⁻⁵.

Two consequences:

  1. Rising corrected-codeword counts on a host port do not prove the optic is bad. A marginal host trace, connector or cage can consume the same budget.
  2. To find the guilty segment, compare the host's FEC counters with the module's own media-side telemetry (per-lane SNR and pre-FEC BER estimates via CMIS), and swap one element at a time.

Reading FEC counters

Counter What it means Healthy pattern
Corrected codewords Codewords that had errors and were repaired Non-zero and steady is normal for PAM4
Uncorrectable codewords Codewords with more than 15 bad symbols; frames are lost Zero. Any increment is a real problem
Symbol-error histogram (bins 0–15) How many codewords had N bad symbols Counts collapse to zero well before bin 15
Pre-FEC BER (derived) Raw error ratio before correction Orders of magnitude below 2.4 × 10⁻⁴

The histogram is the best single margin indicator. A healthy link shows codewords with 0, 1, perhaps 2–3 bad symbols. A tail creeping toward bins 10–15 means the link is close to dropping frames even while uncorrectable counts are still zero.

200G per lane: concatenated FEC

At 200G per lane, 2 km-plus optical links (DR-2, FR4, LR4) cannot meet a 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ raw BER economically. IEEE 802.3dj therefore adds an inner extended Hamming (128,120) code inside the module, decoded with soft information, beneath the end-to-end RS(544,514) outer code; a small padding overhead is why the lane lands at 113.4375 GBd rather than 113.33. The inner code tolerates a raw BER roughly an order of magnitude worse, at the cost of raising the optical lane from 106.25 to 113.4375 GBd. The 500 m PMDs (DR1, DR2, DR4, DR8 and 800GBASE-FR4-500) skip the inner code (802.3dj baseline).

The hosts bracket the outer code and the modules bracket the inner one, so most of the optical segment's errors are corrected before the host ever counts them.

This changes the troubleshooting model: on 2 km-plus 200G links, the module now terminates one FEC layer, so the optical segment's health is visible mainly through module telemetry, not host counters.

Coherent FEC

Coherent links use much stronger FEC, with soft-decision decoding and overheads around 15–21%, tolerating raw BERs around 10⁻². Unlike IM-DD, the coherent module terminates the host's FEC and applies its own across the fiber.

Code Where it is used Character
CFEC (concatenated FEC) OIF 400ZR Staircase outer + Hamming inner; lower power, shorter reach
oFEC (open FEC, from Open ROADM) OpenZR+, 800ZR Stronger, ~15% overhead; longer reach
KP4 + BCH concatenated 800LR Low latency (~55 ns) for campus links

Figures from OIF project presentations (800ZR/800LR).

BER in depth: from SNR to lost frames

BER is a probability set by the signal-to-noise ratio at the receiver's decision point. Three numbers make it operational. PAM4 needs about 9.5 dB more SNR than NRZ for the same BER. KP4 FEC turns a raw 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ into roughly one bad codeword in 10¹². And the margin between a healthy pre-FEC reading and that limit is smaller in dB than the decades suggest.

Four error ratios, four layers.

  • BER. Errored bits over bits sent; pre-FEC is the raw ratio, post-FEC what survives correction.
  • SER. Errored PAM4 symbols over symbols. Gray coding makes most symbol errors a single bit error, so PAM4 BER is about half its SER.
  • FEC symbol errors. RS(544,514) counts 10-bit symbols, so one to ten bit errors inside one symbol cost the same. The symbol-error histogram (above) counts these.
  • CER and FLR. Codewords the FEC could not correct, and frames lost as a result. IEEE 802.3bs set an objective of a BER of 10⁻¹³ or better at the MAC, "or the frame loss ratio equivalent"; one IEEE analysis equates that to an FLR of 6.2 × 10⁻¹¹.

Host-reported pre-FEC BER is derived from corrected symbols or bits, and platforms differ in which they count, so compare trends on one platform rather than absolute values across platforms.

BER vs SNR: why PAM4 needs FEC. With Gaussian noise, BER falls with the eye opening divided by the noise. PAM4's three eyes are each a third the height of NRZ's one eye at the same swing, which costs 20·log₁₀3 ≈ 9.5 dB of SNR.

Without FEC, PAM4 needs 26.4 dB to reach 10⁻¹²; with KP4 it needs only 2.4 × 10⁻⁴, at 20.2 dB. Those 6.2 dB are KP4's coding gain, not a smaller modulation penalty: PAM4 with KP4 still needs about 3.3 dB more than uncoded NRZ, and NRZ with KP4 would need only 10.9 dB.

The FEC cliff. RS(544,514) repairs up to 15 bad symbols per codeword. With random errors, the chance of 16 or more falls so steeply that post-FEC performance has a cliff, not a slope. One IEEE analysis found that random errors need a FEC-input BER below about 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ for an FLR of 6.2 × 10⁻¹¹, the 10⁻¹³ equivalent. 802.3bs gave the optical PMD 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ of that budget and left the rest to the electrical interfaces, so 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ is the optics' share, not the point where the FEC breaks. On 200G-per-lane PMDs that add the inner FEC (200GBASE-DR1-2, the DR2-2, DR4-2 and DR8-2 variants, 800GBASE-FR4 and 800GBASE-LR4), the 802.3dj draft sets the PMD limit at 2 × 10⁻³ instead, so judge their media-side BER against that.

At 10⁻⁴ KP4 leaves about one bad codeword in 10¹⁸; at 10⁻³ it is one in about 6,500, so a link a few times past the limit drops frames continuously.

Pre-FEC BER as margin in dB. Because the BER curve is so steep near the limit, decades of BER are worth little SNR. The table converts readings into margin, computed for Gray-coded PAM4 with Gaussian noise.

Pre-FEC BER Decades below 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ Electrical SNR margin Optical margin, thermal-noise-limited
1 × 10⁻⁴ 0.4 0.6 dB 0.3 dB
1 × 10⁻⁵ 1.4 1.8 dB 0.9 dB
1 × 10⁻⁶ 2.4 2.8 dB 1.4 dB
1 × 10⁻⁸ 4.4 4.2 dB 2.1 dB
1 × 10⁻¹⁰ 6.4 5.3 dB 2.7 dB
1 × 10⁻¹² 8.4 6.2 dB 3.1 dB

A link reading 10⁻⁶ looks two and a half decades clean, yet it is only about 1.4 dB of optical power from the limit, roughly one dirty connector. The optical column assumes a thermal-noise-limited receiver, where 1 dB of optical power is 2 dB of electrical SNR. Reflections (MPI) and laser noise (RIN) flatten the curve into an error floor, so extra power buys even less. This is why section 14 budgets in dB and section 24 trends pre-FEC BER: they are one margin on two scales.

Bathtub curves: BER across the eye. Sweep the sampling point across the eye and BER traces a bathtub: steep walls at the crossings and a floor in the middle. Random jitter is unbounded, so the eye narrows as the target BER falls. In the dual-Dirac model, total jitter is the deterministic part plus the random jitter's spread at the target BER, about 14 times its standard deviation at 10⁻¹². Instruments measure the walls down to a practical depth and extrapolate the rest. For PAM4, each of the three eyes has its own bathtub; the BER is the sum over all three, so the worst eye dominates. Links with KP4 run near 10⁻⁴, not 10⁻¹², which is why 802.3 specifies PAM4 transmitter jitter at about that depth (J4u) and as an rms value (JRMS) rather than as total jitter at 10⁻¹².

The walls are the jitter's tails: random jitter keeps eating into the eye as the target BER falls, so an eye that looks open on a scope is narrower at 10⁻¹², the depth NRZ links were judged at.

Burst errors: when the random assumption breaks. The cliff above assumes independent errors. A decision-feedback equalizer (DFE) subtracts the echo of past symbols, so one wrong decision can push the next ones wrong too, a burst. Ethernet has three defenses.

  • 10-bit FEC symbols absorb short bursts. A burst of up to 10 bits that sits inside one symbol costs one symbol of the 15.
  • Codeword interleaving. 200GBASE-R and 400GBASE-R (802.3bs) symbol-interleave two codewords, so a long burst splits between them. 50GBASE-R and Clause 91 100G PHYs do not; 802.3ck kept Clause 91 as the default for 100G-per-lane backplane and copper links and added an interleaved FEC (Clause 161) that either end can request. In one IEEE analysis with a 0.75 chance of error propagation and an FLR target of 6.2 × 10⁻¹⁰, interleaving tolerated a FEC-input BER of 2.3 × 10⁻⁴, against 5.9 × 10⁻⁵ without it.
  • Precoding and DFE limits. With 1/(1+D) precoding, a typical DFE burst decodes to two errored symbols, but each random error also becomes two; the same analysis found it cut the slicer-output limit for random errors from 3.8 × 10⁻⁴ to 1.7 × 10⁻⁴ (3.3 × 10⁻⁴ at the FEC input), at an FLR of 6.2 × 10⁻¹⁰. 802.3ck's channel-compliance model also caps its reference receiver's first DFE tap at 0.85, which bounds bursts in the model, not in real SerDes.

A burst is dangerous because it lands on top of the random errors already in the same codeword; interleaving and precoding both keep any one codeword's share small.

A symbol-error histogram whose high bins are heavier than a random spread predicts points to bursts: an equalizer with error propagation, in the host SerDes or the module DSP, or short transient events, rather than Gaussian noise.

How long a BER test must run. To claim a BER at confidence CL with no errors seen, a test needs −ln(1 − CL)/BER bits: 3.0/BER at 95% and 4.6/BER at 99%. Allowing 1, 2 or 3 errors raises the 95% factor to 4.7, 6.3 or 7.8.

Target BER Bits, 95% confidence, zero errors Time on a 106.25 Gb/s lane Time on a 212.5 Gb/s lane
2.4 × 10⁻⁴ (KP4 PMD limit) 1.3 × 10⁴ 0.1 µs 0.06 µs
10⁻⁸ 3.0 × 10⁸ 2.8 ms 1.4 ms
10⁻¹² 3.0 × 10¹² 28 s 14 s
10⁻¹³ (MAC objective) 3.0 × 10¹³ 4.7 min 2.4 min
10⁻¹⁵ 3.0 × 10¹⁵ 7.8 h 3.9 h

Pre-FEC BER can be proved in milliseconds. The 10⁻¹³ post-FEC objective takes minutes per lane to bound, and a healthy link's true post-FEC BER is far lower still, so it is bounded or inferred from the cliff, never measured.

Where to read BER.

  • Host FEC counters: corrected and uncorrectable codewords, the symbol-error histogram and derived pre-FEC BER (above).
  • Module telemetry: CMIS VDM pre-FEC BER and SNR, host side and media side (section 12).
  • Out of service: a BERT with PRBS31Q or SSPRQ patterns, lane by lane (section 22).
  • Coherent: pre-FEC BER near 10⁻² and Q margin (sections 18 and 26).
  • Streaming: OpenConfig pre-FEC BER paths for module and port (section 24).

In operations.

  • Alarm in dB, not decades. Use the margin table to set thresholds: two decades below the limit is less than 1.5 dB of optical margin.
  • Treat any uncorrectable codeword as real. On the cliff, one bad codeword means the link is at the edge or bursting.
  • Read the histogram's shape. A binomial spread is noise (optics, fiber, connectors); a heavy tail with a clean average is bursts (an equalizer with error propagation, host or module, or transients).
  • Compare both directions and both ends. FEC is end to end, so the host, the module and the far end all share the budget.
  • Size tests to the claim. A few seconds of PRBS proves the pre-FEC BER, never a post-FEC one.

Bottom line. BER is SNR in disguise. Read pre-FEC BER as dB of margin, expect a cliff past 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ rather than a slope, and remember that a link several decades below the limit can still be one dirty connector away from it.

Sources: 802.3bs BER objective, RS(544,514) limits, FLR equivalence and bursts, RS(544,514) with precoding and interleaving, 802.3dj PMD BER baseline with the inner FEC, 802.3ck Clause 91 and interleaved FEC options, DFE tap limits in the 100G-per-lane reference receiver, precoding and error propagation, BER confidence levels, dual-Dirac and bathtub curves. SNR margins, codeword error ratios and test times are computed here, assuming Gaussian noise and random errors.

AI networks: pros and cons

In AI fabrics FEC shows up as latency and power. 100 ns of FEC equals about 20 m of fiber, and inside a hall propagation delay is small, so the code can be the largest latency term on the link (section 20).

Option Pros in an AI fabric Cons in an AI fabric Best fit
End-to-end KP4 only (500 m DR) Standard 106.25 GBd lanes; no extra FEC power or latency in the module Needs a raw BER of 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ or better, which caps 200G-per-lane links near 500 m Leaf-to-spine inside one hall
KP4 plus inner Hamming (802.3dj, 2 km and longer) Tolerates roughly ten times worse raw BER, so 2 km DR-2 and FR4 links close at 200G per lane 6.8% higher line rate (113.4375 GBd), more DSP power, and about 15 ns for the inner code plus 26–280 ns for its convolutional interleaver, depending on MAC rate (1.6T lowest, 200G highest), unless the interleaver is bypassed Spine to super-spine across a campus
Same KP4, less interleaving (scale-up) UALink keeps RS(544,514) but allows 1-way or 2-way codeword interleaving to cut FEC latency, and adds link-level replay; UEC avoids inner-FEC PHYs and adds link-level retry Needs very short, clean links, with little margin for dirty connectors or aging lasers Inside a scale-up pod, on copper or co-packaged optics

Bottom line. Buy reach with inner FEC only on the links that need it; inside a hall, 500 m optics without it save power and latency on every port.

Section 6 · Products

Grey (IM-DD) optics

7 diagrams · 18 min read
In this sectionThe naming decoderThe PMD reference tableThree architectures, one choiceWavelength plans: CWDM4, LAN-WDM and why cooling decidesBreakout: the lane-matching ruleSame connector, no link: classic interop trapsConnectors and polarityAI networks: pros and consCisco optics by speed: 100G to 1.6T

A PMD name tells you almost everything: 400GBASE-DR4 means 400 Gb/s Ethernet, DR reach class (500 m single-mode), 4 optical lanes. "Grey" means a fixed, non-tunable wavelength that does not need a DWDM line system; IM-DD (intensity modulation, direct detection) is the technique behind it.

The naming decoder

Code Medium Typical reach
CR Twinax copper (DAC) A few meters at 25–100G per lane, about 1 m at 200G
KR Backplane copper Board and backplane traces
VR Multimode 30–50 m
SR Multimode 60–150 m depending on fiber grade
DR Single-mode 500 m
DR-2, FR Single-mode 2 km
LR Single-mode 10 km (LR4-6 = 6 km)
ER Single-mode 30–40 km
ZR Single-mode, coherent DWDM at 400G and up 80 km and beyond
  • The digit after the code is the number of optical lanes: wavelengths for FR/LR, fiber pairs for SR/DR.
  • ".2" means two wavelengths per fiber (400GBASE-SR4.2 runs bidirectionally on 8 fibers).
  • "-6", "-10", "-2", "-20" mark a reach variant in km (LR4-6, DR4-2).
  • IEEE vs MSA vs product names. IEEE names read "400GBASE-FR4". MSA names drop "BASE" (100G-CWDM4, 100G-PSM4, 100G-LR1-20). Product names such as "2×FR4" or "DR4+" are not standards; they describe two engines in one module, or a reach-extended variant.

Figures marked ~ are pre-publication baselines. The 200G-per-lane PMDs are from IEEE 802.3dj, in final ballot as of October 2026.

Three architectures, one choice

  • Parallel (SR4, DR4, DR8). One wavelength, one fiber per lane per direction. The simplest optics, the most fibers, and the natural choice for breaking out to lower-speed ports.
  • WDM duplex (CWDM4, FR4, LR4). Several wavelengths multiplexed onto one fiber pair. Fewer fibers and reach to 10 km, but a mux and demux inside the module and no breakout.
  • BiDi. Two wavelengths travel in opposite directions on each fiber. Its main purpose is reusing an existing duplex multimode plant at a higher speed.

Fiber count, not reach, is often the deciding factor: parallel optics are simplest but need four times the fibers of a WDM duplex link.

Wavelength plans: CWDM4, LAN-WDM and why cooling decides

Every WDM-duplex grey optic sits on one of two O-band plans, and the choice is about temperature as much as dispersion.

Plan Lane centers (nm) Spacing Allowed drift Laser Used by
CWDM4 1271, 1291, 1311, 1331 20 nm ±6.5 nm, a 13 nm box Uncooled DFB or EML 100G CWDM4, 400GBASE-FR4 and LR4-6, 800G 2×FR4 and 800GBASE-FR4
LAN-WDM 1295.56, 1300.05, 1304.58, 1309.14 about 4.5 nm (800 GHz) about ±1 nm TEC-cooled DFB or EML 100GBASE-LR4 and ER4, 200GBASE-LR4 and ER4, 400GBASE-LR8 and ER8 (an eight-lane grid reaching down to 1273.54 nm), 800GBASE-LR4
Parallel (DR) 1311 on every fiber none ±6.5 nm Uncooled; in silicon photonics one laser can feed several lanes DR1, DR4, DR8

The arithmetic of drift. A DFB's wavelength moves about 0.1 nm per °C, so an uncooled laser wanders 7 nm over a 0–70 °C case range. That fits inside a 13 nm CWDM box but not inside a 2 nm LAN-WDM box, which is why every LAN-WDM optic carries a thermoelectric cooler (TEC) holding its lasers near a fixed temperature, at a cost of roughly 0.5–1 W and a control loop. The TEC is also why LAN-WDM optics tolerate hot chassis less gracefully: when the cooler saturates, the wavelength walks toward the edge of the mux passband and power drops before any temperature alarm fires.

The arithmetic of dispersion. CWDM's outer lanes at 1271 and 1331 nm sit 20–40 nm from λ₀ (up to 53 nm at the lane edge against the worst-case λ₀) and see about −4 and +2 ps/(nm·km); the four-lane LAN-WDM grid sits within 15 nm of 1310 nm and sees at most about 3 ps/(nm·km) even at the λ₀ = 1324 nm corner (IEEE budgets −28 ps/nm over 10 km for its lowest lane). At 100G per lane IEEE held CWDM4 to 6 km (400GBASE-LR4-6) and reached 10 km only with the single-wavelength 100GBASE-LR1; at 200G per lane, where the symbol is 8.8 ps (113.4375 GBd with the inner FEC) and the signal about 0.65 nm wide, 800GBASE-LR4 adopted the four-lane LAN-WDM grid with a 3.9 dB TDECQ limit, while 800GBASE-FR4 stayed on CWDM for 2 km.

Inside the module. A WDM optic adds a multiplexer on the transmit side and a demultiplexer on the receive side, usually thin-film filters or an arrayed-waveguide grating, each costing on the order of 1–2 dB per pass that the transmitter's power budget absorbs; the receive demux must also be wide enough to pass a lane that has drifted to the edge of its box. An optical isolator in front of each laser keeps reflections from connectors out of the cavity, where they would raise RIN; reflections are also why single-mode PAM4 optics specify APC connectors and limit discrete reflectance in the plant.

Operations. A LAN-WDM optic reports laser temperature and, through VDM, TEC current; a TEC current climbing toward its limit on a hot day is the earliest warning of a wavelength walk. CWDM optics report temperature only, and their failure mode at the hot corner is power or TDECQ, not wavelength.

Sources: 10 km PMD lane plans, 800GBASE-LR4 baseline, 802.3cu dispersion by lane.

Breakout: the lane-matching rule

A high-speed port can split into several lower-speed ports only when each optical lane on one end matches a whole port on the other, in rate and in modulation.

Port optic Can break out to Cannot break out to
400G DR4 (4 × 100G PAM4) 4 × 100G-DR or 100G-FR1 100G-PSM4 or CWDM4 (4 × 25G NRZ inside)
800G DR8 (8 × 100G PAM4) 8 × 100G-DR, or 2 × 400G-DR4 Anything with 25G or 50G lanes
800G 2×FR4 2 × 400G-FR4 100G ports (lanes are wavelength-multiplexed)
1.6T DR8 (8 × 200G PAM4) 8 × 200G-DR1, or 2 × 800G-DR4 100G-lane optics

Breakout needs three things to agree: the host's port-split configuration, the module's selected application (section 12), and a fiber path that maps each transmit lane to the right far-end receiver.

Each far-end module receives one DR4 lane unchanged; the breakout is purely a fiber re-mapping, plus a port-split setting on the host.

Same connector, no link: classic interop traps

  • 100G on duplex single-mode comes in at least three incompatible flavors. LR4 (LAN-WDM, 4 × 25G NRZ), CWDM4 (CWDM, 4 × 25G NRZ) and FR1/LR1 (one 100G PAM4 wavelength) all use duplex LC and none talk to each other.
  • APC vs UPC. Single-mode parallel optics use angled (APC) MPO ferrules to suppress reflections, which PAM4 is sensitive to. Mating APC to flat UPC causes high loss and can damage end faces.
  • MPO-12 vs MPO-16. Different key offsets: they do not mate by design.
  • Multimode patch on single-mode optics, or the reverse. Light passes, links may even come up briefly, then errors climb. Check the jacket color and the label, not just the connector.

Connectors and polarity

  • LC duplex. The default for duplex optics.
  • MPO-12 / MPO-16. Multi-fiber push-on connectors for parallel optics; a 4-lane module uses 8 of the 12 fibers.
  • Very-small-form-factor (VSFF) connectors (SN, MDC, CS). Fit two to four duplex connections in one module face, enabling breakout without fanout cables.
  • Polarity. Every transmit fiber must land on a receive position at the far end. Parallel optics usually expect a key-up-to-key-up trunk that flips fiber order (commonly called Type B or Method B). Wrong polarity means lanes see darkness, not low power.

AI networks: pros and cons

Two choices decide most of an AI cluster's grey optics bill: multimode or single-mode, and parallel fibers or wavelengths.

Option Pros in an AI fabric Cons in an AI fabric Best fit
Multimode SR (VCSEL) Lowest cost and power per port; relaxed alignment and simple installation; 800G eSR8 showed multi-vendor interoperability in June 2026, and 1.6T SR8 modules have been demonstrated over 30 m of OM4; IEEE P802.3ds targets 30 m and 50 m at 200G per lane Reach shrinks with each lane-rate step (about 100 m at 100G per lane, about 30 m at 1.6T); the multimode plant may not carry to the next generation NIC-to-leaf links within a row, and active optical cables
Single-mode DR, FR, LR 500 m to 10 km on one fiber type that carries across generations; DR breaks out to lower-speed ports; almost all 1.6T optics shipping in 2026 are DR-type More power and cost per port than SR; tighter connector cleanliness Leaf-to-spine and anything leaving the row
Parallel (DR4, DR8) One wavelength and simple optics; breakout to 4 or 8 lower-speed ports; lowest cost at 500 m or less 4 to 8 fiber pairs per port, MPO trunks, polarity management and more end faces to keep clean Leaf-to-spine in one hall with plenty of fiber
Wavelength-multiplexed (FR4, 2×FR4) One or two fiber pairs per port; 2 km reach; duplex patching Mux and demux loss and four wavelength-specific lasers per group raise power and cost; no lane-level breakout Across buildings, or where fiber and duct space are scarce

Bottom line. Inside one hall, parallel single-mode (DR4 or DR8) is the AI default because breakout and cost win. WDM earns its premium only where fiber is scarce or links leave the building, and multimode survives where links stay inside a row.

Sources: multimode status, July 2026, 1.6T shipments by type.

Cisco optics by speed: 100G to 1.6T

This is the guide's one vendor-specific section: Cisco's pluggable optics as its data sheets list them in October 2026, by speed and reach. Data sheets describe the optic, not the host, so confirm each PID and minimum software release for a platform in Cisco's Transceiver Module Group (TMG) compatibility matrix.

Reading a Cisco PID. A grey PID reads form factor, then speed, then PMD, then a suffix. Coherent PIDs follow a separate scheme that starts with DP.

Grey PIDs read left to right in that order; coherent PIDs pack the speed and form factor into their first eight characters.

The map. Cisco covers every reach class at 100G and 400G. At 800G the data-sheet set is VR8, DR8 and 2 km parts, with LPO, 10 km and NIC-style variants named for later in 2026. At 1.6T, only the platform and the optic family are announced so far.

Solid cells ship on a Cisco data sheet today; dashed cells are named for later in 2026; the 1.6T cell is a family without published PIDs.

What is inside each variant. The host lanes, the DSP and the fibers decide what a variant can break out to and what it can face at the far end.

Parallel parts use one fiber pair per optical lane, so DR8 and VR8 need 16 fibers; WDM parts fold four lanes onto one pair.

No Cisco 1.6T coherent pluggable was announced as of October 2026.

Breakout with Cisco PIDs. A breakout works when each far-end module receives exactly one lane group of the near module (the lane-matching rule above).

Breakout reach is the shorter of the two ends: a DR4 lane feeding an FR-S still stops at 500 m.

Where they plug in, Nexus 9000.

Platform Ports Optics
Nexus 9300-GX (N9316D-GX, N93600CD-GX) 16 × 400G QSFP-DD; or 8 × QSFP-DD plus 28 × QSFP28 400G QSFP-DD and 100G QSFP28
Nexus 9300-GX2 (9364D-GX2A, 9348D-GX2A, 9332D-GX2B) 32 to 64 × 400G QSFP-DD 400G; 4 × 100G and 2 × 200G breakout
Nexus 9500 (N9K-X9716D-GX) and 9400 (N9K-X9400-8D) 16 or 8 × 400G QSFP-DD per card 400G; 4 × 100G breakout on the X9716D-GX; 9400 breakout not stated
N9364E-SG2-O, N9364E-SG2-Q (Silicon One G200) 64 × 800G OSFP, or 64 × 800G QSFP-DD800 800G; 2 × 400G and 8 × 100G breakout

In operations.

  • Check host support per PID, not per speed. The platform data sheets name no optics; the TMG compatibility matrix gives the supported PIDs and minimum release per platform.
  • Dual MPO-12 or one MPO-16. The OSFP VR8 and DR8 come both ways, with the same optics inside; QDD-800G-VR8 is dual MPO-12 only. Pick the version that matches the trunk plant.
  • APC or UPC. APC MPO: the 800G parallel parts, the 400G SR8, VR4, DR4 and 4X100G-FR/LR, and QSFP-100G-PSM4-S. UPC: every other 100G part, including the SR4-S and SL4 MPOs, plus QDD-400G-SR4.2-BD, QDD-2X100-SR4-S (MPO-24) and all LC and CS parts. A mismatch is the classic trap described above.
  • Breakout is a host setting too. The NX-OS breakout map must match the module's selected application (section 12) and the fiber mapping.
  • Read the data sheets critically. The current 400G and 800G sheets label some VR parts as SR or DR in their ordering tables. Trust the PMD and connector columns, and confirm in the compatibility matrix.
  • -S suffix. No Cisco sheet defines it. The 40G sheet calls these parts S-Class and lists per-part limits, such as Ethernet rate only and no FCoE; newer PIDs drop the suffix.

Bottom line. For AI back-ends on Nexus today, the core set is 800G OSFP DR8, with VR8 inside a row and breakout to 400G DR4 or 100G DR. OSFP-2X400G-FR4 or QDD-8X100G-FR covers 2 km, and 800G LPO and 1.6T OSFP arrive on the SG2X and G300 platforms as their PIDs publish.

Sources: Cisco data sheets for 100G QSFP28, 400G QSFP-DD, 400G QSFP112, 800G OSFP, 800G QSFP-DD800, 400G ZR and ZR+, low-power 400G ZR and ZR+, 400G high-power, its reach, 400G ER1, 400G CFP2 BiDi, 800G ZR and ZR+, 100ZR, 40G, for the -S suffix; end-of-sale notices for QDD-400G-LR8-S, QDD-2X100-SR4-S and QDD-2X100-CWDM4-S; Cisco Live 2026 optics session; G300 and 1.6T OSFP announcement; N9364F-SG3 and 800G LPO; platform data sheets for N9364E-SG2, N9364E-SG2X, 9300-GX, 9300-GX2, 9500 and 9400.

A form factor fixes the electrical lane count, the mechanics and the power and thermal envelope, not the optics inside. The same QSFP112 cage can hold a 100 m SR4, a 2 km FR4, a copper DAC or a coherent module. Read every form-factor name as "lanes × lane rate".

Power and thermal

Figures above 400G are vendor-listed (1.6T, 800G LPO, 400ZR datasheet); the 100G and 400G grey rows are approximate.

  • Power classes. Each MSA defines classes. The module advertises its power class and maximum power in its CMIS memory map (Page 00h bytes 200–201); the host compares that with what the port can supply and cool, and keeps the module in low-power mode if it cannot support it.
  • Ports are not equal. High-power coherent or 1.6T modules may be supported only in ports with better airflow. Temperature alarms on one port but not its neighbor often point to airflow, not the module.

Compatibility rules of thumb

  • A larger cage usually accepts the smaller module of the same family (QSFP28 in QSFP-DD, SFP28 in SFP56), running at the smaller module's speed if the host supports it.
  • The reverse never works mechanically.
  • Adapters exist (QSFP-to-SFP for 10G/25G in a QSFP port; OSFP-to-QSFP), but they add a host-support question.
  • "400G QSFP-DD" alone does not tell you the host lane rate: 8 × 50G and 4 × 100G hosts both exist, and some modules only support one.
Section 8 · Products

Coherent optics and DCI

2 diagrams · 6 min read
In this sectionWhy coherent, in one tableAnatomy of a coherent pluggableThe standards and MSA landscapeDWDM in five ideasIP over DWDMGrey vs coherent: the decisionAI networks: pros and cons

Coherent optics mix the incoming light with a local laser, which lets a DSP recover amplitude, phase and polarization. That one trick unlocks three things IM-DD cannot do: undo dispersion electronically, pack 8 or more bits into each symbol, and tune to any DWDM channel, so a single wavelength carries 400G–1.6T over tens to hundreds of kilometers.

Why coherent, in one table

Grey IM-DD Coherent
What the receiver sees Optical power only Full field: I, Q, two polarizations
Bits per symbol 1–2 per lane 4–8+ per wavelength
Dispersion handling Avoid it (stay near 1310 nm, short reach) Compensate it in the DSP
Wavelength Fixed, O-band Tunable across the C-band, and the L-band for some 800G ZR+ parts (DWDM)
Amplification Not used EDFAs extend reach
Cost and power per module Lower Higher, falling fast
Sweet spot Inside the building and campus, ≤ 10 km DCI and metro, 40 km and beyond

Anatomy of a coherent pluggable

  • Transmit. A narrow-linewidth tunable laser feeds a dual-polarization IQ modulator: nested Mach-Zehnder modulators driven by the DSP's DACs, one pair for each polarization.
  • Receive. The incoming light and a local-oscillator laser enter a polarization-diverse 90° optical hybrid. Balanced photodiodes and TIAs produce four electrical signals (XI, XQ, YI, YQ), which four ADCs hand to the DSP (section 4).
