  • DCO vs ACO. A digital coherent optic carries its DSP inside the module and presents a plain Ethernet electrical interface. An analog coherent optic leaves the DSP on the host card. Pluggable DCOs now dominate.

Light stays light until the photodiodes; from there on, everything that makes coherent work happens in the receive DSP.

The standards and MSA landscape

Spec Rate and format Reach and line system FEC Status
OIF 400ZR 400G, DP-16QAM, ~60 GBd 80–120 km amplified on a 75 or 100 GHz grid; unamplified single-wavelength mode (~11 dB budget) CFEC First release 2020; v2.0 Nov 2022
OpenZR+ MSA 100/200/300/400G, QPSK to 16QAM Metro and regional; v3.0 adds high-power (0 dBm) modes for ROADM networks oFEC v3.0 Sep 2023
OIF 800ZR 800G, DP-16QAM, ~118 GBd 80–120 km amplified, single span; 150 GHz channels oFEC (~15%) Published Nov 2024
OIF 800LR 800G, DP-16QAM, ~124 GBd Up to 10 km, unamplified, fixed wavelength KP4 + BCH (~21%), low latency Published Apr 2025
IEEE 802.3dj coherent PMDs 800G, single wavelength 10 km (LR1), 20 km (ER1-20), 40 km (ER1) — In final ballot, Oct 2026
OIF 1600ZR 1.6T, 16QAM, ~235 GBd (project-stage figure) Up to 120 km amplified oFEC Published Sep 2026

Sources: 400ZR IA, OpenZR+ documents, 800ZR release, 800LR release, 800ZR/LR parameters, 802.3dj objectives, 1600ZR release, 1600ZR project report. IEEE's own 400GBASE-ZR project (802.3cw) was withdrawn in 2024 (project page), so the OIF 400ZR agreement is the interoperability reference at 400G.

  • "ZR" vs "ZR+". ZR means a low-power, standardized, point-to-point DCI profile with low launch power (about −10 dBm for 400ZR). "ZR+" means more reach: stronger FEC, multi-rate operation, and in high-power variants about 0 dBm launch power to survive ROADMs and amplifier cascades (OIF OFC 2024 demo slides).
  • Coherent-lite. Simplified, lower-power coherent for 2–20 km campus links, sometimes in the O-band. Its future depends on how far PAM4 can stretch: an analyst view from July 2026 is that 800LR saw little deployment once 200G-per-lane PAM4 matured (Cignal AI).

DWDM in five ideas

  1. The grid. ITU-T G.694.1 defines channel center frequencies. Fixed grids use 12.5, 25, 50 or 100 GHz spacing; flexible grids place channel centers on a 6.25 GHz grid and allocate slot widths in 12.5 GHz multiples.
  2. Channel width follows baud. A ~60 GBd 400ZR signal fits a 75 GHz slot; a ~118 GBd 800ZR needs about 150 GHz. Doubling the rate per wavelength does not double fiber capacity.
  3. Fiber capacity. The C-band holds about 64 × 75 GHz channels, so 64 × 400ZR is roughly 25.6 Tb/s per fiber pair (demo report).
  4. The line system. Passive mux/demux combine channels; EDFAs amplify all of them at once; ROADMs use wavelength-selective switches to add, drop or route individual channels without converting them to electrical.
  5. OSNR is the coherent budget. Optical signal-to-noise ratio is signal power against amplifier noise (ASE). Every amplifier adds noise, so doubling the number of identical spans costs about 3 dB of OSNR. Denser formats need more OSNR, which is why reach falls as rate per wavelength rises.

A ROADM lets individual wavelengths leave or join without converting the rest to electrical; its filters add a small penalty each time a channel passes through.

IP over DWDM

Putting coherent pluggables directly in routers and switches removes the separate transponder shelf: the router port is the DWDM transmitter. It saves power, space and cost, and it moves wavelength management into the IP team's world, which is an operational decision as much as a technical one.

Grey vs coherent: the decision

Distance Fiber situation Usual answer
≤ 2 km Plenty of fiber Grey: DR or FR
2–10 km Plenty of fiber Grey LR; coherent-lite where PAM4 runs out
10–40 km Few fibers or leased Grey ER struggles at 100G+ per lane; coherent increasingly wins
40–120 km DCI, amplified 400ZR / 800ZR / 1600ZR
> 120 km or ROADM network Shared line system High-power ZR+ / OpenZR+, or embedded transponders

Fiber scarcity tips the decision earlier: if a fiber pair is expensive, DWDM multiplies what each pair carries, and that favors coherent even at short distances. Beyond about 120 km, reach is set by amplifier noise, fiber nonlinearity and the margins operators hold back; section 26 explains each.

AI networks: pros and cons

AI training increasingly spans buildings and sites, which brings two coherent decisions into the fabric: how to run 2–10 km campus links, and how to connect sites.

Option Pros in an AI fabric Cons in an AI fabric Best fit
200G-per-lane PAM4 (DR-2, FR4, LR4) Lowest power and cost per bit up to 10 km; the same DSP family, management and spares as the optics inside the hall Reach stops near 10 km with shrinking margin; dispersion and reflections limit it; no wavelength multiplication of the fiber Campus links on owned fiber
Coherent-lite (800LR class) Large margin and tolerance of fiber impairments; a path to more capacity per fiber More power and cost than PAM4 at the same rate; little deployment once 200G PAM4 matured (analyst view, July 2026) Where PAM4 runs out of margin or fiber pairs run out
ZR and ZR+ pluggables in routers and switches No transponder shelf, so less power, space and cost; multi-vendor (400ZR, 800ZR, OpenZR+, with 1600ZR specified in September 2026); high-power ZR+ crosses ROADM networks Less reach and capacity per wavelength than embedded transponders; 20 W-plus ports need the right cages and airflow; optical operations move to the IP team Metro links between AI sites, up to about 1,000 km with 800G ZR+ in field trials
Embedded transponders Highest rate and reach per wavelength: up to 1.6T at about 200 GBd, and 800G beyond 1,500 km in field trials Separate shelves with more power and space; vendor-specific line systems and management Regional, long-haul and subsea links between AI regions (section 26)

Bottom line. Keep PAM4 as far as it reaches inside the campus, use ZR and ZR+ pluggables for metro distances between AI sites, and save embedded transponders for regional and long-haul spans where reach and spectral efficiency decide the cost.

Section 9 · Products

AI fabric and next-gen optics

9 diagrams · 19 min read
In this sectionThe trade-offs at a glanceThree networks, three media200G per lane: the current generationCopper's shrinking reachAI networks: pros and consCable technologies: from passive copper to slow-and-wide lightCo-packaged and near-packaged opticsThe 400G-per-lane horizonReliability is now a network metricAlso on the horizon

AI clusters turned optics into a first-order cost, power and reliability problem: a non-blocking fabric needs several transceivers for every GPU-facing port, and a single flapping link can stall a training job across thousands of GPUs. The industry's four answers are faster lanes (200G now, 400G next), fewer DSPs (LPO, LRO), shorter electrical paths (CPO), and copper wherever it still reaches.

The trade-offs at a glance

Every tier of an AI cluster faces its own optics trade-off, and the sections that cover each one close with an “AI networks: pros and cons” callout.

Read from the GPU outward: close to the GPU, latency and power dominate; farther out, reach, fiber count and interoperability decide.

Three networks, three media

Network What it connects Typical reach Dominant media
Scale-up GPUs inside a rack or pod, with memory-semantic links ~1–2 m today Copper: backplanes, cable cartridges, DAC; optics is the next frontier for multi-rack pods
Scale-out (back-end) GPU NICs to leaf to spine, RDMA traffic 2 m to 2 km AEC or DAC in the rack; DR4/DR8/2×FR4 optics at 400G–1.6T beyond it
Front-end Storage, management, users Data-center scale Conventional data-center optics

Why the optics count explodes. Every link has a transceiver at each end. A non-blocking three-tier fabric has three link layers per GPU-facing port (host to leaf, leaf to spine, spine to super-spine), so each port implies about six transceivers if every layer is optical, or four if the host-to-leaf hop is copper.

When the NIC-to-leaf hop fits on copper, the optics count per port drops from six to four, which is why in-rack leaf placement and AEC reach matter so much to cluster cost.

200G per lane: the current generation

  • Standards. IEEE 802.3dj (200G-per-lane electrical and optical, 800GbE and 1.6TbE) is in its final ballot recirculation as of October 2026, with submission targeted for later that month and approval at the December 2026 RevCom meeting (agenda). Its PMD family spans 200G to 1.6T: DR (500 m), DR-2 (2 km), FR4 (2 km), LR4 (10 km), coherent LR1/ER1, plus CR copper and KR backplane.
  • Modules. 1.6T OSFP modules (DR8 and 2×FR4 on 200G lanes; see section 11) entered volume shipment in 2026, with analysts expecting a steep ramp alongside continued 800G growth (LightCounting).
  • Silicon. 102.4 Tb/s switches (512 × 200G) in production make 64 × 1.6T or 128 × 800G ports per switch the new building block.

Copper's shrinking reach

Higher baud means more loss per meter of twinax, so copper reach roughly halves with each lane-rate doubling.

Medium What is inside Reach at 100G/lane Reach at 200G/lane
DAC (passive) Twinax only; host SerDes does all equalization ~2–3 m ~1 m
ACC / linear active copper Linear redriver at the ends Longer than DAC ~1–2.5 m
AEC (active electrical cable) Retiming DSP in each connector ~7 m ~3 m+ (vendor claim)
AOC (active optical cable) Optics permanently attached Tens of meters Tens of meters

Sources: 802.3dj objectives, AEC claims, 200G cable catalog. The 100G DAC figure is approximate.

AI networks: pros and cons

The first decision in any AI rack is how far copper can go, because every copper hop removes two transceivers.

Option Pros in an AI fabric Cons in an AI fabric Best fit
Passive copper (DAC) No power in the cable; lowest cost and latency; no lasers, so very reliable About 1 m at 200G per lane; thick cables crowd racks; the host SerDes does all the equalization Inside a rack or tray: GPU to switch tray, NIC to top-of-rack
Active copper (ACC, AEC) About 1–2.5 m with linear redrivers, or about 3 m and beyond with retimed AEC (vendor claim), on thinner cable; still no lasers; vendors claim 25–50% less power than active optical cables The retimer in each plug draws power and adds latency; still meters, not tens of meters Adjacent racks; NIC-to-leaf when the leaf sits in the row
Optics (pluggable, linear or co-packaged) Tens of meters to kilometers; light, dense cabling; the only option for multi-rack scale-up and for every switch tier above the leaf Highest power and cost per link; lasers are the leading failure source; more connector end faces to keep clean Anything beyond a few meters

Bottom line. Use copper wherever it reaches: each copper hop takes two transceivers, and their lasers, out of the power and failure budget. Every lane-rate step shortens copper, which is why the 400G-per-lane generation pushes optics into the scale-up domain.

Sources: copper reach as in the table above; AEC power claim; 1.6T SR8 reach.

Cable technologies: from passive copper to slow-and-wide light

At 200G per lane, passive copper stops at about 1 m and pluggable optics start at tens of meters. The 1–50 m between them, where most AI rack and row links fall, is now contested by seven cable types, as of October 2026. Four ship today: passive copper, linear active copper, retimed copper and active optical cables (AOCs so far only at 100G per lane). Three are emerging, with first products or product demonstrations expected in 2026–2027: RF over plastic waveguide, terahertz waveguide and micro-emitter (microLED) "slow and wide" optical cables.

Every row has the same two plugs and the same host interface; what changes is the electronics in each plug and the medium between them. Terahertz waveguide cables follow the RF row's pattern at higher carrier frequency.

The family at a glance, October 2026

Cable Inside each plug Reach at 200G per lane Power per end (1.6T unless noted) Status
Passive copper (DAC) ID memory only; the host SerDes drives the whole channel IEEE objective at least 1 m; one 1.6T data sheet lists 1 m at 26 AWG, and one large AI vendor lists none at 200G per lane Under 0.1 W Shipping
Linear active copper (ACC, also LACC) A linear redriver per lane; no clock recovery Catalogs list 1–2.5 m; vendors claim 3–4 m About 1.8–4.3 W (about 1.1–2.7 pJ/bit; the low end is a vendor claim) Shipping
Retimed copper (AEC) A retimer DSP; can also change lane rate and count Catalogs list 1–3 m; second-generation claims exceed 6 m 22 W typical and 27 W maximum in one catalog (about 14–17 pJ/bit); a second-generation DSP alone claims 12.8 W 1.6T in catalogs; second generation sampling
Active optical (AOC) A full optical module at each end (DSP or linear driver, lasers and photodiodes), with the fiber bonded in 800G: 30 m on OM3 in one data sheet; VR8-class optics reach 50 m on OM4 800G: up to 14 W (about 17.5 pJ/bit) 800G shipping; no shipping 1.6T AOC found
RF over plastic waveguide A millimeter-wave radio chip; each plastic core carries two 224G carriers Claims range from 10 m (2025) to 10–20 m Target about 3 pJ/bit (claim) Evaluation kits; small volumes reported for the second half of 2026
Terahertz waveguide A radio chip with carriers near 1 THz on thin dielectric guides 4 m demonstrated; 20 m projected Not published Prototype; product demonstrations promised for late 2026
Micro-emitter (microLED) optical A gearbox, a microLED array and a photodiode array: hundreds of slow channels over a multicore fiber bundle Evaluation kits (reach not published); one 1.6T cable targets up to 50 m One 1.6T design claims 12 W (about 7.5 pJ/bit); a modeled 800G research design needs 5.3 W as a pluggable (3.1 W co-packaged) Evaluation kits now; first product announced for 2027

Reach and power in the last three rows are vendor claims or research models, not measured products. The pJ/bit figures divide the stated power per end by the line rate.

Why copper keeps getting shorter

  • Loss rises with frequency. Twinax loses more per meter as frequency rises, through skin effect and dielectric loss. Since the move to PAM4 at 50G, each lane-rate doubling doubles the frequency the cable must carry: about 26.6 GHz at 100G, 53.1 GHz at 200G, and over 100 GHz if 400G stays PAM4.
  • IEEE reach objectives shrank with each step, then stopped. Twinax objectives went from 5 m at 25G per lane (with RS-FEC) to 3 m at 50G, 2 m at 100G and 1 m at 200G. The 400G-per-lane project (P802.3dv, approved September 2026) keeps 1 m, because 1 m is the shortest useful rack link: a mid-rack switch to the top or bottom of the rack, plus slack.
  • 802.3dj trades host loss against cable loss. It does not fix a cable length. It sets a 40 dB end-to-end loss budget and four cable-assembly loss classes (19, 24, 29 and 34 dB), so a low-loss host leaves more of the budget for the cable.
  • Thicker wire buys reach at the cost of bulk. One 1.6T DAC at 26 AWG is 10.5 mm across with a 90 mm bend radius. One 800G (8 × 100G) AEC line uses 34 AWG (6.4 mm) for 1–3 m, stepping through 32 and 30 AWG to 28 AWG (10.9 mm) for 4–6 m.

The ladder stops shrinking at 1 m because the rack sets the floor; anything longer than that at 400G per lane will need active electronics or optics.

Active copper: linear or retimed

  • Linear (ACC). A redriver boosts the high frequencies the cable lost but does not recover the clock. The host SerDes still equalizes the whole channel, so a cable works only with hosts it was tuned for: one catalog's 1.6T splitter cables, when plugged into one switch model, can link only to one NIC model. Latency added is under 100 ps (claim).
  • Retimed (AEC). A DSP in each plug recovers the clock and sends a clean signal, so each host drives only the short channel to its own plug, as with an optical module. AECs can change lane rate and count for breakouts, run link training and report telemetry through CMIS. The costs are power and latency, tens of nanoseconds in earlier generations; no figure is published for 1.6T.
  • The power surprise. First-generation 1.6T AECs draw 22 W typical per end in one catalog, about two-thirds of the 33.5 W the same catalog lists for its 1.6T (2 × 800G) twin-port optical module. Second-generation 3 nm DSPs claim 12.8 W for the DSP and more than 6 m (sampling, October 2026).

Active optical cables

  • What they are. An AOC is two optical modules with the fiber bonded in. One 800G AOC data sheet lists VCSEL multimode, 8 × 106.25G, 30 m on OM3 and up to 14 W per end. Two 800G VR8 modules plus fiber reach 50 m on OM4 at 12.9 W typical per end. Linear (no-DSP) and half-retimed (retimed transmit, linear receive) 800G AOCs were shown in OIF interoperability demonstrations at ECOC 2024.
  • Why use one. It costs less than two modules plus fiber, because only electrical testing is needed at the factory.
  • Why not. One failed end replaces the whole cable, and lengths are fixed. Lasers remain a reliability weak point: the microLED research paper below puts short-reach optical links at a few hundred FIT, against under 10 for passive copper. At 1.6T, the 200G-per-lane multimode PHY is still in IEEE P802.3ds, and no shipping 1.6T AOC was found.

Slow and wide cables: micro-emitters and fiber bundles

Section 10 introduced slow and wide at the package. The same idea now reaches cables. The plug splits the host's few fast lanes into hundreds of slow channels and sends each on its own microLED through a multicore "imaging" fiber, the kind endoscopes use. Each channel runs at a few Gb/s with on-off NRZ signaling. There are no lasers and no DSP. The host's Ethernet FEC still runs; the research design adds only a lightweight Hamming-style code across channels, not a second FEC. Added latency is a few nanoseconds (research estimate).

The host sees an ordinary 800G module. In each direction the cable uses 460 light sources: 400 carry data and 60 carry a cross-channel error-correcting code.

  • A peer-reviewed research design (SIGCOMM 2025).
    • Prototype. Measured 2 Gb/s per channel at 20 m with a BER below 10⁻⁶, and below 10⁻¹² to 10 m.
    • Modeled 800G design. 400 data channels on a 20 × 20 microLED array under 1 mm², plus 60 parity channels. It reaches 50 m in simulation and draws 5.3 W per end as a pluggable (3.1 W co-packaged). The paper's reference 10 m 800G AOC draws 9.8–12 W (data sheets list up to 14 W), so the saving is 56–68%.
    • Timeline. Its owners expect commercialization with partners in late 2027.
  • Evaluation kits. One startup ships 1 Tb/s kits: 335 microLED channels at up to 3 Gb/s each over a multicore fiber bundle (August 2026). It showed a connectorized version in an MPO-form-factor connector in September 2026.
  • A first product announcement. A retimer vendor announced a 1.6T micro-emitter cable on 12 October 2026, shipping in 2027. Its claims:
    • up to 50 m, at 12 W per end, about 30% below the vendor's own AEC baseline;
    • spare channels with hitless failover;
    • a 100-million-hour MTBF target;
    • ten times lighter than an AEC.
  • Other paths.
    • An LED maker showed a 10 m engine at 3 Gb/s or more per channel and under 2 pJ/bit (claim), and targets a market launch in 2027.
    • A thin-film micro-VCSEL array (850 nm) showed error-free 32 Gb/s NRZ over a connectorized multicore fiber, claiming multimode-fiber compatibility (private demonstration, September 2026). It is still slow and wide, with fewer, faster channels.

Why LEDs. A microLED has no lasing threshold and needs no wavelength control. It comes from display-industry manufacturing, and spare channels turn a dead emitter into a remap inside the cable rather than a link down. The research design's reliability model projects under 20 FIT per link, against a few hundred for short-reach optics. That is a model, not field data.

What limits them

  • Dispersion. A microLED's spectrum is over 10 nm wide, against under 1 pm for a laser, and visible light disperses strongly in silica. That bounds reach to tens of meters, and measured reach (20 m) still trails modeled reach (50 m).
  • Channel speed. Each LED runs at a few Gb/s, so 1.6T needs hundreds of channels and a gearbox to map 200G host lanes onto them. In the research design the whole digital back end, gearbox included, draws only 0.4 W per end; the host electrical interface (2.4 W pluggable, 0.2 W co-packaged) costs more.
  • Bundles and connectors. Multicore bundles stiffen quickly as they grow, and a connectorized link, claimed as the first, was shown only in September 2026.
  • No standard yet. An Open Compute Project workstream, Short-Reach Micro-Emitter Optics (SRMO), started on 12 October 2026 and targets approval in 2027. It has published no technical parameters, and no IEEE or OIF project covers these links.

RF and terahertz over plastic waveguide

These cables modulate a radio carrier and guide it through a plastic (dielectric) core instead of sending light or a baseband electrical signal. Loss per meter is far lower than twinax at the same data rate, and neither uses lasers; the millimeter-wave chips are 28 nm CMOS.

  • Millimeter wave.
    • Construction. A 1.6T cable has eight metal-clad plastic cores. Each core can carry 448 Gb/s as two 224G carriers at about 90 and 225 GHz, so eight cores give about 3.6 Tb/s in total. That is enough for 1.6T each way if four cores serve each direction, one carrier per 200G host lane; the sources do not state the split. The cable is 8.1 mm across, about half the volume of an AEC.
    • Claims. 10–20 m reach, about a third of optics' power (target about 3 pJ/bit), and latency far below DSP optics.
    • Status. Evaluation kits. A press report, not confirmed by the company, puts small-volume shipments to a cloud provider in the second half of 2026 and volume in 2027.
  • Terahertz. Carriers near 1 THz run over guides about 200 µm across, with as little as 0.3 dB/m of loss. It was demonstrated over 4 m in April 2025; 20 m is projected, and first product demonstrations were promised for late 2026.
  • No MSA covers either. Both vendors plan pluggable cables first; the terahertz parts had not yet been integrated into a pluggable as of December 2025.

Inside the box: flyover and co-packaged copper

  • Why the cable moves inward. At 200G per lane, board traces (about 1.1 dB per inch in a host model proposed to 802.3dj) eat the loss budget. So the long run moves into twinax: flyover cables from a connector beside the ASIC to the front panel, or co-packaged copper at the package (section 10).
  • Status. A 102.4T switch package with co-packaged copper (512 × 200G lanes through substrate-level cable connectors) was shown physically at OFC 2025. Copper channel modeling for AI systems (SFF-TA-1043) is under way in SNIA SFF, and no shipping co-packaged-copper switch was found.
  • 448G. A member study at an OIF 448G workshop (April 2025) targeted about 2 m end to end for a scale-up channel and modeled cables only up to 1.6 m. It found negative COM margin and suggested an inner FEC to recover it. It concluded that attaching cable directly at the package might be the only viable option.

The emerging cables sit in the empty corner of the chart: tens of meters at a fraction of today's optical power. Every one of those points is a claim or a model.

Where each cable competes: copper owns the rack, optics own the row and beyond, and every emerging cable aims at the 3–50 m between them.

AI networks: pros and cons

Option Pros in an AI fabric Cons in an AI fabric Best fit
Passive copper (DAC) Near-zero power and latency; no lasers; cheapest About 1 m at 200G per lane; thick, stiff cables block airflow; the host SerDes carries the whole channel Inside a tray, or the shortest in-rack runs
Linear active copper (ACC) A few watts per end; under 100 ps of added latency (claim) Tuned to particular hosts; no clock recovery, so host and cable are qualified together; 1–2.5 m in catalogs In-rack links on one qualified host and cable pairing
Retimed copper (AEC) Isolates each host from the cable channel; breakout and lane-rate options; CMIS telemetry; no lasers First-generation 1.6T draws optics-class power; adds latency; still only a few meters NIC to switch and switch to switch within a rack or to the next rack
Active optical cable (AOC) Tens of meters; cheaper than two modules plus fiber The whole cable is replaced on any failure; fixed lengths; lasers remain; no shipping 1.6T AOC found Row-scale links that do not need structured cabling
RF over plastic waveguide Reach beyond copper at a fraction of optics' power (claim); no lasers Not yet in volume; a single supplier; no MSA; reach claims vary from 10 to 20 m Adjacent-rack scale-up, once qualified
Micro-emitter (microLED) optical Very low energy per bit (claims and models); spare channels absorb emitter failures; no DSP and nanosecond latency Not yet a product; dispersion limits reach to tens of meters; new connectors and bundles; no standard yet Row-scale scale-up from 2027, if the claims hold

Bottom line. Copper stays the default wherever it reaches, because it has no lasers to fail. At 200G per lane that means about 1 m passive and a few meters active. From a few meters to 50 m, today's answer is an AOC or two modules and fiber. The emerging cables all target that gap with the same bet: replace lasers and DSPs with radio chips or many slow LEDs. Treat their reach and power as claims until independent measurements and a standard exist.

In operations

  • Copper links take longer to come up. CR PHYs auto-negotiate (Clause 73) and run link training. Training timers grew with each generation, from 0.5 s at 25G to 3 s at 50G and 12 s at 100G, and an early 200G draft set a 60 s auto-negotiation retry timer that was expected to change. Allow for slow link-up after a reseat before calling it a failure.
  • Know which copper is in the port. A DAC, an ACC and an AEC look alike in the rack. The module's CMIS memory reports its media interface technology, and linear cables carry host-compatibility lists. Check both before swapping one for another.
  • Budget an AEC like an optic. At 22 W typical and 27 W maximum per end, a 1.6T AEC counts against the port's power class and thermal budget just as an optical module does.
  • Bulk is a cooling problem. Thick 26 AWG bundles with a 90 mm bend radius block airflow. Prefer thinner-gauge active cables where intake space is tight.
  • New cables bring new telemetry. For micro-emitter cables, ask for spare-channel counts and per-channel error counters. For every emerging cable, qualify each host and cable pairing, since none has a compliance specification yet.
  • Count flaps, not just errors. In AI training one link flap can stall a job, so track flaps per cable type during qualification.

Filled dots have happened; hollow ones are announcements, targets or projections, to check as each date arrives.

What to watch as these emerge

  • IEEE 802.3dj (200G per lane, at least 1 m of twinax) is in its final IEEE SA recirculation ballots and targets approval at the December 2026 RevCom meeting.
  • IEEE P802.3dv (400G per lane, still at least 1 m of twinax) started in September 2026 and projects submission for final approval in September 2029.
  • OIF CEI-448G projects (VSR chip-to-module and LR backplane, launched February 2026) will set 448G electrical channel budgets; twinax reach at 400G per lane is set in IEEE P802.3dv.
  • IEEE P802.3ds (200G per lane on multimode fiber) is what 1.6T VCSEL AOCs need.
  • Second half of 2026. Small-volume RF waveguide shipments (press report) and terahertz product demonstrations (promised).
  • 2027. The first micro-emitter cable shipments (announced), the OCP SRMO specification (target), and commercialization of the microLED research design (late 2027, target).

Sources: 802.3dj objectives, 802.3dj RevCom plan, 802.3dj September 2026 motions, 802.3ck objectives, 802.3cd objectives, 802.3by cable types, P802.3dv, P802.3dv PAR, P802.3dv objectives, why 1 m at 400G per lane, 802.3dj cable-assembly classes, 802.3dj host trace loss proposal, copper link-training timers, 200G cable catalog with AEC, linear-cable and optics power, second-generation 1.6T AEC DSP, 1.6T DAC data sheet, AEC wire gauges, linear redriver claims, 4 m linear redriver claim, 800G AOC data sheet, 800G VR8 data sheet, AOC trade-offs, linear and half-retimed AOC demonstration, P802.3ds, CMIS 5.2, microLED research paper, its commercialization target, microLED evaluation kits, connectorized microLED link, 1.6T micro-emitter cable announcement, SRMO launch, SRMO workstream, microLED limits, LED-maker microLED engine, its 2027 launch target, micro-VCSEL arrays, RF and terahertz waveguide cables, RF waveguide targets, RF waveguide shipment report, terahertz demonstration plans, co-packaged copper switch demonstration, SFF copper channel work, 448G scale-up channel study, OIF 448G projects. Power per bit is computed here from stated watts; all emerging-cable figures are vendor claims or research models.

Co-packaged and near-packaged optics

CPO, NPO, XPO and the other packaging choices now have their own section (section 10).

The 400G-per-lane horizon

The next step is P802.3dv: 400G per lane for 400G, 800G and 1.6T Ethernet over copper and single-mode fiber up to 500 m, targeting completion around 2029 (PAR). Modulation (PAM4 vs PAM6), whether pluggables survive at that rate, and how much CPO takes over are the defining open questions of the late 2020s.

Reliability is now a network metric

  • Synchronous training stalls on the slowest or broken link, so a link flap can force a whole job back to its last checkpoint.
  • Operators therefore track per-link flap counts, FEC margin trends and module temperature as capacity-planning signals, and pull optics on degrading margin before they fail.
  • Laser type, operating temperature and burn-in screening drive failure rates. One reason silicon photonics is attractive is that one well-cooled laser can feed several lanes.

Also on the horizon

  • Optical circuit switches reconfigure fabric topology with mirrors instead of packets. They favor bidirectional or WDM optics that tolerate the switch's insertion loss (section 19).
  • Hollow-core fiber carries light mostly through air, cutting latency by about a third, which matters for distributed training across data-center campuses (section 17).
Section 10 · Products

Optics packaging: pluggable, LPO, XPO, NPO and CPO

11 diagrams · 20 min read
In this sectionThe five approaches side by sideWhy distance is the leverXPO: the pluggable answer to densityNPO: the middle pathWhat NPO hardware looks likeExternal or built-in lasers: pros and consDense NPO: when the engine needs retimingCPO: the end pointFast and narrow vs slow and wideScale-up from the package: CPC and OCIAI networks: pros and consChoosing among them

The same optical engine can sit in five places relative to the switch ASIC, and moving it closer shortens the electrical path. A shorter path needs less equalization, so the SerDes and DSP shrink and power per bit falls; the price is serviceability, thermal complexity and multi-vendor freedom. Section 25 opens up the engine itself.

The top three rows keep the optics at the faceplate as replaceable modules; the bottom two move them beside or onto the ASIC and run fiber to the panel instead.

The five approaches side by side

Approach Where the optics sit, and the electrical path Cooling and power Serviceability Status, Oct 2026
Retimed pluggable Front-panel cage; ~10–30 cm of board trace or flyover cable; DSP in the module Air; ~20–26 W for a 1.6T module Hot-swap one port at a time; any compliant vendor Mainstream at 800G and 1.6T
LPO / LRO Same cage and path; DSP removed (LPO) or kept only on transmit (LRO) Air; under 10 W (LPO) to ~11–15 W (LRO) at 1.6T Hot-swap, but each host and module pairing must be qualified LPO MSA specs since 2025; 1.6T LPO and LRO modules listed in 2026
XPO Front panel, one large module carrying 64 × 200G lanes (12.8 Tb/s) Liquid cold plate, up to ~400 W per module Hot-swap, but one module is eight 1.6T ports' worth MSA announced Mar 2026; demos at OFC 2026; no released spec or shipping product found
NPO (near-packaged) Optical engine on the board or an interposer next to the ASIC; a few cm (up to ~15 cm); fiber to the panel Liquid cooling in the OIF project; lasers often external Engine replaceable without replacing the switch ASIC OIF 12.8T NPO module project launched May 2026; pilots in 2026, deployments expected from 2027
CPO (co-packaged) Optical engines on the ASIC's package substrate; millimeters (≤ ~5 cm); fiber to the panel; lasers in front-panel ELSFPs Lowest power per bit; switch-level cooling Lasers hot-swap; engines do not 51.2T and 102.4T CPO Ethernet switches in production

Sources: XPO announcement, XPO lanes and density, XPO ecosystem status, OIF 12.8T NPO project, NPO deployment outlook, 1.6T LPO, 1.6T LRO. Power figures are vendor-listed.

Why distance is the lever

  • Loss sets SerDes power. At 200G per lane, every centimeter of board trace costs signal. A host SerDes driving a pluggable must equalize a long, lossy channel; one driving a co-packaged engine sees a channel of about 10 dB, and one driving an NPO engine about 13 dB (OIF channel classes, XSR and XSR+).
  • Energy per bit follows. A ~30 W pluggable carrying 1.6 Tb/s works out to roughly 19 pJ/bit. CPO vendors claim 65–70% lower optics power, or 3.5–5× better efficiency per port; these are vendor claims (102.4T CPO, CPO efficiency).
  • Density follows too. Faceplate area, not silicon, limits how many pluggables fit a 1RU switch. XPO answers by packing eight ports into one liquid-cooled module (about 204.8 Tb/s per rack unit, by its sponsors' figures); NPO and CPO answer by moving the optics off the faceplate entirely.

XPO: the pluggable answer to density

XPO (eXtra-dense Pluggable Optics) is a multi-source agreement announced in March 2026 for a large, liquid-cooled pluggable with 64 electrical lanes at 200G, or 12.8 Tb/s per module. One XPO occupies the faceplate of roughly eight OSFPs and is meant to carry DR, FR, LR, SR and coherent ZR/ZR+ optics. It keeps the pluggable model (replaceable modules from multiple vendors) while accepting liquid cooling at up to ~400 W per module. As of October 2026 it is at the demonstration stage, and adoption depends on switch silicon built around it.

NPO: the middle path

Near-packaged optics put the optical engine on a high-performance substrate or interposer beside the ASIC rather than on the ASIC's own package. That keeps most of CPO's electrical benefit while letting the engine be tested, sourced and replaced separately, and it keeps the most failure-prone part away from the hottest chip. Some in the industry describe NPO as a practical way to implement co-packaging rather than an alternative to it. The OIF started a 12.8T NPO module implementation agreement in May 2026, covering 6.4T and 12.8T engines at 200G per lane with liquid cooling and laser-source definitions.

  • On-board optics (COBO) is the older relative: optics on the main board near the chip, with a longer electrical path than NPO.

What NPO hardware looks like

No NPO engine specification has been published yet: the OIF project began in May 2026, and a socketed-engine MSA formed in March 2026 has not released one. The picture below is assembled from their published scopes and from 2026 demonstrations, so read the drawings as schematics rather than as any one product.

The front panel loses its transceiver cages. What remains is fiber adapters and slots for external laser modules, with fiber running inside the chassis from each engine to the panel.

The engine

  • Capacity. 3.2 Tb/s engines are in early deployments. The socketed-engine MSA defines 6.4 Tb/s as 32 × 200G lanes, with a roadmap to 12.8 Tb/s and 448G lanes; the OIF project covers 6.4T and 12.8T engines at 200G per lane.
  • What is inside. The same parts as a CPO engine (section 25): a photonic IC with modulators and detectors, an electronic IC with drivers and TIAs, and a fiber attach unit. The difference is the engine's own substrate, which plugs into a socket or high-density connector instead of being soldered to the ASIC package.
  • Light. Most designs take continuous-wave light over fiber from external laser modules at the front panel, as CPO does. At least one engine shown in September 2026 builds its lasers in: 7.2 Tb/s as 36 × 200G channels, driven linearly with no DSP. A 3.2T line shown in March 2026 uses VCSELs, for multimode links.
  • Cooling. Liquid. The OIF project defines cooling and power delivery alongside the electrical, optical and mechanical interfaces.

The ASIC and the engine share the board, often under one cold plate. Only the socket separates the engine from the switch, and that is what makes it replaceable.

The system

  • Layout. Engines ring the ASIC a few centimeters away. A 102.4 Tb/s switch needs 16 × 6.4T or 8 × 12.8T engines.
  • Electrical path. An XSR+ class channel of about 13 dB, compared with about 10 dB for CPO, so the host SerDes drives the engine directly with no retimer or module DSP.
  • Front panel and fiber. Fiber adapters (MPO or very-small-form-factor) and laser-module slots replace transceiver cages. The internal fiber from every engine to the panel becomes a design and service item of its own.
  • Service model. Lasers swap from the front panel, an engine unplugs from its socket inside the chassis, and the ASIC stays. With pluggables you swap one port at the faceplate; with CPO only the lasers are replaceable.

External lasers and a stacked EIC are the common pairing today; built-in lasers trade front-panel serviceability for fewer fibers and connectors.

Status, October 2026

  • Two large cloud operators beta-tested 3.2T NPO configurations in mid-2026 and plan 6.4T variants for 2027; wider deployment is expected from about 2027.
  • Specifications in progress: the OIF NPO implementation agreement, the socketed-engine MSA, and open engine specifications from an OCP initiative due in Q4 2026 (section 27).
  • Not yet public: engine dimensions, the connector type, the number of lasers per engine and the fiber count per engine.

Sources: socketed-engine MSA, OIF NPO project scope, 7.2T engine with built-in lasers, its expo showing, NPO as an interim step, 3.2T VCSEL line and beta tests, NPO vs CPO overview, CPO vs NPO vs XPO.

External or built-in lasers: pros and cons

Lasers are the least reliable and most heat-sensitive part of an engine, so where they sit decides efficiency, serviceability and what a failure costs. Nearly every CPO design keeps them outside in front-panel ELSFP modules. NPO reopens the question, because the engine itself is replaceable.

The external laser keeps the light source cool and swappable; the built-in laser skips the connector, the coupler, the splitter and the PM fiber, but sits next to the heat.

External laser (ELSFP) Built-in laser
Laser temperature + Front-panel airflow, away from the ASIC and EIC; one 8-laser module is rated for a 0–70 °C case − Sits near the hottest parts; threshold and slope efficiency worsen exponentially with temperature, and dense laser arrays heat each other
Power and loss budget − Light crosses a connector, a fiber-to-chip coupler and often a splitter, so lasers run at high power (over 20 dBm per lane in current modules) + No coupling loss on the source; a 2021 model found built-in designs drew less system power even though each laser was less efficient
Serviceability + The most failure-prone part hot-swaps from the front panel without touching the engine − A laser failure means an engine swap: a socket change inside the chassis, not a front-panel hot-swap
Failure blast radius − One laser often feeds several lanes through a splitter, so a failure takes out a group + Can be one laser per lane, though the engine is the replaceable unit
Fiber and front panel − Adds polarization-maintaining fiber and laser slots on the panel; high power makes connector cleanliness critical + No laser fiber or laser slots; the panel and fiber attach carry only data
Engine build, yield and test + The engine is passive photonics plus the EIC, with no III-V material; lasers can be cooled, higher power and shared − III-V bonding or attach lowers yield, complicates burn-in and narrows the supplier base
Ecosystem + OIF ELSFP is a published, multi-vendor agreement − Each design is proprietary
Operations − One more managed device per engine group; correlate laser output with the engine's receive power + Self-contained; triages more like a pluggable

Why NPO shifts the balance. CPO's strongest argument for external lasers is that a dead laser should not strand a whole switch. A socketed NPO engine weakens it: a built-in laser failure costs an engine swap, and an engine a few centimeters from the ASIC can be cooled on its own, so the heat penalty is smaller than on the ASIC package. That is likely why the first NPO engine shown with built-in lasers (September 2026, a vendor claim) took that route. What does not change is the size of the outage: an engine swap takes 6.4–12.8 Tb/s offline in a maintenance window, while a laser swap is a front-panel hot-swap.

Rule of thumb.

  • Choose external lasers for fleet-scale front-panel operations, multi-vendor laser sourcing, or when the engine cannot be kept cool.
  • Choose built-in lasers when power per bit and fiber and connector count dominate, the engine has liquid cooling, and engine-level spares and maintenance windows are acceptable.

The modeling figures come from a 2021 study aimed at 51.2 Tb/s switches: cooled external lasers reached about 125 mW against about 75 mW for built-in lasers running uncooled at 70 °C, cooling built-in lasers improved link budgets by 2–4 dB, and at 70 °C built-in designs needed backup lasers to hold about a 1% annual failure rate. Vendor claims, such as 66% lower power and 10× reliability for one built-in-laser engine (against its own earlier design) or 4× fewer lasers from sharing external ones, are not independently verified.

Sources: external vs integrated light sources, JLT 2021, thermal scaling of hybrid laser arrays, OIF ELSFP 2.0, 8-laser ELSFP datasheet, built-in-laser engine, shared external lasers in production.

Dense NPO: when the engine needs retiming

NPO keeps most of CPO's power saving only if the ASIC's SerDes can drive each engine directly, with no retimer in between. That works inside an electrical budget of about 13 dB, and packing more engines around the ASIC pushes some of them outside it.

The inner engines get short traces and can run linear; the second row needs one of the fixes in the flow further down.

The budgets that decide it

Interface class Reach and loss What it connects
CEI-112G-XSR (CPO) About 50 mm, about 10 dB ASIC die to an engine on the same package
CEI-112G-XSR+ (NPO) Up to 150 mm, 13 dB ASIC to an engine a few centimeters away
CEI-224G-XSR Up to about 50 mm of package-substrate trace Die to die and die to engine (in development)
CEI-224G-VSR 200 mm host, 20 mm module, one connector Chip to module: pluggable, NPO or CPO
CEI-224G-MR and LR 500 mm; 1,000 mm with two connectors Chip to chip; backplane and copper cable
CEI-224G-Linear and EEI-224G-RTLR Projects Fully linear and half-retimed optics for LPO, NPO and CPO

Why density makes it harder

  • Escape geometry. A 102.4 Tb/s ASIC must route 512 × 200G lanes to 16 × 6.4T or 8 × 12.8T engines. Only so many engines fit in the inner ring; the rest sit farther out and need more routing layers.
  • 224G halves the reach. Doubling the lane rate roughly doubles the Nyquist frequency, to about 56 GHz, and board loss per centimeter rises roughly in step, so the same 13 dB covers about half the trace length it did at 112G.
  • The socket is a tax. The socket or connector that makes an NPO engine replaceable adds loss and reflections that CPO does not pay, and tighter lane pitch adds crosstalk.
  • 448G tightens it again. OIF's 448G electrical work so far covers only the VSR and LR classes.

What each fix costs

  • The yardstick. Every 1 pJ/bit on a 102.4 Tb/s switch is about 100 W.
  • Retimed engine. A retimer puts another SerDes pair on every lane; OIF's 224G framework notes that removing one repeater halves the SerDes count per switch port. A full DSP also brings back part of the pluggable's latency.
  • Bigger host SerDes. No retimer, but the ASIC pays: one 224G long-reach SerDes was demonstrated at about 4 pJ/bit across a 48 dB channel.
  • Cut the loss. Flyover cable from the package to the engines, lower-loss laminate or a shared substrate keeps linear drive and its power saving, at the cost of mechanical complexity.

Where it stands, October 2026

  • Linear NPO exists at 200G per lane: one 7.2 Tb/s engine (36 × 200G) drives its optics linearly with no optical DSP.
  • Pure linear drive is harder at 224G because optical nonlinearity grows, so hybrid designs add gain control and clock recovery, moving toward half-retimed.
  • OIF's CEI-224G-Linear and EEI-224G-RTLR projects cover the fully linear and half-retimed cases; the OIF 12.8T NPO agreement, which will fix the engine's electrical interface, is not yet published.

In operations. A linear NPO link is one long equalized channel from the ASIC's SerDes, through the engine and fiber, to the far end, so the host SerDes counters are the only per-lane view, and a dirty connector, an aging laser and a weak lane look alike. Retimed engines restore segment-by-segment telemetry; it is the same trade as LPO against retimed pluggables (section 4).

Bottom line. Dense NPO stays linear and low-power only if every engine fits inside a budget of roughly 13 dB, and both density and 224G shrink that budget. Expect linear or half-retimed inner engines, and flyover cable, retimed engines or bigger host SerDes for the rest, each giving back part of the power saving.

Sources: XSR and XSR+ channel classes, OIF CEI-224G projects, OIF current work, CEI-224G framework, CEI-224G-Linear, 224G linear drive, 224G long-reach SerDes, linear 7.2T engine.

CPO: the end point

Co-packaged optics place optical engines on the same package substrate as the switch ASIC, so the electrical path shrinks to millimeters and the pluggable DSP disappears.

  • The laser problem. Lasers are the least reliable, most heat-sensitive part, so CPO keeps them in front-panel external laser source modules, standardized by the OIF as ELSFP (v2.0, January 2025) (spec).
  • What is shipping. 51.2T CPO Ethernet switches are deployed; 102.4T CPO switches have sampled since late 2025, and a GPU-fabric vendor's CPO Ethernet switches entered full production in August 2026 (production report).
  • Reliability data. The early fear was that a failed engine would strand a switch. One hyperscaler reported about 15 million CPO device-hours with roughly 5× the MTBF of pluggables, and later too few failures to compute an MTBF at all (report).
  • Scale-up next. GPU vendors have shown photonics for multi-rack scale-up domains, where copper's ~1 m reach at 200G per lane runs out.
  • What you give up. Engines cannot be swapped at the faceplate; the supply chain concentrates around the switch vendor; and fault isolation tools are less mature than for pluggables.

Fast and narrow vs slow and wide

There are two ways to move a given bandwidth off a chip. Fast and narrow runs a few lanes at the highest rate the electronics allow (200G PAM4 per lane today, 400G next), with DSP equalization and FEC. Slow and wide runs many more lanes at a modest rate, typically 16–64 Gb/s NRZ, with little or no equalization and no FEC, and gets its bandwidth from lane count: many wavelengths per fiber, many fibers, or a wide parallel electrical interface.

Both carry 1.6 Tb/s in the drawing. Fast and narrow spends its effort in the SerDes and DSP; slow and wide spends it in packaging, lasers and fiber count.

Fast and narrow Slow and wide
Lane rate 200G PAM4 now, 400G next 16–64 Gb/s NRZ per lane or wavelength; current optical I/O runs 32–56 Gb/s
What makes it work Faster SerDes, DSP equalization, FEC Lane count: dense WDM (8–16 wavelengths per fiber), parallel fibers or micro-LED arrays, advanced packaging
Energy and latency Higher pJ/bit; the DSP and FEC add latency Lower pJ/bit; no FEC, latency in nanoseconds
Reach Meters to kilometers, on IEEE PMDs Short: package to rack scale (one micro-LED design targets about 10 m)
Shoreline density Limited by SerDes area and package escape High with 2.5D and 3D packaging; one 3D-stacked engine spreads I/O across the whole die
Interoperability Standard Ethernet PMDs from many vendors Mostly proprietary; the OCI MSA and UCIe-based chiplets are the first open steps
Where it fits in AI Scale-out: NICs, leaf, spine, between buildings Scale-up: GPU to GPU and GPU to memory inside a pod

Examples, October 2026

  • Fast and narrow. 1.6T modules on 8 × 200G lanes are the volume product, and 400G-per-lane DSPs are sampling (section 25).
  • Slow and wide, by wavelength. Optical I/O chiplets with ring-based dense WDM run 32 Gb/s NRZ per wavelength with no FEC. One 3D-stacked CPO engine runs 16 wavelengths per fiber at 56 Gb/s NRZ (800 Gb/s per fiber), or 106/112 Gb/s PAM4 (1.6 Tb/s per fiber), with availability claimed for 2026.
  • Slow and wide, by fiber count. A micro-LED prototype drives hundreds of 10 Gb/s channels through a multicore imaging fiber, about 3 Tb/s at under 1 pJ/bit over about 10 m.
  • In between. The OCI MSA's 200G PHY uses 4 wavelengths at 53 GBd NRZ per direction rather than one 200G PAM4 lane (section 27).
  • Electrically. UCIe runs 4–64 GT/s per lane (64 GT/s since UCIe 3.0, August 2025). Standard 2D packages allow about 25 mm at a 100–130 µm bump pitch; 2.5D cuts the pitch to 25–55 µm with about 2 mm of reach and much higher shoreline density.

Bottom line. Fast and narrow wins where reach, standards and multi-vendor plugs matter, which is the scale-out network. Slow and wide wins where energy, latency and shoreline density matter over short reach, which is the scale-up domain. The two meet in CPO and NPO engines, which can be built either way.

Sources: serial vs parallel optical PHYs, UCIe over optics, WDM optical I/O, 3D-stacked CPO engine, micro-LED links, OFC 2026 status. Shoreline and energy figures are vendor or analyst claims.

Scale-up from the package: CPC and OCI

Scale-up links (GPU to GPU, and GPU to scale-up switch inside a pod) are moving their connection point from the faceplate to the package. Two concepts lead. Co-packaged copper (CPC) keeps copper but plugs it in at the package, and the OCI MSA defines an open optical PHY for the links copper cannot reach.

Inside the rack, copper wins on cost and has no lasers to fail; once a link leaves the rack, it needs light.

Co-packaged copper (CPC)

  • What it is. A twinax cable assembly that plugs into a socket on or beside the ASIC's package substrate, next to the SerDes, instead of a connector at the board's edge. The signal skips the lossy board trace and runs in cable to the front panel, a backplane or the next tray. Compression-mount, solderless sockets keep the cable field-replaceable.
  • Why now. At 224G the board trace is the weakest part of the channel. A long-reach 224G SerDes demonstrated in 2026 ran 2.5 m of cable (two 0.75 m co-packaged cables and a 1 m backplane), 48 dB bump to bump, at about 4 pJ/bit with a bit error ratio around 10⁻¹¹.
  • One socket, two media. Package sockets are being designed to take either copper or optics. One connector supplier shows CPC and CPO on the same substrate of 95 mm or less, with 16- and 64-pair sockets around the chip for 1,024 off-chip lanes, and claims about 5 dB less loss than near-packaged connections (vendor claim).
  • Limits. Copper reach still halves with each lane-rate step. The 448G work is weighing PAM4 against PAM6, with 336G PAM4 as a fallback, and 448G co-packaged cable systems are prototypes. No industry standard defines CPC yet.

OCI: an open optical PHY for scale-up

  • What it defines. A 200G-per-direction link on one fiber: 4 wavelengths × 53.125 GBd NRZ each way, the forward group at 1308.0–1314.9 nm and the reverse group at 1327.7–1334.8 nm, for links under 100 m with a budget good to about 500 m (section 27).
  • Why it looks this way. It is slow and wide in miniature: NRZ lanes need little equalization and no heavy DSP, four wavelengths share each direction, and sending both directions on one fiber halves the fiber count. The reference design uses silicon micro-ring modulators fed by ELSFP external lasers.
  • Where it goes. A second generation doubles to 400G per direction, with 3.2 Tb/s per fiber on the longer roadmap, in pluggable, on-board, co-packaged and chiplet form factors; UALink can run over it.

The two wavelength groups sit about 13 nm apart, so a simple filter at each end separates what it sends from what it receives.

AI networks: pros and cons

Option Pros in an AI fabric Cons in an AI fabric Best fit
Board-routed copper (DAC or AEC at the faceplate) Mature, standard and cheapest Board trace plus connector loss limits reach at 224G; AEC retimers add power In-rack links at today's rates
Co-packaged copper (CPC) Takes the board out of the channel, so long-reach SerDes copper reaches about 1–2.5 m; no lasers; the cable is field-replaceable at the package No standard yet; cable bulk around the package; reach halves again at 448G Tray-to-tray and in-rack scale-up at 224G
OCI optics Open, multi-vendor PHY; NRZ lanes with little DSP and low latency; one bidirectional fiber per link; tens of meters New ecosystem; external lasers and ring control loops to manage; first specification only Multi-rack scale-up pods
CPO or NPO optics on 200G PAM4 lanes Highest bandwidth per fiber pair today; shares the Ethernet optics supply chain PAM4 lanes need KP4 FEC and more equalization, adding latency Scale-out, and scale-up links that bridge into the Ethernet fabric

Bottom line. Inside a rack, CPC stretches copper by taking the board out of the channel. Across racks, OCI gives scale-up an open optical PHY built for low power and latency rather than reach. Watch for package sockets that accept either medium, because that is how one switch or GPU design can serve both.

Sources: co-packaged copper, co-packaged interconnects at DesignCon 2026, 224G long-reach SerDes over co-packaged copper, OCI MSA formation, 200G-OCI PHY write-up, OCI MSA.

AI networks: pros and cons

In an AI fabric the packaging decision comes down to power at cluster scale, how much fails together, and who can supply the parts.

Option Pros in an AI fabric Cons in an AI fabric Best fit
Retimed pluggable Multi-vendor sourcing; hot-swap one port at a time; mature tooling and telemetry Highest power per bit (about 14 W per 800G, roughly 17.5 pJ/bit); faceplate area limits ports per rack unit The default, and any fabric that mixes vendors or generations
LPO or LRO pluggable Keeps the pluggable model at roughly half the module power or less (section 4) Per-pairing qualification; tight margins at 200G per lane Short links in tightly controlled clusters
XPO 12.8T per liquid-cooled module, about eight OSFPs' worth, while keeping pluggable sourcing Demonstration stage; one module failure takes out eight ports' worth of traffic; liquid cooling at the faceplate Future high-density pluggable switches
NPO Most of CPO's electrical benefit, with socketed, field-replaceable engines and a path to multi-sourcing The Open CPX specification was published in September 2026, and products are pre-production; an engine swap needs a maintenance window; fiber management inside the chassis 2027-onward switches that want CPO-class power with serviceability
CPO Lowest power per bit (vendor claims of about 4.4–6.9 pJ/bit); fewer lasers; positive production reliability data (about 5× pluggable MTBF at one hyperscaler) Engines are not field-replaceable; supply concentrates around the switch vendor; fault-isolation tools are less mature Large single-vendor AI fabrics at 102.4T and beyond

Bottom line. Pluggables stay the default while AI fabrics mix vendors and generations. CPO wins where one vendor owns the whole switch and power is the binding constraint. NPO and XPO are the two bets on keeping serviceability while closing the power gap.

Choosing among them

  • Need multi-vendor optics and per-port replacement: retimed pluggables.
  • Short, controlled links and a power target: LPO or LRO, after qualifying the exact host and module pair.
  • Faceplate density at 1.6T and beyond, while keeping pluggables: watch XPO and the 400G-per-lane USFP.
  • Lowest power per bit at scale, accepting switch-level integration: CPO, with NPO as the more serviceable middle ground.
Section 11 · Products

1.6T in depth

1 diagram · 4 min read
In this sectionThe arithmeticHost interfaces: 8 lanes or 16The 1.6T module familyPower and thermalCoherent 1.6TStatus and what comes next

A 1.6T port is eight 200G PAM4 lanes: the host drives 8 × 212.5 Gb/s, and the module carries them on eight fiber pairs (DR8), two groups of four fiber pairs (2×DR4), or two groups of four wavelengths (2×FR4). A 102.4 Tb/s switch therefore offers 64 × 1.6T ports, or 128 × 800G when each module is split in two.

DR8 and 2×DR4 are the same optics with different connectors; 2×FR4 swaps parallel fibers for wavelengths so it can run over duplex single-mode.

The arithmetic

  • Lanes. 8 × 200G. Each electrical lane runs 106.25 GBd PAM4 (212.5 Gb/s with RS(544,514) overhead).
  • Optical lane rate. 106.25 GBd on 500 m DR links; 113.4375 GBd on 2 km-plus links that add the inner Hamming code inside the module (section 5).
  • Switch math. 512 × 200G SerDes = 102.4 Tb/s = 64 × 1.6T. The same silicon can also be built with 1,024 × 100G SerDes, which is where 16-lane 1.6T modules come in (102.4T launch).
  • Per-GPU vs per-port. 2026 GPU platforms advertise 1.6 Tb/s of scale-out bandwidth per GPU, but one leading NIC's datasheet lists 800G per port, so "1.6T per GPU" can mean two 800G ports (NIC datasheet). Check which one a design means.

Host interfaces: 8 lanes or 16

IEEE 802.3dj defines an 8-lane 1.6T attachment interface as the main option and allows a 16-lane one (objectives). A 16 × 100G host can drive 200G-lane optics through a gearbox module: one OSFP-XD 1.6T DR8 listing pairs 16 × 106.25G host lanes with 8 × 212.5G optical lanes at about 22 W (datasheet). Most 1.6T deployment, though, pairs 8 × 200G hosts with OSFP1600 modules.

The 1.6T module family

Variant Optical lanes Connector Reach Splits into
1.6T DR8 8 × 200G, one wavelength; MPO-16 or dual MPO-12 MPO-16 APC 500 m 8 × 200G-DR1, or 2 × 800G-DR4
1.6T DR8-2 (DR8+) 8 × 200G MPO-16 or dual MPO-12 APC 2 km Same as DR8
2×DR4 2 × (4 × 200G) Two MPO-12 APC 500 m or 2 km 2 × 800G
2×FR4 2 × (4 wavelengths × 200G) Two duplex LC 2 km 2 × 800G-FR4
1.6T LPO / LRO DR8 8 × 200G, linear or half-retimed As DR8 500 m class As DR8
1.6T AEC (copper) 8 × 200G electrical, retimed — Up to ~2 m —

Sources: DR8 / 2×DR4 datasheet, DR8, DR8-2 and 2×FR4 modules, retimed and LPO 1.6T, 1.6T AEC.

  • Standards vs products. IEEE 802.3dj's 1.6T optical objectives cover 8 fiber pairs at 500 m and 2 km; there is no 1.6T FR or LR objective. 2×FR4 modules are two 800G FR4 engines in one shell.
  • Laser technology. Both EML and silicon photonics designs ship (section 25 compares them); one analyst firm reports that almost all 1.6T optics shipping in 2026 are DR-type silicon photonics (Cignal AI).
  • Form factors. OSFP1600 dominates, in finned-top and riding-heatsink versions; QSFP-DD1600 is specified; OSFP-XD carries 16-lane hosts and is the path to 3.2T.

Power and thermal

1.6T module type Listed power
DSP-retimed (DR8, 2×FR4) ~20–26 W
Half-retimed (LRO) ~11–15 W
Linear (LPO) under 10 W

Vendor-listed figures (DSP and LRO, LRO datasheet, LPO). 3 nm DSPs for 8 × 200G claim over 20% lower module power than the previous node (3 nm DSP). A switch with 64 retimed 1.6T modules spends well over a kilowatt on optics alone, which is the case for LPO, LRO, NPO and CPO in section 10.

Coherent 1.6T

  • 1600ZR. The OIF published the 1600ZR implementation agreement on 9 September 2026: one wavelength carrying a 1.6TbE client over up to 120 km of single-span amplified DWDM, with interop demos planned (announcement). Project-stage figures pointed to about 235 GBd 16QAM with oFEC.
  • 1600ZR+. In progress since January 2024, aimed at roughly 1,000 km (OIF 1600G page).
  • Coherent-lite at 1.6T. O-band and C-band designs target 2–20 km campus links, but strong 200G PAM4 has slowed adoption (section 8).

Status and what comes next

  • Volume. One analyst firm expects more than 10 million 1.6T units in 2026, with shipments growing about 50% quarter on quarter in early 2026 (Cignal AI, above).
  • Standard. IEEE 802.3dj, which defines the 1.6TBASE-R PCS and PMDs, was not yet approved as of early October 2026; submission for approval was planned for October, targeting the December 2026 standards board meeting (PAR extension). Today's modules are built to the near-final drafts.
  • Next. 3.2T arrives either as 16 × 200G (OSFP-XD's future option, or XPO at 64 lanes) or 8 × 400G (P802.3dv, PAR approved September 2026; a 16-lane 400G-per-lane USFP pluggable was announced in October 2026); 400G-per-lane DSPs have already been announced, and analysts expect nearly half of 1.6T-plus-3.2T transceivers over the next five years to use 400G lanes. XPO targets 12.8T per module.
Section 12 · Operations

Management and diagnostics

2 diagrams · 7 min read
In this sectionThe management specsDOM basics (every generation)CMIS concepts worth masteringCMIS in depth: the memory map and the bring-up sequenceIdentity and coding

Every pluggable carries a small management memory map that the host reads over a two-wire (I²C-style) bus. SFP-class modules use SFF-8472, QSFP28-era modules use SFF-8636, and everything 400G and newer uses CMIS, now at version 5.4 (May 2026) under the OIF (IA list). Knowing which map a module speaks tells you what you can see and control.

The management specs

Spec Used by What it adds
SFF-8472 SFP, SFP+, SFP28 Digital diagnostics (DOM/DDM) with alarm and warning thresholds
SFF-8636 QSFP+, QSFP28 The same for four lanes, with per-lane values
CMIS QSFP-DD, OSFP, QSFP112, SFP-DD and beyond Module and data-path state machines, application selection, VDM telemetry, firmware upgrade, many lanes via banks
C-CMIS Coherent modules CMIS extensions for coherent: tuning, CD, OSNR and SNR estimates, laser frequency

Identifier byte values that say which module type is plugged in are defined in SFF-8024.

DOM basics (every generation)

  • Five monitors. Module temperature, supply voltage, laser bias current, Tx optical power and Rx optical power, per lane where the module has lanes.
  • Four thresholds per monitor. High alarm, high warning, low warning, low alarm, written by the module vendor. Warnings mean "drifting"; alarms mean "out of spec".
  • Latched flags. On QSFP (SFF-8636) and CMIS modules a flag stays set until read and drives the interrupt line, so a short excursion is still caught. On the SFP family (SFF-8472) the flags are live and clear on their own, so only polling catches an excursion.
  • Accuracy. SFF-8472 allows about ±3 dB on optical power readings (summary), so DOM power is excellent for trends and lane-to-lane comparisons and weak as an absolute meter.
  • Average, not OMA. DOM reports average optical power (SFF-8472 lets a module declare OMA instead, A0h byte 92 bit 3, so check it before comparing dBm); for PAM4 eye quality, use the module's SNR or BER telemetry.

CMIS concepts worth mastering

  1. Module state machine. Low power → powering up → Ready (or Fault). A module stuck in low-power mode often means the host has not granted its power class.
  2. Data-path state machine. Each data path (a group of lanes forming one port) moves from deactivated through initialization to activated. Per-port problems after breakout often sit here.
  3. Applications (AppSel codes). The module advertises the host-interface and media-interface pairs it supports, for example "400GAUI-8 to 400GBASE-DR4" or "4 × 100GAUI-2 to 4 × 100GBASE-DR". The host selects one per data path. Breakout and speed changes are application changes.
  4. VDM (versatile diagnostics monitoring). Per-lane media-side SNR, pre-FEC BER (current, minimum, maximum, average), errored-frame counts, laser temperature and more. VDM is how you see the optical segment's health separately from the host's FEC counters.
  5. CDB (command data block). A command channel used mainly for module firmware upgrades. Module firmware is now a real operational variable.
  6. Built-in test. Many modules offer host-side and media-side loopbacks and PRBS generators and checkers, which let you isolate the electrical and optical segments without test equipment.

A port that never comes up is usually stuck in one of these boxes: low power (power class not granted) or a data path that never leaves initialization (unsupported application).

CMIS in depth: the memory map and the bring-up sequence

The concepts above become concrete once you can picture the memory map a host reads over I²C, and the order in which it must write it.

The memory map. Lower memory (bytes 0–127) is always visible: management-interface revision, module state, global and lane-flag summaries, temperature, supply voltage and the page and bank select registers at bytes 126–127. Everything else is paged. Upper pages 00h, 01h and 02h hold identity and advertising: vendor, part and serial numbers, date code, power class and maximum power (page 00h bytes 200–201), the application descriptors (host interface, media interface, lane counts), the durations the module needs for each state transition, and the alarm and warning thresholds. Page 10h is control, banked per group of eight lanes: data-path deinit, transmitter disable and squelch, and the staged control sets (bytes 145–152 for control set 0: AppSel, data-path ID, the explicit-control bit, and the signal-integrity settings when explicit control is on). Page 11h is its mirror for status: data-path state per lane, latched flags with their masks, per-lane receive and transmit power and laser bias, and the active control set the module is really using. Pages 13h and 14h hold the built-in test engines: host- and media-side loopbacks, PRBS generators and checkers, and per-lane error counts. Pages 20h–2Fh are VDM, and page 9Fh is the CDB command window.

Bringing a data path up.

  1. Power. The module starts in low power after reset. The host reads its power class and MaxPower, checks that the cage can supply and cool it, and releases LPMode (a pin or a software bit) so the module can move to ModuleReady.
  2. Discover. The host reads the advertised applications and the transition durations (MaxDurationDPInit and its siblings). A module that does not advertise the host's intended application cannot be made to run it; this is where a 400G module refuses a 4 × 100G breakout.
  3. Stage. With the data path deactivated, the host writes a control set: which application, which lanes form the data path and, if it takes explicit control, the host-side equalizer settings. Nothing takes effect yet.
  4. Apply. The host sets ApplyDPInit (page 10h byte 143) for the lanes. The module validates the staged set, reports per-lane acceptance or rejection codes, and moves the data path from DPDeactivated through DPInit to DPInitialized within the advertised duration. A rejected set is the commonest silent cause of a port that never comes up after a configuration change.
  5. Activate. The host enables the transmitter; the data path goes to DPActivated and light appears. Lane state and the latched flags on page 11h are now meaningful.
  6. Watch. Flags are latched, so a transient fault stays visible until read; the interrupt pin tells the host something changed. VDM thresholds warn before failure.

VDM: what to watch and why. Each observable has a current value, with high and low alarm and warning thresholds; the host reads descriptors to learn which observables the module supports.

Observable What it tells you Why it matters
Media-side pre-FEC BER, per lane and per data path The raw error ratio the module's own FEC or the host FEC sees on the optical segment Separates optical health from host-channel health; a distance to the FEC cliff
Media-side eSNR The DSP's estimate of signal quality after equalization, in dB Falls before BER rises; tracks dirt, dispersion and aging
Host-side pre-FEC BER and eSNR The same for the electrical segment Convicts or clears the host channel without test gear
Errored frames (FERC) Frames the FEC could not correct, as a count and a rate The number that should match the host's uncorrectable counter
Laser temperature and TEC current Thermal state of each laser Early warning of wavelength walk (LAN-WDM) and of laser aging
Laser bias current, Tx and Rx power per lane The classic DOM set Bias creeping up at constant power is an aging laser
Laser age, percent The module's own estimate of consumed life A fleet-replacement signal

Signal-integrity controls. With explicit control the host can set, per lane, the module's host-side input equalizer and its host-side output pre-cursor and post-cursor emphasis and amplitude; without it the module uses its application defaults. Platforms usually expose these only through debug commands, and the right setting depends on the host trace, which is why a module that is marginal in one slot may be fixed by a host-side SI profile rather than a replacement.

What the versions mean. CMIS 3 (2018) defined the data-path state machine, applications and staged control sets; CMIS 4 (2019) added VDM and CDB; the CMIS 5.x releases added form-factor, Fibre Channel, CPO and ELSFP, link-training and advertising extensions (5.3 in 2024, 5.4 in 2026). OIF's coherent CMIS (C-CMIS) adds the observables a ZR module needs (OSNR, chromatic dispersion, PMD, state of polarization) and the frequency and power controls, and its 2026 CMIS-LT adds out-of-band, per-lane, per-direction link tuning for any module type, with linear optics as the main driver. A host that implements an older revision than the module advertises will still see identity and DOM but may not see VDM or be able to stage applications, which shows up as a module that works but cannot be configured.

Sources: CMIS 3.0, CMIS 4.0, CMIS 5.3 release, CMIS-LT and C-CMIS 1.5 approval.

Identity and coding

The memory map also holds vendor name, part number, serial number, date code and compliance codes. Hosts may check these to decide whether a module is supported, so a module can be optically perfect and still be refused or run with warnings. Know your platform's policy before blaming the optic.

Section 13 · Operations

Troubleshooting and operations

2 diagrams · 7 min read
In this sectionThe layered methodSymptom to causeToolsOperational hygieneOptical power and laser safety: the numbers behind the rule

Work the link from the glass upward and from the module toward the host. Most optical link problems are dirty or damaged connectors, the wrong fiber or polarity, or a mismatch in lane rate, FEC or application, not a dead laser.

The layered method

  1. Is the module accepted? Present, identified, in the Ready state, power class granted, a supported application selected. If not, nothing optical matters yet.
  2. Is light leaving? Per-lane Tx bias and Tx power inside thresholds; no Tx fault or Tx disable. A lane with normal bias but low Tx power points to the laser or its coupling.
  3. Is light arriving? Per-lane Rx power between the receiver's sensitivity and its overload point. Near-end Tx minus far-end Rx, lane by lane, estimates the path loss.
  4. Is the signal clean? Media-side SNR and pre-FEC BER from the module (VDM), and the host's FEC counters and symbol-error histogram. Corrected errors rising over time means margin is draining.
  5. Do both ends agree? Same speed, same lane rate and modulation, same FEC mode, matching breakout mode and application, link training on copper.
  6. Is it stable? Flaps correlate with temperature, marginal Rx power, reflections, mechanical seating or firmware. Look at timestamps against module temperature and Rx power history.

The order matters: each check assumes the ones above it passed, so a FEC problem is only worth chasing once power levels are known to be good.

Symptom to cause

Symptom Most likely causes First check
Link down, Rx loss of signal on all lanes Polarity (Tx into Tx), unplugged or wrong patch, fiber break Far-end Tx power, then trace the path
Some lanes dark on a parallel optic Dirty or damaged MPO fibers, wrong MPO polarity type, MPO-12 vs MPO-16 mix Inspect the MPO end face, check trunk type
Link up, corrected FEC errors climbing Dirty connector, marginal power, reflections (MPI), tight bend, weak host channel Clean and inspect; compare module VDM with host FEC
Uncorrectable codewords, CRC errors Margin exhausted on at least one segment Find the worst lane in VDM; swap one element at a time
Rx power above the overload point ER-, ZR-class or amplified optics on a short patch (IEEE DR, FR and LR optics are specified for a 0 dB channel) Add an attenuator; never loop a long-reach optic back on itself unattenuated
Link flaps Thermal limits, Rx power near sensitivity, firmware, loose cage latch Correlate flap times with temperature and Rx power
Module not recognized or held in low power Unsupported coding, power class beyond the port, unsupported application Read module identity and state; check the host's support list
Breakout ports dead Lane rate or modulation mismatch, port not split on the host, wrong application Check the lane-matching rule (section 6)
Copper link will not come up Auto-negotiation or link-training mismatch; cable too long for the lane rate Align negotiation settings on both ends
Coherent link down Channel or frequency mismatch, mode mismatch (400ZR vs OpenZR+), low OSNR, wrong Tx power for the line system Compare frequency and mode at both ends; read OSNR and CD estimates

Tools

  • Fiber inspection scope. Inspect before you connect, every time, against the IEC 61300-3-35 pass/fail zones. Cleaning without inspecting is guessing.
  • Cleaning. Dry-clean first with a click cleaner sized for the connector (LC or MPO), then inspect again. Wet-dry cleaning only for stubborn contamination.
  • Optical power meter and light source. Measures real loss more accurately than DOM.
  • OTDR. Locates breaks, bad splices and high-loss connectors on longer runs.
  • Visual fault locator. A red laser that shows continuity and bends on short patches.
  • Module loopbacks and PRBS. Isolate host channel vs optics without lab equipment.
  • Swap discipline. Change one thing at a time (module, port, patch, trunk) and record the result. Two simultaneous swaps teach you nothing.

Operational hygiene

  • Baseline DOM and FEC values at turn-up, so later readings have something to be compared with.
  • Trend corrected-FEC rates and symbol-error histograms, not just alarms; alarms fire after margin is gone.
  • Keep caps on every unused port and patch end. Most contamination happens during moves, adds and changes.
  • Track module firmware versions like any other software.
  • Laser safety: never look into a fiber or port, and treat amplified DWDM systems as hazardous even when "nothing is lit".

Optical power and laser safety: the numbers behind the rule

The rule in the list above, never look into a fiber or port, is right. An expert should also know where the real hazards sit, because the answer has shifted as ports add lanes and external lasers arrive.

Classes and hazard levels. IEC 60825-1 classifies the product; IEC 60825-2 classifies the fiber system by the power accessible at any point, as hazard levels 1, 1M, 2, 2M, 3R, 3B and 4. Class 1 and hazard level 1 mean safe to view even with the naked eye under reasonable conditions; 1M means safe to the naked eye but not through magnifying optics such as a loupe or an inspection microscope held to a bare fiber. The limit depends on wavelength because the eye's lens and vitreous absorb the longer wavelengths before they reach the retina: under IEC 60825-2 Ed. 4.0 (2021), built on IEC 60825-1:2014, hazard level 1 in single-mode fiber is about +22 dBm at 1310 nm and +10 dBm at 1550 nm (1M: about +24 and +21 dBm), while at 850 nm in 50 µm multimode, where the retina is exposed, hazard level 1 is +5.9 dBm (3.9 mW) and 1M +8.8 dBm (7.5 mW). The 1310 nm figure moved a long way between editions: the 2004 table gave about +12 dBm, which is the number still quoted in many module datasheets, so check which edition a label refers to (Table D.1 values by edition).

Where the power adds up. A single DR lane launches +1 dBm nominal and at most +4 dBm, but an MPO carries eight transmit fibers: 8 × +1 dBm is +10 dBm and 8 × +4 dBm is +13 dBm through the ferrule. At 1310 nm that is still 9 dB below the 2021 hazard level 1, and the measurement aperture (7 mm at 100 mm) captures only a fraction of each fiber's divergent output; IEEE nonetheless assesses the worst-case combination of lanes on, and at 850 nm, where the limit is +5.9 dBm, an SR8 port at about +8 dBm total is why multi-lane multimode PMDs have been classified hazard level 1M rather than 1 (802.3cd assessment). The devices that cross a limit outright are a different class: an external laser source feeding a CPO package (the OIF ELSFP implementation agreement specifies power per wavelength per core in classes up to 26 dBm, targets hazard level 1, and limits any fiber to 24.5 dBm where an automatic power reduction loop acting within 250 ms, rather than an interlock, protects an open connector), an EDFA booster at +17 to +20 dBm, well above the +10 dBm level-1 limit at 1550 nm, and a Raman pump at +27 to +30 dBm, a Class 3B or 4 source that will damage connector end-faces and skin, not only eyes. A 400ZR module is tame by comparison at about −10 dBm (high-power ZR+ variants reach 0 to +1 dBm).

Mechanisms that keep it safe.

  • Automatic laser shutdown (ALS, ITU-T G.664) on amplified line systems: when a fiber breaks, the loss of the return signal turns the amplifier output down to a safe level within seconds and probes periodically for restoration. Automatic power reduction (APR) does the same for Raman pumps. Nothing of the kind exists in a grey pluggable, which keeps transmitting into an open connector.
  • Interlocks on external-laser ports. High-power ELS connectors are keyed and their sources are designed to reduce power on an unmated or broken connection, the same loop ALS runs on a line system.
  • Signal detect and Tx disable in pluggables are for link management, not safety: a module with its transmitter disabled is Class 1 by design in any case, and is not "safe because it is off" when the host re-enables it.

Practice. Inspect with a video scope, never a bare eye, and prefer scopes that image through the connector to loupes; cap unused ports and pigtails, since safety and cleanliness are the same habit; treat any amplifier, Raman pump, ELS or unknown long-haul fiber as hazardous even when the management system says the port is down, because the pump may be on while the data path is not; and remember that 1310 nm and 1550 nm light is invisible, so "no light" means nothing. Power meters, not eyes, are the instrument.

Sources: IEC 60825-2 Table D.1 by edition, 802.3cd hazard assessment, OIF ELSFP 02.0, 400ZR launch power.

Section 14 · Operations

Link budgets made intuitive

2 diagrams · 6 min read
