In this sectionThe budget in one lineWorked example: a 2 km 400G FR4 linkMeasuring the real lossWorked budgets: standard-grade against low-loss plantThe coherent version: an OSNR budget

A grey link closes when the weakest legal transmitter, minus every loss and penalty on the path, still lands above the weakest legal receiver's sensitivity, with margin left for aging and repairs. IEEE packages this as one number per PMD, the maximum channel insertion loss, so in practice the question is: does my measured or estimated path loss fit under it?

The budget in one line

Margin = PTx,min − SensitivityRx − (fiber loss + connector loss + splice loss) − penalties
  • Fiber loss = length × attenuation (about 0.4–0.5 dB/km in the O-band for budgeting; 3.5 dB/km at 850 nm on multimode).
  • Connector loss = number of mated pairs × per-pair loss (budget 0.75 dB per standard-grade mated pair of any type (TIA-568.3), about 0.35 dB for low-loss MPO and 0.25 dB for low-loss LC; IEEE's channel figures assume 0.5 dB averages).
  • Penalties = dispersion, reflections, transmitter quality (TDECQ) allowances, carved out of IEEE's power budget before the channel-loss figure is set, so never subtract them again when comparing a measured loss with that figure.
  • Overload is the other edge: too much power saturates the receiver. Check the data sheet's overload and damage thresholds: IEEE DR, FR and LR modules are specified for a 0 dB channel, so a back-to-back loop is in spec; attenuators are for ER- and ZR-class optics, APD or SOA receivers and amplified links.

Worked example: a 2 km 400G FR4 link

The lesson: at data-center distances, connectors, not fiber, consume the budget. Each extra patch-panel hop costs as much as a kilometer of fiber. A dirty connector can add several dB on its own, which is how a 1 dB-headroom link becomes an errored one.

Measuring the real loss

  • Best: an optical loss test set (light source and power meter) at turn-up.
  • Good enough to trend: near-end Tx power minus far-end Rx power from DOM, lane by lane. Treat absolute values as ± a couple of dB, but trust changes over time and differences between lanes.
  • A single bad lane on a parallel optic almost always means one dirty or damaged fiber position in an MPO, not a fiber-wide problem.

Worked budgets: standard-grade against low-loss plant

The FR4 example above counts hops. This one puts the current TIA-568.3 grades to the three most common single-mode links, because connector grade is the difference between a design that closes and one that does not.

Component Standard grade Low-loss hardware
LC or SC mated pair 0.75 dB maximum (TIA-568.3) 0.25 dB typical maximum (vendor)
MPO mated pair 0.75 dB maximum 0.35 dB typical maximum
Fusion splice 0.3 dB (budget) 0.1 dB or less
OS2 fiber at 1310 nm 0.5 dB/km planning, 0.35 typical same
  • 400GBASE-DR4 over 500 m (3.0 dB allowed). Fiber 500 m × 0.5 = 0.25 dB. A typical structured path has four mated MPO pairs (two patch panels, each with a jumper on both sides): at 0.75 dB that is 3.0 dB, 3.25 dB in total, over budget before anything is dirty. With low-loss hardware (two MPO pairs at 0.35 and two LC pairs at 0.25 through a breakout cassette) connectors cost 1.2 dB and the total is 1.45 dB: 1.55 dB of margin.
  • 400GBASE-FR4 over 2 km (4.0 dB allowed). Fiber 1.0 dB. Six mated pairs across two buildings' panels at 0.75 dB is 4.5 dB, 5.5 dB in total: it does not close. The same path with low-loss hardware (6 × 0.35 = 2.1 dB) totals 3.1 dB, with 0.9 dB to spare.
  • 100GBASE-LR4 over 10 km (6.3 dB allowed). At the 0.5 dB/km planning figure the fiber alone is 5.0 dB and two standard pairs make 6.5 dB, which does not close on paper; at a measured 0.43 dB/km it is 4.3 + 1.5 = 5.8 dB, which does. LR links are the one place where fiber, not connectors, dominates, and where the optical loss test, not the planning number, decides.

The rules that fall out.

  1. Count mated pairs first, then fiber. At DR and FR distances each standard-grade pair costs as much as 1.5 km of fiber.
  2. Specify low-loss hardware for any 400G-and-up single-mode path that crosses more than two panels; it is cheaper than the margin it buys back.
  3. IEEE's power budget already sets aside the dispersion, reflection and transmitter penalties for the PMD's reach (FR4: 7.8 dB budget, 3.8 dB of penalties); what is left, the maximum channel insertion loss, is what a measured loss is compared with directly, and adding penalties again double-counts. The 0 dB case is covered too: DR, FR and LR optics are specified to work back to back, so an attenuator is needed only for ER, ZR and amplified links.
  4. Keep about 1 dB for aging and repair: a field splice after a cut adds 0.1–0.3 dB, and connector end-faces degrade with every mating cycle.
  5. Multimode budgets are tighter than they look: 100 m of OM4 at 3.0 dB/km is only 0.3 dB, but the 1.8–1.9 dB budget must hold two pairs at 0.75 dB and still leave room for the modal-bandwidth penalty, which is why MMF structured cabling at 100G per lane is practically limited to two connections.

Sources: channel loss and penalty allocations, link-loss planning values, TIA-568.3 connector and splice values.

The coherent version: an OSNR budget

Amplified coherent links are rarely limited by received power, because amplifiers restore it. They are limited by accumulated noise. The budget becomes: delivered OSNR (set by span count, span loss, amplifier noise figure and launch power) must exceed the transceiver's required OSNR plus penalties for filtering through ROADMs, nonlinearity and aging. Two intuitions carry most of it:

  • Doubling the number of identical spans costs about 3 dB of OSNR.
  • Raising launch power improves OSNR until fiber nonlinearity starts adding its own noise, so there is an optimum launch power, not a "more is better".

The link-budget instrument in Optics Bench lets you move each of these numbers and watch the headroom respond.

A coherent budget in numbers. For N identical spans, each amplifier adding noise set by its noise figure (NF) and the span loss it makes up,

OSNRdB ≈ 58 + Plaunch,dBm − Lspan,dB − NFdB − 10·log10 N

where 58 dB is the quantum ASE constant: the noise an ideal amplifier chain adds, hν × 12.5 GHz = −58 dBm in the 0.1 nm reference bandwidth at 1550 nm. Two cases. A single amplified 120 km span for 400ZR, with +1 dBm per channel launched by the booster, 0.2 dB/km plus 1 dB for connectors (25 dB) and a 5 dB preamplifier noise figure: 58 + 1 − 25 − 5 = 29 dB against the 26 dB a 400ZR receiver requires, 3 dB of margin before ROADM filtering (1–2 dB) and aging; the module's ±2,400 ps/nm dispersion tolerance caps it near 140 km in any case. The same arithmetic for eight 80 km spans (640 km and about 10,900 ps/nm, inside a 400G OpenZR+ module's 12,000 ps/nm): 58 + 1 − 17 − 5 − 9 = 28 dB against about 23.5 dB required with oFEC, 4.5 dB of margin, and a tenth span would cost another 1 dB before the dispersion limit is reached (one module's published OSNR and dispersion tolerances). Doubling the span count costs 3 dB; raising launch power to +4 dBm buys 3 dB back, until nonlinear noise (section 26) takes it away again.

Section 15 · Operations

Selection framework

2 min read
In this sectionStep 1: the host fixes the form factor and lane rateStep 2: reach and fiber narrow the PMDStep 3: breakout and topologyStep 4: power, cost and operabilityThe pre-deployment checklist

Choose an optic by answering four questions in order: what lanes the host drives, what distance and fiber you have, whether the port must break out, and what power and cost you can afford. The first two usually leave only two or three candidates.

Step 1: the host fixes the form factor and lane rate

The switch or NIC port decides the form factor (QSFP-DD vs OSFP), the host lane rate (50G, 100G or 200G) and the supported power class. Everything later must fit inside that.

Step 2: reach and fiber narrow the PMD

Reach Existing fiber 100G-lane choice (400G/800G) 200G-lane choice (800G/1.6T)
≤ 3 m, in rack — DAC; AEC if longer DAC to ~1 m; AEC beyond
≤ 30 m — AOC or SR AOC or DR
≤ 100 m Multimode trunk SR4 / SR8 / SR4.2 BiDi Single-mode DR (multimode options thin out)
≤ 500 m Single-mode parallel (MPO) DR4 / DR8 DR4 / DR8
≤ 2 km Single-mode duplex FR4, 2×FR4 FR4, DR-2 variants
≤ 10 km Single-mode duplex LR4 (LR4-6 to 6 km) LR4; coherent LR1
10–40 km Single-mode duplex ER-class grey or coherent Coherent ER1-20 / ER1
40–120 km DWDM, amplified 400ZR 800ZR / 1600ZR
ROADM or > 120 km Shared line system High-power ZR+ / OpenZR+ High-power ZR+

Step 3: breakout and topology

  • Need to split a port into lower-speed links? Choose parallel optics (DR4, DR8) and confirm the lane-matching rule.
  • Running a new plant? Single-mode MPO trunks keep every future option open.
  • Fiber scarce or leased? Favor WDM duplex or DWDM.

Step 4: power, cost and operability

Priority Leans toward
Lowest power per bit LPO or LRO where host and reach allow; CPO at system level
Plug-and-play interoperability Fully retimed, standards-based PMDs
Best diagnostics Retimed modules with full CMIS VDM; coherent for long links
Lowest capex in rack DAC, then AEC
Longest life of fiber plant Single-mode everywhere

The pre-deployment checklist

  • Host supports the module type, power class and required applications in those exact ports
  • Lane rate and modulation match at both ends, including breakout partners
  • FEC mode agreed on both ends
  • Connector type, APC vs UPC and MPO-12 vs MPO-16 match the plant
  • Polarity method verified end to end
  • Loss budget calculated with real connector counts, and attenuators for long-reach optics on short links
  • Telemetry (DOM, VDM, FEC counters) collected and baselined at turn-up
  • Spares and firmware versions tracked
Section 16 · Deep dives

Fiber plant design

3 diagrams · 5 min read
In this sectionTopologiesMPO polarity: making transmit meet receiveBend-insensitive fiberFiber density for AI clustersCleanliness and records at scaleFiber connectivity: today and next

In an AI data center the fiber plant is a product in its own right: tens of thousands of MPO links whose polarity, bend radius, connector count and cleanliness decide whether the optics work on day one. One fiber maker estimates AI data centers need more than 10× the fiber of traditional ones (Corning).

Topologies

  • Direct patch. Module to module with one cable. Fewest connectors and lowest loss, but it does not scale and is hard to change.
  • Structured cabling. Permanent MPO trunks between rows, ending in patch panels or cassettes, with short patch cords to the equipment. Every panel adds mated pairs, which spend the link budget (section 14).
  • Interconnect vs cross-connect. An interconnect patches equipment directly to the trunk; a cross-connect adds a second panel so moves happen without touching the trunk, at the cost of more connectors.
  • Breakout at the panel. Cassettes or harnesses split MPO trunks into duplex LC or VSFF ports, which is how DR4 and DR8 breakouts are usually built (section 6).

MPO polarity: making transmit meet receive

  • Type A trunk (straight). Position 1 lands on position 1; keys run up-to-down.
  • Type B trunk (reversed). Position 1 lands on position 12; keys run up-to-up. This is the natural fit for parallel optics: a DR4's transmit fibers 1–4 arrive on the far module's receive fibers 9–12.
  • Type C trunk (pair-flipped). Each adjacent pair swaps (1↔2, 3↔4 ...); used for duplex channels.
  • Methods A, B and C (TIA-568) combine a trunk type with matching patch cords so that every duplex or parallel channel crosses over exactly once. Mixing trunk types or patch cords within a channel is the most common cause of a parallel link with every lane dark.
  • MPO-16 has an offset key so it cannot mate with MPO-12, and single-mode parallel links use angled (APC) ferrules (section 6).

Bend-insensitive fiber

ITU-T G.657 defines single-mode fibers that tolerate tight bends, which matters in dense trays and cassettes.

Category Minimum bend radius Works with standard G.652.D fiber
G.657.A1 10 mm Yes
G.657.A2 7.5 mm Yes
G.657.B2 (merged into A2 in the 2024 edition) 7.5 mm No
G.657.B3 5 mm No

Figures from a secondary summary of the recommendation (source).

Fiber density for AI clusters

  • Rollable ribbon cables pack fibers loosely bonded in ribbons that fold into round cables: one maker offers 1,728 fibers in a 1.25-inch duct, 3,456 in 1.5-inch and 6,912 in 2-inch (FlexRibbon).
  • Thinner fiber. 200 µm-coated fiber (vs the classic 250 µm) raises the count a conduit can hold by about 1.5× from the coating alone, up to 2× combined with rollable ribbon, and 160 µm is next (analysis).
  • Multi-core fiber multiplies count again without more strands (section 17).

Cleanliness and records at scale

  • Inspect every end face before connecting, including new patch cords out of the bag; MPO end faces need MPO-specific cleaners and scopes.
  • Keep dust caps on every unused port and connector.
  • Record for every link: trunk ID, trunk type and polarity method, panel positions, and turn-up loss test results. Those records turn a two-hour hunt into a two-minute lookup, and they seed the telemetry baselines in section 24.

Fiber connectivity: today and next

AI fabrics multiply fiber. A 102.4 Tb/s switch with DR-type optics terminates over a thousand fibers, and CPO and NPO move the first connector from the module's face to the chip itself. Every hop from the engine to the far end now has a denser option on the way.

In use today

Connector or method Fibers Where it is used Notes
LC duplex 2 Duplex pluggables (FR4, LR4) and patching The long-time baseline
VSFF duplex (SN, MDC, CS) 2 Breakouts and dense patch panels Several duplex ports in one LC's space
MPO-12 and MPO-16 12 or 16 Parallel optics (DR4, DR8, SR8) and trunks MPO-16 matches 8-lane modules; polarity matters (above)
MT-12 laser port 12 (8 used) External laser modules (ELSFP) Polarization-maintaining fiber
Fiber array unit pigtails Tens to hundreds CPO and NPO engines Bonded at the factory; edge or grating coupled (section 25)
High-fiber-count ribbon cable Hundreds to thousands Building and campus trunks Pre-terminated or fusion-spliced

What is coming

Option What it changes Status, October 2026
MMC (TMT ferrule) 16–32 fibers in about half an MPO's size, up to 3× MPO density, 250 µm pitch; an expanded-beam version mates blind and tolerates debris Shipping from several suppliers, aimed at AI rows, NPO and CPO
SN-MT 8 or 16 fibers in the SN duplex footprint, 2.7× the density of a 16-fiber MPO; up to 3,456 fibers in a 1RU panel, 64 fibers into an OSFP or QSFP-DD New; target specifications; aimed at 800G, 1.6T and CPO
Detachable fiber-to-chip connectors Replace glued pigtails so the engine and its fibers can be serviced separately; an edge-coupled glass-waveguide design was shown in September 2025, with a vertically coupled version in development Demonstrations

Connectors shrink the panel; wavelengths and cores shrink the fiber count. Moving from DR to 16 wavelengths per fiber cuts the strands for one switch from 1,024 to 64.

AI networks: pros and cons

Option Pros in an AI fabric Cons in an AI fabric Best fit
MPO-12 and MPO-16 Mature and multi-vendor; every test and cleaning tool supports them Large footprint; polarity and end-face cleaning at scale; limits panel density Today's pluggable fabrics
VSFF multi-fiber (MMC, SN-MT) About 2.7–3× MPO density; more fibers into modules and panels Newer ecosystem with less mature test, inspection and cleaning tooling; two competing families Dense AI rows, and NPO and CPO front panels
Detachable fiber-to-chip Engine and fiber serviced separately; better assembly yield Adds a connector's loss and contamination risk right at the chip Next-generation CPO and NPO engines
Fewer fibers through WDM or bidirectional optics 4–16× fewer fibers and connectors to clean Mux loss, more lasers or wavelength-specific parts, no lane-level breakout Fiber-scarce links and scale-up optical I/O
Multi-core or hollow-core fiber Four cores per strand, or lower latency New connectors, splicing, fan-outs and test methods Duct-limited campuses; latency-bound training sites

Bottom line. A dense AI row needs both levers: VSFF multi-fiber connectors at the panel today, and WDM, bidirectional or multi-core links as fiber counts grow with every switch generation.

Sources: MMC connectors, SN-MT connector, 8-laser ELSFP datasheet, detachable glass-waveguide connector, polymer waveguide CPO. Fiber counts are arithmetic for 512 × 200G lanes.

Section 17 · Deep dives

Fiber frontiers: hollow-core, multi-core and few-mode

1 diagram · 4 min read
In this sectionHollow-core fiber (HCF)Multi-core fiber (MCF)Few-mode fiber and space-division multiplexingComparisonAI networks: pros and cons

Two new fiber types have left the lab. Hollow-core fiber guides light through air, cutting latency by roughly 30% while losing less light than glass. Multi-core fiber puts several cores in one standard-size strand, multiplying capacity per duct. Few-mode fiber remains mostly in research.

Hollow-core fiber (HCF)

How it works. The core is air. Thin glass membranes around it (nested antiresonant nodeless designs, NANF, and double-nested DNANF) reflect light back into the core by anti-resonance rather than total internal reflection, so almost none of the light travels in glass.

Property Standard SMF (G.652) Hollow-core (DNANF)
Propagation delay ~4.9 µs/km (group index ~1.47) ~3.3–3.4 µs/km (group index ~1.003)
Best reported loss ~0.14 dB/km (record silica) 0.091 dB/km at 1550 nm (2025 record)
Low-loss window O to L bands with care Under 0.2 dB/km across 1250–1730 nm
Chromatic dispersion at 1550 nm ~17 ps/nm/km ~2–4 ps/nm/km
Nonlinearity Reference Roughly 1,000× lower
Delay change with temperature ~40 ps/km/K ~2 ps/km/K

Sources: Nature Photonics, Sep 2025, coverage, 2026 review preprint (not peer-reviewed; the dispersion, nonlinearity and thermal figures come from it). Headlines quote latency savings from 30% to 47% depending on how they are expressed; ~30% lower latency is the conservative figure.

Why data centers care.

  • Latency is distance. At the same latency budget, HCF reaches about 45% farther, so AI campuses linked by HCF can sit farther apart and still behave like one cluster.
  • Stable delay. Low thermal sensitivity keeps timing stable, which helps time distribution (section 20).
  • Wide, low-loss spectrum and low nonlinearity leave room for more wavelengths and higher launch power.

Deployment status (October 2026).

  • One hyperscaler reported 1,280 km of HCF carrying live traffic by September 2025, including hybrid cables with 32 hollow-core and 48 standard fibers between two data centers, and has announced a 15,000 km rollout supported by multiple fiber manufacturers (IEEE Spectrum, rollout).
  • Other cloud and telecom deployments are reported in secondary sources.
  • In July 2026 ITU-T Study Group 15 opened a work item for a technical report, "Hollow-core fibre technologies and systems", and liaised IEC SC86A; no Recommendation is in progress yet (SG15 summary).

What is still hard. HCF needs its own connectors, splicers and test methods; every hollow-to-solid transition costs loss and must keep reflections very low; and production volume and cost are still scaling.

Multi-core fiber (MCF)

  • Uncoupled MCF. Each core is an independent fiber, spaced far enough apart that crosstalk is negligible. Standard transceivers attach through fan-in/fan-out devices or MCF-aware connectors. A 4-core fiber in the standard 125 µm cladding fits existing cable and connector dimensions; one 2023 result reached 0.155 dB/km with crosstalk below −60 dB per 100 km (result).
  • Coupled-core MCF. Cores sit close enough to couple, which improves density and lowers some impairments but requires MIMO DSP at the receiver, as in coherent systems.
  • Where it is deployed. Subsea adoption began with a 2023 commitment to use two-core MCF on a trans-Pacific system; the first at-scale MCF transatlantic cable (24 pairs of two-core fiber) was announced in September 2026 for 2029 service (announcement). In March 2026 four companies formed the SDM4 MSA to standardize 4-core fiber for short-reach O-band links inside and between AI data centers (MSA); its v1.0 specification followed in September 2026, and in July 2026 ITU-T SG15 extended its G.650.1 revision to weakly coupled MCF geometry, with new WC-MCF Recommendations and test methods planned.
  • Why data centers care. A 4-core fiber carries four times the links in the same strand and duct space, which attacks the fiber-count problem in section 16.

Few-mode fiber and space-division multiplexing

Few-mode fiber carries several spatial modes in one larger core, each as a separate channel. Modes mix as they travel, so receivers need MIMO DSP to unscramble them. As of 2026 it lives in research and field testbeds rather than production networks (testbed). Space-division multiplexing (SDM) is the umbrella term for adding capacity in space (more cores or modes) rather than in wavelength or modulation.

Comparison

Fiber What it improves What it needs Status, Oct 2026
Standard SMF (G.652/G.657) Baseline Nothing new Universal
Hollow-core Latency, loss, nonlinearity, spectrum New connectors, splicing, test methods Early hyperscale production; ITU-T technical report in development
Uncoupled MCF Capacity per strand and per duct Fan-in/fan-out or MCF connectors Subsea and early data-center use; MSA and ITU-T work started
Coupled-core MCF Density, impairment averaging MIMO DSP Research and trials
Few-mode Capacity per core MIMO DSP, mode-matched components Research and testbeds

AI networks: pros and cons

Option Pros in an AI fabric Cons in an AI fabric Best fit
Standard single-mode fiber Universal and cheap; every connector, splice and test tool works Light travels about 30% slower than in hollow-core, which limits how far apart sites can sit for synchronous training Everything inside a building, and most links between buildings
Hollow-core fiber About 30% lower latency per km, so sites can sit about 45% farther apart for the same latency budget; very low nonlinearity and a wide low-loss spectrum New connectors, splicing and test methods; few suppliers; higher cost; early production Multi-building or multi-site training clusters where the latency budget binds
Multi-core fiber (4-core) Four cores per strand and per connector, easing duct and tray congestion; SDM4 MSA v1.0 published in September 2026 Fan-in and fan-out devices, new connectors and an immature test ecosystem Dense AI campuses where duct space, not distance, is the limit

Bottom line. Hollow-core buys distance for latency-bound training, multi-core buys density for space-bound campuses, and standard single-mode fiber remains the answer everywhere else.

Section 18 · Deep dives

Advanced coherent and DCI

1 diagram · 2 min read
In this sectionPoint-to-multipoint coherent with digital subcarriersMore spectrum: C, Super C, L and beyondManaging coherent optics and line systems with open models

Beyond point-to-point ZR links, three ideas stretch coherent optics further: splitting one transceiver into independently routed subcarriers, using more of the fiber's spectrum, and managing transceivers and line systems through open data models.

Point-to-multipoint coherent with digital subcarriers

A coherent DSP can build its signal from many narrow Nyquist subcarriers instead of one wide carrier. If each subcarrier can be routed separately, one hub transceiver (for example 400G as 16 × 25G) can talk to several smaller leaf transceivers at once (for example four 100G leaves with four subcarriers each), over a passive splitter or a ROADM (concept).

  • Why it matters. Metro and aggregation networks are hub-and-spoke by nature. Point-to-multipoint optics replace the intermediate aggregation boxes that would otherwise terminate many 100G links at the hub, and capacity can be re-assigned between leaves by software.
  • Status. The Open XR Optics Forum publishes interoperable specifications: 400G first, then in September 2025 100G specifications for bidirectional single-fiber point-to-point, dual-fiber point-to-multipoint, and an overlay on passive optical networks (forum update). Multiple vendors offer pluggables that support both modes; large-scale deployment is still emerging.

More spectrum: C, Super C, L and beyond

Band Approximate usable width Status
Standard C (1530–1565 nm, 4.4 THz) ~4 THz Universal
Extended C ~4.8 THz Common in modern line systems
"Super C" ~6 THz Vendor-specific extension
C+L ~10–12 THz Deployed on long-haul and high-capacity DCI; L-band coherent pluggables sampling since 2025
S+C+L and wider 15.6 THz demonstrated; 37.6 THz across O to U bands in research Research

Sources: band widths, L-band ZR+ pluggables, S+C+L result, O–U band result.

Adding the L band roughly doubles capacity per fiber pair without new fiber, at the cost of L-band amplifiers, filters and transceivers. Bands beyond C+L need new amplifier types (for example thulium-doped amplifiers for the S band) and are not yet in deployed systems.

Managing coherent optics and line systems with open models

When coherent pluggables live in routers (IP over DWDM), the optical layer is configured and monitored through the router's management interface. Two open model families do this:

  • OpenConfig. openconfig-terminal-device and openconfig-platform-transceiver cover the transceiver; openconfig-optical-amplifier and openconfig-wavelength-router cover amplifiers and ROADMs.
  • Open ROADM MSA. Common device, network and service models for multi-vendor ROADM networks; release 19.1.0 was published in July 2026 (repository).

Example OpenConfig telemetry for a coherent link (schema docs):

/components/component/optical-channel/state/frequency
/components/component/optical-channel/state/target-output-power
/components/component/optical-channel/state/chromatic-dispersion
/components/component/optical-channel/state/osnr
/terminal-device/logical-channels/channel/otn/state/pre-fec-ber/instant
/terminal-device/logical-channels/channel/otn/state/q-value
/terminal-device/logical-channels/channel/otn/state/esnr
/optical-amplifier/amplifiers/amplifier/state/actual-gain

These paths turn section 8's physics into numbers you can trend: estimated CD tells you the fiber length the DSP sees, OSNR and ESNR show margin, and Q-factor and pre-FEC BER show how close the link sits to its FEC threshold.

Section 19 · Deep dives

Optical circuit switching

1 diagram · 3 min read
In this sectionHow a MEMS OCS worksWhy AI and cloud fabrics use OCSWhat OCS demands of the opticsTechnologies and marketAI networks: pros and cons

An optical circuit switch (OCS) steers light from any input fiber to any output fiber with tilting mirrors or liquid crystals. It never looks at packets, so it carries any data rate, wavelength or protocol at very low power. The trade is speed: it reconfigures in milliseconds, so it rewires topology rather than forwarding traffic.

How a MEMS OCS works

The best-documented example is a 136 × 136 switch built from two arrays of 2D MEMS mirrors. Light from each input fiber hits a mirror in the first array, which tilts on two axes to aim it at a mirror in the second array, which aims it into the chosen output fiber. A camera watches the beams so one control loop can align every mirror. Insertion loss is typically under 2 dB, and return loss is typically −46 dB (Apollo paper).

Why AI and cloud fabrics use OCS

  • Rate-agnostic. The same switches have carried four generations of optics, 40G through 400G, because a mirror does not care what the light encodes.
  • Replace the spine. One hyperscaler replaced its spine layer with OCS-connected aggregation blocks and reported about 30% lower capex and 41% lower power (Jupiter paper).
  • Reconfigurable topology. A 4,096-chip AI system uses OCS to rewire its interconnect into the shape each job needs (for example a twisted 3D torus) and to route around failed hosts, with OCS and optics under 5% of system cost and under 3% of system power (TPU v4 paper).

What OCS demands of the optics

  • Extra loss budget. Every pass through the switch costs a couple of dB. Transceivers tuned for OCS links absorb up to 3 dB of extra loss while keeping 2 km or 6 km reach (OCS optics).
  • Circulators and bidirectional links. A circulator lets transmit and receive share one fiber, roughly halving the switch ports and fibers needed per link.
  • WDM transceivers. Multi-wavelength optics (CWDM4-class) put more bandwidth through each switch port than parallel optics would.
  • Low reflections and fast re-link. Reflections from the switch path add MPI noise, and every reconfiguration forces the link to retrain, so CDR lock and link bring-up time become part of the design.

Technologies and market

Technology How it switches Notes
3D MEMS mirrors Tilting micro-mirrors Most deployed; 300 × 300 products announced for AI clusters
Liquid crystal Polarization steering, no moving parts 300 × 300 product announced in 2024
Piezoelectric beam steering Actuated collimators Specialist products
Robotic patch panel A robot moves fiber connectors Slow; for automation and reconfiguration, not dynamic switching
Silicon photonics On-chip switch matrices Emerging

One analyst firm forecast a $2.5B OCS market by 2029 in December 2025 and raised that outlook by more than 40% in February 2026, but notes that outside one hyperscaler, OCS was still at proof-of-concept and trial stage in early 2026 (forecast, update). Demonstrations at OFC 2026 paired 300 × 300 MEMS switches with standard optics for AI scale-up networks.

AI networks: pros and cons

Option Pros in an AI fabric Cons in an AI fabric Best fit
OCS layer in place of the electrical spine About 30% lower capex and 41% lower power in one hyperscaler's fabric; rate-agnostic, so it survives optics upgrades; rewires topology per job and routes around failed hosts Reconfigures in milliseconds, so it cannot switch packets; insertion loss eats optical budget and needs optics built for it; still at trial stage outside one hyperscaler in early 2026; needs SDN control and planning Large single-operator AI fabrics with predictable, job-shaped traffic
Electrical packet spine Per-packet load balancing and any-to-any connectivity; standard operations and tooling Power and optics for every spine port; upgraded with each lane-rate generation The default, and multi-tenant or general-purpose fabrics

Bottom line. OCS pays off for operators who control the whole stack and can schedule topology around jobs; everyone else keeps a packet spine and watches the trials.

Section 20 · Deep dives

Latency and timing

1 diagram · 2 min read
In this sectionA latency budgetFrequency and time over opticsWhere asymmetry hides in optical links

Optics add latency in two ways: propagation, about 5 ns per meter of standard fiber, and processing in FEC and DSPs, from a few ns (an inner code) through about 100 ns (KP4) to microseconds (coherent DSP plus soft-decision FEC). For time synchronization the problem is different: what matters is not how long the path is, but whether it is equally long in both directions.

A latency budget

Element Added latency Equivalent fiber
Standard single-mode fiber ~4.9–5 µs per km (~5 ns per m) —
Hollow-core fiber ~3.3–3.4 µs per km ~30% less than SMF
RS(544,514) KP4 FEC ~100 ns ~20 m
802.3dj inner FEC with interleaver ~15 ns ~3 m
800LR concatenated FEC ~55 ns (end-to-end target under 300 ns) ~11 m
PAM4 DSP in a retimed module Not consistently published; LPO removes it —
Coherent ZR-class DSP and soft-decision FEC Well above IM-DD; check the module datasheet —

Sources: KP4 latency, inner FEC latency, 800LR, 800LR target.

Inside a data center, FEC and DSP latency can rival propagation: 100 ns of FEC equals 20 m of fiber. That is why AI scale-up fabrics, which are latency-sensitive and short, care about lighter FEC, LPO and CPO.

Frequency and time over optics

  • SyncE (frequency). Each link's transmit clock is traced to a reference, and the receiver locks to the clock it recovers from the line, passing frequency hop by hop. Quality levels travel in ESMC messages (overview).
  • PTP (IEEE 1588, time). Two devices exchange timestamped messages in both directions and assume the forward and reverse delays are equal. Any difference, the asymmetry, appears as a time offset of half the asymmetry.

Where asymmetry hides in optical links

Source Size of the effect
Length mismatch in a duplex fiber pair ~2.5 ns of time error per meter of mismatch
BiDi optics (different wavelength each way) 1310/1550 nm pairs: ~1.6–2.5 ns of delay difference per km
Module DSP and FEC Transmit and receive latency can differ inside 50G-plus modules
Amplifiers and dispersion compensators Can add hundreds of ns on long-haul paths

Sources: asymmetry figures, module contributions.

For scale, the ITU-T G.8273.2 boundary-clock classes allow constant time error of 50 ns (class A), 20 ns (class B) and 10 ns (class C) (summary). A 4-meter patch-cord mismatch alone uses the whole class C budget. Industry groups have proposed storing calibrated transmit and receive delays in module memory so hosts can compensate.

Section 21 · Deep dives

Link encryption and physical-layer security

1 diagram · 3 min read
In this sectionMACsec in briefWhere encryption runs at 800G and 1.6TPhysical threats to the fiberAI networks: pros and cons

MACsec encrypts and authenticates Ethernet frames hop by hop at line rate, protecting what crosses the fiber between two devices. It does not stop anyone from tapping the fiber; it makes what they capture useless.

MACsec in brief

  • Standard. IEEE 802.1AE defines the frame protection; keys are negotiated by the MACsec Key Agreement protocol (MKA, part of IEEE 802.1X).
  • Ciphers. AES-GCM with 128- or 256-bit keys. The extended packet number (XPN) suites raise the frame counter to 2⁶⁴ so high-rate links do not rekey every few seconds: with small frames a 32-bit packet number wraps in about 5 minutes at 10G, under 30 s at 100G and about 7 s at 400G (802.1AEbw).
  • Overhead. A security tag and an integrity check value add 24–32 bytes per frame: about 2% of goodput at 1,500-byte frames but 20–30% at minimum-size frames (a 64-byte frame occupies 84 bytes on the wire, 116 with MACsec), which is why MACsec-heavy fabrics care about average frame size.
  • Scope. Hop by hop: each device decrypts, forwards and re-encrypts, so traffic is in clear inside each switch.

Where encryption runs at 800G and 1.6T

Location How Notes
Switch or NIC ASIC Inline MACsec engines on the ports Simplest when the silicon supports line rate on every port
External PHY or retimer MACsec in the PHY chip A 1.6T PHY with 256-bit MACsec was announced in 2022 to offload the ASIC (announcement)
Pluggable module DSP MACsec inside the optic OIF launched a project in May 2026 to write a technical white paper on MACsec support in 1.6T pluggables, driven by hyperscalers deploying shallow-buffer switches at every tier (OIF)
Coherent DCI modules AES-256-GCM in the coherent module Used for data-center interconnect, including a 2025 QKD demonstration

Physical threats to the fiber

  • Tapping. Bending a fiber tighter than its minimum bend radius leaks a little light, and a clip-on coupler can collect it without breaking the link. The victim sees only a small drop in received power.
  • Detection. Watch for unexplained steps in per-lane Rx power on a stable link (section 24), use OTDR or distributed fiber sensing to locate events, and keep physical security on panels and pathways. Research using machine learning on fiber-monitoring data flagged anomalies with about 97% F1 score, classified clip-on taps at about 98% accuracy and located them within about 0.2 m, on a laboratory testbed (study).
  • Quantum key distribution (QKD). Uses single photons to distribute keys with eavesdropping detection. A December 2025 demonstration ran QKD over 21.8 km of live commercial fiber between data centers, feeding AES-256-GCM encryption at 800G; it remains early-stage (demo).

AI networks: pros and cons

Option Pros in an AI fabric Cons in an AI fabric Best fit
Encrypt every hop (MACsec in switch and NIC silicon) Protects against taps anywhere, including inside shared or colocated facilities; runs at line rate in current silicon Adds power and some latency per port; key management across tens of thousands of links; not every switch supports it at full rate, which is why the OIF began a white paper on MACsec in 1.6T pluggables in May 2026 Shared or colocated facilities, and regulated workloads
Encrypt only links that leave the building Keeps cost, power and latency off the latency-sensitive back-end fabric while protecting the links most exposed to tapping In-building fiber relies on physical security alone Back-end fabrics inside a single, physically secure hall

Bottom line. Encrypt wherever fiber leaves your physical control; inside a secure hall, weigh per-hop MACsec against its power, latency and key-management cost.

Section 22 · Deep dives

Test and measurement

3 diagrams · 6 min read
In this sectionTest patternsTransmitter and receiver testsOMA, extinction ratio and TDECQ: reading a transmitter's numbersIn the lab and in the fieldReading an OTDR trace

Every number on an optics datasheet comes from a defined test: a specific pattern, reference receiver and reference equalizer. Knowing those definitions tells you what a spec promises and what it does not.

Test patterns

Pattern Length Used for
PRBS7, PRBS9 127 / 511 bits Quick NRZ checks, loopback tests
PRBS31 2³¹ − 1 bits NRZ BER testing; long and stressful
PRBS13Q 8,191 symbols PAM4 checks; easy to capture, mild stress
PRBS31Q 2³¹ − 1 symbols PAM4 BER testing; stressful but too long to capture whole
SSPRQ 65,535 symbols PAM4 transmitter tests such as TDECQ; a short pattern built from PRBS31 segments to keep the stress
QPRBS13 31,096 bits PAM4 backplane (Clause 94) testing

Sources: 802.3bs pattern discussion, pattern definitions. PAM4 patterns are Gray-coded.

Transmitter and receiver tests

  • Transmitter (TDECQ). The transmitter sends SSPRQ through a reference receiver (a 4th-order Bessel-Thomson filter) into a sampling scope, and software applies a reference equalizer, then adds Gaussian noise until the symbol error ratio reaches the target (4.8 × 10⁻⁴); TDECQ is the dB shortfall in tolerable noise against an ideal transmitter. At 100G per lane that equalizer is a 5-tap FFE; for 200G per lane, 802.3dj drafts use a 15-tap FFE, with later draft text adding one DFE tap (200G reference equalizer, draft discussion).
  • Receiver (stressed receiver sensitivity). A reference transmitter is deliberately impaired with ISI, jitter, interference and noise until its signal is as bad as the worst legal transmitter; the receiver under test must still reach the target BER (concept).
  • The pairing is the point. A link is guaranteed because the worst legal transmitter, after the worst legal channel, still meets the worst legal receiver. A module that passes TDECQ with little margin may still work today, but it has spent margin the rest of the link was counting on.

OMA, extinction ratio and TDECQ: reading a transmitter's numbers

Three numbers describe a PAM4 transmitter, and they are easy to confuse with the one DOM reports.

Average power is what DOM reports; OMA is what the link needs. A receiver decides on the swing between levels, not on the average. Outer optical modulation amplitude is the difference between the top and bottom levels, P3 − P0, and it relates to average power through the extinction ratio ER = P3 / P0:

OMAouter = 2 · Pavg · (ER − 1) / (ER + 1)

At the IEEE single-mode minimum ER of 3.5 dB (3.0 dB for SR PAM4 optics) the OMA is 1.2 dB below the average power; at 6 dB it is 0.8 dB above it. Two modules showing the same DOM transmit power can therefore differ by 2 dB in the quantity the far receiver cares about, and a transmitter that passes on "Tx power" can fail on OMA, which is why every transmitter and receiver limit in the standard is written in OMA.

TDECQ: the noise tolerance a transmitter gives away. Transmitter and dispersion eye closure quaternary asks a precise question. Through a reference receiver (a fourth-order Bessel-Thomson filter at half the symbol rate: 26.6 GHz for 53 GBd, 53.1 GHz for 106 GBd) and a reference equalizer (a 5-tap FFE at 100G per lane; 15 taps plus one DFE tap in the 802.3dj drafts for 200G per lane), how much Gaussian noise can be added to this transmitter's signal before the symbol error ratio reaches the target (4.8 × 10⁻⁴ for the 100G-per-lane PMDs, twice the 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ BER because a PAM4 symbol carries two bits; the 802.3dj inner-FEC PMDs use a higher target because the concatenated code tolerates a worse raw error ratio), compared with an ideal transmitter of the same OMA? That ratio in dB is TDECQ, and the limit is 3.4 dB for most 100G-per-lane PMDs (3.9 dB for 800GBASE-LR4, 4.5 dB for SR8). The equalizer is in the definition on purpose: eye closure that a receiver's equalizer can recover does not count, and closure that it cannot (noise, nonlinearity, jitter, residual ISI beyond the tap span) does. The pattern is SSPRQ, a short sequence chosen to exercise the worst PAM4 transitions, and the scope's bandwidth must exceed the filter's so that the filter can be applied numerically.

How the three interlock in the standard. The transmitter must launch at least a minimum OMA, and separately at least a minimum of OMA minus TDECQ; a transmitter with a worse TDECQ must launch more OMA to compensate, up to its maximum. The receiver's stressed sensitivity is measured with a signal whose stressed eye closure (SECQ) equals the TDECQ limit. Put together, the chain "minimum OMA at the TDECQ limit, minus the maximum channel loss, meets the stressed sensitivity measured at that same SECQ" is the guarantee behind the reach figure, with only 0.1–0.8 dB left over (DR4: −2.2 + 3.4 − 3.0 = −1.8 against −1.9 dBm). An optic that reports a TDECQ of 3.3 dB is compliant; it has also spent the whole allowance that the receiver, the fiber and the connectors were assuming would be shared.

What replaced what. NRZ-era optics were judged by transmitter and dispersion penalty (TDP) and an eye mask; PAM4 dropped the mask because a PAM4 eye through a real receiver is never open without equalization, and replaced TDP with TDECQ (the Q is for quaternary). Other transmitter numbers that still matter: relative intensity noise (RIN, in dB/Hz, with an OMA-referenced variant in the PMD tables), side-mode suppression ratio (SMSR, at least 30 dB, so that a DFB is single-wavelength), and the transmitter's wavelength and drift, which decide whether a WDM lane stays in its box (section 6).

Sources: TDECQ method, reference equalizer, 802.3dj TECQ and TDECQ equalizer, SR8 extinction ratio and TDECQ.

In the lab and in the field

Instrument What it answers
BERT (pattern generator and error detector) What is the BER, lane by lane?
Sampling oscilloscope Eye quality, TDECQ, OMA, extinction ratio
Optical spectrum analyzer Wavelengths, side-mode suppression, OSNR
Power meter and light source True link loss
OTDR Where the loss and reflections are along the fiber
Inspection scope Is the end face clean and undamaged?

In the field, a module's built-in PRBS generator, checker and loopbacks (section 12) stand in for a BERT.

Reading an OTDR trace

An OTDR sends light pulses and plots the light scattered back over distance. The trace slopes down with fiber attenuation; events interrupt it (application note).

  • Reflective events (spike plus step): connectors, mechanical splices, breaks and the open fiber end.
  • Non-reflective events (step only): fusion splices and bends. Bends lose more at longer wavelengths, so testing at two wavelengths separates bends from splices.
  • Dead zones. After a strong reflection the detector is blinded: the event dead zone is the minimum distance to see a second event; the attenuation dead zone is the distance until loss can be measured again. A launch fiber moves the first connector out of the dead zone, and a receive fiber lets you measure the last one.
  • Ghosts. Echoes between strong reflections appear at multiples of a real event's distance, with no loss. Index-matching gel, shorter pulses or lower power, and a range of 1.5–2× the fiber length help expose them, since a ghost then lands beyond the fiber end where no real event can be (ghost events).
Section 23 · Deep dives

Interoperability, qualification and reliability

1 diagram · 2 min read
In this sectionThe bathtub curveTemperature gradesEnvironmental qualification (Telcordia GR-468)FIT, MTTF and what they mean for a fleetThird-party optics and compatibilityQualifying a new optic for a fleet

An optic that meets its datasheet can still fail in your network. Temperature grade, environmental qualification, burn-in, firmware and host compatibility decide how it behaves in a hot switch for five years.

The bathtub curve

Failure rate over a population's life has three phases: early failures from manufacturing defects (screened out by burn-in), a long flat period of random failures (the number a FIT rate describes), and a rising wear-out phase, which for optics is mostly laser aging.

Temperature grades

Grade Case temperature Typical use
Commercial 0 to 70 °C Data-center switches with controlled airflow
Extended Varies by vendor (typically up to 85 °C) Harsher indoor sites
Industrial −40 to 85 °C Outdoor cabinets, mobile and edge sites

The rating is module case temperature, not room temperature. A commercial module in a poorly cooled port can exceed 70 °C in a 25 °C room (grades).

Environmental qualification (Telcordia GR-468)

GR-468 is the common reliability standard for optoelectronic devices. One vendor's 400G DR4 report shows how it is applied (report, test categories):

Test Example condition
Mechanical shock 500 g, 1 ms
Vibration 20 g, 20–2,000 Hz
Thermal shock Screening temperature cycling is −40 to 70 or 85 °C for 20 cycles; GR-468 thermal shock proper is 0 to 100 °C liquid to liquid (MIL-STD-883 Method 1011), and qualification cycling runs 100–1,000 cycles
Temperature cycling −40 to 70/85 °C, hundreds of cycles
Damp heat 85 °C and 85% relative humidity
High-temperature operating life 2,000 hours at 70 °C case
ESD Handling robustness

FIT, MTTF and what they mean for a fleet

FIT is failures per billion device-hours; in the flat part of the bathtub, MTTF = 10⁹ ÷ FIT hours (definition). Fleet arithmetic makes it concrete:

Expected failures per year = Nmodules × 8,760 h × FIT × 10−9

At an illustrative 100 FIT, a 100,000-module fleet expects about 88 failures a year, nearly two a week. In an AI cluster, each one can interrupt a training job, which is why section 24's early-warning telemetry matters.

Third-party optics and compatibility

  • Coding. Hosts read vendor name, part number and compliance codes from the module's memory map (section 12) and may refuse, warn on, or fully support a module based on them.
  • Firmware. Modules run firmware that is upgraded through CMIS; module firmware versions belong in change control.
  • Interop events. Industry plugfests and OIF interoperability demonstrations test multi-vendor combinations before they reach networks.

Qualifying a new optic for a fleet

  • Host accepts the module, power class and every application (speed and breakout mode) you will use
  • Multi-hour PRBS or traffic soak shows the expected pre-FEC BER on every lane, against several host ports
  • Worst-case thermal: hottest port, lowest fan speed, highest inlet temperature
  • DOM readings checked against a power meter
  • Firmware upgrade and rollback work in place
  • Breakout and interop tested against the far-end optics actually deployed
  • LPO or LRO modules qualified per host and module pairing
  • Baselines recorded so fleet telemetry starts from known-good values
Section 24 · Deep dives

Fleet telemetry and predictive analytics

1 diagram · 2 min read
In this sectionWhat to collectSignals that predict failuresMaking it predictive

At fleet scale, optics are run on data: stream every module's diagnostics and FEC counters, baseline every link at turn-up, and act on trends before a link flaps. Absolute DOM values are only accurate to a few dB, but changes against a link's own baseline are precise and early.

What to collect

Signal OpenConfig path Subscription Why
Per-lane Rx power /components/component/transceiver/physical-channels/channel/state/input-power/instant SAMPLE Contamination, bends, fiber faults, taps
Per-lane Tx power .../physical-channels/channel/state/output-power/instant SAMPLE Transmitter health
Per-lane laser bias .../physical-channels/channel/state/laser-bias-current/instant SAMPLE Laser aging
Module pre-FEC BER /components/component/transceiver/state/pre-fec-ber SAMPLE Optical-segment margin
Port FEC counters /interfaces/interface/ethernet/state/counters/fec-corrected-blocks and fec-uncorrectable-blocks SAMPLE End-to-end margin and frame loss
Port pre-FEC BER /interfaces/interface/ethernet/state/pre-fec-ber SAMPLE Margin seen by the host
Link state /interfaces/interface/state/oper-status ON_CHANGE Flaps
Coherent quality /terminal-device/logical-channels/channel/otn/state/q-value, esnr, pre-fec-ber SAMPLE DCI margin (section 18)

Sources: openconfig-platform-transceiver, openconfig-if-ethernet (FEC counters and pre-FEC BER were added in late 2025). Power and bias leaves also offer avg, min and max.

Subscription modes. gNMI streams with SAMPLE (at a fixed interval, optionally suppressing unchanged values with a heartbeat) or ON_CHANGE (on events) (gNMI spec). A reasonable starting point is analog values every 30–60 s, FEC counters every 10–30 s, and link state on change. An example with the open-source gnmic client:

gnmic -a leaf1:6030 subscribe --mode stream --stream-mode sample --sample-interval 30s \
  --path /interfaces/interface/ethernet/state/counters/fec-corrected-blocks

Signals that predict failures

Pattern Likely cause Action
Laser bias rising while Tx power holds steady Laser aging: the control loop pushes more current for the same light Schedule a swap before end of life
Rx power steps down on one lane after maintenance Contaminated or damaged connector Inspect and clean that path
Slow Rx power drift on many links sharing a trunk Fiber plant: bend, crushed cable, cassette Inspect the shared path
Pre-FEC BER rising with Rx power steady Transmitter quality, reflections (MPI), or host channel Compare both ends; swap one element
Corrected FEC bursts that track temperature Thermal or airflow limit Check fans, port placement, grade
Flaps with clean optics and steady power Firmware, host SerDes or power Check firmware cohorts and host logs
Unexplained small Rx power drop on a stable, untouched link Possible tap or physical disturbance Investigate (section 21)

Making it predictive

  • Baseline every link at turn-up, per lane and both ends, and alert on change rather than absolute value.
  • Compare cohorts. Group by part number, vendor, firmware and manufacturing lot; one bad batch shows up as a cohort trend long before individual alarms.
  • Correlate. Both ends of a link, links sharing a trunk or panel, and links on the same switch tell you whether the cause is the module, the fiber or the host.
  • Watch the FEC histogram tail (section 5): codewords drifting toward the correction limit are the earliest sign of lost margin.
  • Automate the response. In AI fabrics, drain a degrading link before it flaps and stalls a training job, then schedule cleaning or a swap during a quiet window.
Section 25 · Deep dives

Silicon photonics and optical engines

7 diagrams · 24 min read
In this sectionWhy silicon, and what it cannot doThe building blocksModulators: Mach-Zehnder, ring, EAM and TFLNGetting light onto the chip: lasersGetting light off the chip: fiber couplingInside an optical engineEngines in 2026 productsOptical I/O chiplets for scale-upManufacturing, test and yieldLimits and next steps: 400G per laneAI networks: pros and consWhat it means in operations

An optical engine is the part of every optical link that turns electrical lanes into light and back: a photonic chip, the electronics that drive and read it, a light source and a fiber attach, built as one subassembly. Section 10 covers where the engine sits; this section covers what is inside it, and why those choices show up in power, reliability and troubleshooting.

Most engines built in 2026 are silicon photonic. An analyst firm expects modules using silicon photonic modulators to pass half of transceiver sales in 2026, up from 10% in 2018 and a third in 2024 (LightCounting). The reason is manufacturing: the optical circuit is built on CMOS-style wafers, one laser can feed several lanes, and every die can be tested before assembly.

Read the transmit path left to right and the receive path right to left. Each part has a subsection below: lasers, modulators, couplers and fiber attach, and the electronic IC.

Why silicon, and what it cannot do

Silicon photonics borrows CMOS manufacturing: the same wafers, lithography and process control, so thousands of identical optical circuits come off one 200 or 300 mm wafer. The price is four physical gaps, and every engine design is a set of workarounds for them.

  • The platform. Silicon-on-insulator (SOI): a 220 nm silicon layer on about 2 µm of buried oxide, with single-mode waveguides about 450–500 nm wide (foundry review). Silicon's refractive index (3.48) is far above the oxide's (1.44), so light is held tightly and a waveguide can turn a corner in a few micrometers. That density is the platform's main strength.
  • Gap 1: no laser. Silicon has an indirect bandgap, so it emits light very inefficiently (review). Every engine borrows its light from an indium phosphide (InP) laser, attached in one of four ways (see lasers, below).
  • Gap 2: no fast linear electro-optic effect. Silicon's crystal is centrosymmetric, so it has no Pockels effect. Modulators instead move free carriers, and 10¹⁷ carriers per cm³ shift the index by only about 10⁻⁴ (modulator review). A weak effect means long devices or resonant ones, and several volts of drive.
  • Gap 3: transparent at 1310 and 1550 nm. Silicon cannot detect the light it guides, so photodiodes use germanium grown on the silicon.
  • Gap 4: heat moves everything. Silicon's index changes by about 1.86 × 10⁻⁴ per kelvin, roughly 18 times the oxide's (thermal study). Broadband devices barely notice; resonant devices drift about 0.1 nm per kelvin and need heaters and control loops.

One more mismatch shapes the whole engine. The guided mode is about 0.5 × 0.3 µm, while standard single-mode fiber's mode is 9.2 µm across at 1310 nm (coupling review, fiber spec). Bridging that 20-fold gap is the coupling problem.

At the same scale the waveguide's light is a speck inside the fiber's. The high index contrast that makes silicon circuits dense is the same thing that makes coupling to fiber hard.

Silicon is one of four photonic platforms, and real engines often combine them.

Platform What it does well What it lacks Where it is used in 2026
Silicon (SOI) CMOS-scale wafers, dense circuits, germanium detectors, wafer-level test Lasers; modulators much beyond 100 GHz DR4/DR8 pluggables, NPO and CPO engines, optical I/O
Indium phosphide (InP) Lasers, EMLs, optical amplifiers, modulators beyond 100 GHz Small, costly wafers; less integration The light source for every platform; EML transceivers; coherent
Silicon nitride on silicon Low loss (below 0.5 dB/cm for LPCVD nitride), low thermal drift Passive only Filters, multiplexers and low-loss routing layers
Thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) Pockels effect: more than 100 GHz at low drive voltage Young supply chain 200G–400G-per-lane modulators; coherent

Sources: foundry platform review, InP EML above 110 GHz, TFLN at 140 GHz.

The building blocks

A photonic IC is built from a small library of devices, most of them passive. Foundries ship them as characterized cells in a process design kit, and an engine designer mostly wires them together.

Block Job in an engine Typical figure Watch-out
Strip and rib waveguides Route light between devices 1–2 dB/cm (strip); 0.7–1 dB/cm (rib) Negligible over the few millimeters of a DR engine
Splitters (Y-junction, MMI, directional coupler) Share one laser across lanes; form modulator arms Under 0.3 dB excess loss for a good Y-junction Each 1:2 split also halves the light per lane (3 dB)
Wavelength multiplexers (AWG, echelle grating, cascaded Mach-Zehnder) Combine CWDM or LAN-WDM lanes onto one fiber 1.5–2.6 dB insertion loss in published designs FR and LR engines pay it twice (mux and demux); DR engines skip it
Polarization splitter-rotator Turn the fiber's random polarization into the chip's single mode 1.2–1.5 dB insertion loss Needed on receive, because SOI waveguides are strongly polarization-dependent
Thermo-optic phase shifter (heater) Bias MZMs, lock rings, trim filters About 20–25 mW per π of phase shift Microseconds, not picoseconds: for tuning, never for data
Germanium photodiode Detect light 0.8–1.0 A/W at 1310 nm (the quantum limit is 1.06 A/W), typically 0.7–1.0 A/W at 1550 nm; 50–70 GHz in foundry kits Bandwidth and dark current set the receive limit
Monitor photodiode (tap) Feed the bias, lock and power control loops Taps a small fraction of the light Source of the per-lane telemetry an engine reports

Sources: foundry review, foundry efforts review, Y-junction, AWG, echelle, splitter-rotator, phase shifters, germanium photodiodes.

A DR engine is the simplest circuit: one laser split across several modulators, each with its own output fiber, and one photodiode per receive fiber. An FR4 engine adds a multiplexer and a demultiplexer. Coherent engines add the IQ modulator and 90° hybrid from section 8, which are often built in silicon too.

Modulators: Mach-Zehnder, ring, EAM and TFLN

The modulator sets an engine's bandwidth, drive voltage, size and temperature behavior, and 2026 products split along it. Mach-Zehnders dominate pluggables and one CPO family; micro-rings drive another CPO family and most optical I/O chiplets; electro-absorption modulators appear where III-V material is bonded onto silicon; thin-film lithium niobate is the bandwidth bet for 400G per lane.

  • Mach-Zehnder modulator (MZM). Light splits into two arms, a reverse-biased PN junction in each arm shifts its phase, and the arms recombine and interfere, turning phase into amplitude. Because silicon's effect is weak, the arms are a few millimeters long: one foundry kit lists a Vπ of 5.9 V for a 4 mm device and 29–40 GHz of bandwidth (platform review). Long devices need traveling-wave electrodes, and the drive swing exceeds what advanced CMOS supplies deliver, so drivers often use SiGe processes. The reward is a broadband, temperature-tolerant device that works at any wavelength in the band. With on-chip equalization, one 2025 result reached 90 GHz for 200G per lane (OFC 2025).
  • Micro-ring modulator (MRM). A ring a few to ten micrometers in radius sits beside a bus waveguide. At resonance, light couples into the ring and the bus transmission dips; a PN junction in the ring shifts the resonance, so a laser parked on the dip's slope sees large intensity changes. Rings are tiny (a few hundred µm²) with only a few femtofarads of capacitance, so modulation costs a few femtojoules per bit (ring result), and research devices exceed 110 GHz (2025 result). Each ring acts on one wavelength only, which makes dense WDM natural: several rings on one bus, each tuned to its own wavelength. The cost is temperature: the resonance moves about 0.1 nm per kelvin, and a drift of more than about 1 K can break the link without a heater and a feedback lock (thermal study).
  • Electro-absorption modulator (EAM). An electric field shifts a material's absorption edge, so the device absorbs more or less light at the laser's wavelength. Germanium-silicon EAMs are compact and reach about 50 GHz but work in the C and L bands (GeSi EAM, review); O-band EAMs use III-V quantum wells bonded onto silicon. The absorption edge moves with temperature, about 0.8 nm/°C in one GeSi study (study).
  • Thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN). Lithium niobate has the Pockels effect that silicon lacks, so a thin film bonded onto an insulator or onto silicon gives a fast, linear, low-voltage MZM. A 2025 demonstration used 140 GHz TFLN modulators for 8 × 448G over 2 km (OFC 2025). Its manufacturing base is younger than silicon's or InP's.

The MZM's curve depends only on drive voltage, so it works at any wavelength. The ring's dip sits at one wavelength, and heat moves it the same way the data signal does; a drift of about 1 K is enough to break the link, which is why every ring needs a lock loop.

Modulator Size Bandwidth Drive Temperature behavior Wavelengths Used in
Silicon MZM Millimeters 30–50 GHz in foundry kits; 90 GHz with equalization (record) Several volts; SiGe drivers common Tolerant Any in the band Most pluggables; one CPO family
Micro-ring About 10 µm radius Over 110 GHz in research; 200G PAM4 in production About 2 V peak-to-peak Drifts about 0.1 nm/K; needs a lock loop One per ring, so WDM-friendly One CPO family; optical I/O
EAM (GeSi, or III-V on silicon) Tens of micrometers About 50 GHz (GeSi); 400G-per-lane III-V demos About 2 V peak-to-peak Absorption edge moves about 0.8 nm/°C GeSi: C/L band; III-V: O-band III-V-on-silicon DR8 PICs; optical I/O
TFLN Millimeters Over 100 GHz (140 GHz demo) Low Vπ Stable Any in the band 400G-per-lane candidates; coherent

Both MZMs and rings are nonlinear: an MZM follows a cosine and a ring follows its resonance curve, so PAM4's outer levels compress unless the driver or DSP pre-distorts them. That is the level-linearity (RLM) failure from section 2, created inside the engine.

Try it: the Modulators tab of the Optics Bench lab puts an MZM and a ring side by side. Move the bias, drive swing, laser offset and temperature, switch the ring's lock off, and watch the four light levels, OMA and RLM respond.

Getting light onto the chip: lasers

Every silicon engine gets its light from an InP laser. How that laser is attached decides coupling loss, thermal design, whether the laser can be tested before assembly, and what gets replaced in the field. There are four approaches; 2026 products mostly use the first two, and heterogeneous lasers also ship.

Moving down and right, the laser gets closer to the waveguide: less coupling loss and assembly, but more heat in the chip and less freedom to test or replace the laser on its own.

Approach How it works Strengths Weaknesses Status in 2026
External laser source Laser in its own module, often a front-panel ELSFP; light arrives over polarization-maintaining fiber Cool location; replaceable; testable alone; shareable across lanes Extra connector and fiber loss; needs high-power lasers; eye-safety controls Standard in CPO; defined by the OIF ELSFP agreement
Hybrid (flip-chip or micro-optic) Known-good InP laser die placed beside or on the PIC, butt-coupled or coupled through lenses Lasers tested before assembly; mature process Sub-micron alignment for every die Most silicon photonic pluggables; tens of millions of units a year
Heterogeneous III-V material bonded onto the silicon wafer, then patterned into lasers aligned to the waveguides Sub-dB coupling; wafer-level test; many lasers per chip Heat removal and thermal-expansion mismatch Shipping: one vendor reported over 32M on-chip lasers by mid-2024; another platform passed GR-468 in 2025
Monolithic Laser material, often quantum dots, grown directly on silicon Lowest assembly cost, eventually Crystal defects and lifetime still being solved Research and development: 300 mm wafer-scale demos in 2025

Sources: integration review, heterogeneous volumes, GR-468 qualification, 300 mm lasers, quantum-dot lasers.

  • One laser, several lanes. A continuous-wave laser can be split across lanes, which is silicon's structural advantage over one-EML-per-lane designs. 800G DR8 PICs use 2 lasers for 8 lanes (product); 1.6T DR8 designs use 1 to 4 lasers (MZM design, EAM design, TFLN design); and one CPO switch feeds 4 transmit lanes from each laser (developer blog).
  • Sharing needs power. Each 1:2 split halves the light per lane, so shared lasers are high-power parts: 100 mW uncooled or 300 mW cooled DFBs for pluggables (laser), and 400 mW-class lasers at 50–55 °C for CPO (CPO laser).
  • ELSFP. The OIF's ELSFP-02.0 (January 2025) defines the front-panel laser module: a blind-mate MT-ferrule connector carrying 4 or 8 polarization-maintaining fibers, power classes from 11 to 26 dBm per wavelength per fiber, 1311 nm or CWDM4 wavelengths, and eye-safety rules that cut power within 250 ms if an unprotected optical path opens (spec). A separate OIF agreement (September 2024) manages ELSFPs through CMIS (OIF agreements).
  • Multi-wavelength sources. Ring-based dense WDM needs many precisely spaced wavelengths, because a ring's resonance is only 20–40 GHz wide (feature). The CW-WDM MSA (2021) defines 8-, 16- and 32-wavelength O-band grids for such sources (release). 2026 products include a 16-wavelength source built to that MSA (product) and an 8-wavelength comb ELSFP with more than 1 W of output (report).
  • Why lasers move away from heat. Laser wear-out speeds up with temperature. One published model uses an activation energy of 0.5 eV, which works out to roughly 1.6–1.9× faster aging per 10 °C (model); the familiar "halves every 10 °C" rule is not universal (analysis). Putting the laser in a cool front-panel module, away from a switch ASIC, is the CPO answer.

Getting light off the chip: fiber coupling

Matching a 9 µm fiber mode to a sub-micron waveguide is where silicon engines lose the most light, and where assembly yield is won or lost. Two coupler types exist; they trade testability against loss and bandwidth.

A grating coupler sends light up out of the chip's surface, so a probe can reach it anywhere on the wafer. An edge coupler sends light straight out of the chip's side through a taper, losing less light over a wider band but needing the fiber aligned five times more precisely.

Grating coupler Edge coupler
How it works An etched grating diffracts light up out of the chip toward a fiber tilted a few degrees from vertical A taper at the chip's edge expands the mode to match a fiber held in a V-groove
Loss per coupler About 2.5–4.5 dB in standard foundry kits; under 1 dB in optimized designs About 1–2 dB per facet in foundry kits; under 1 dB in optimized designs
Optical bandwidth Roughly 20–40 nm (1 dB) About 100 nm
Polarization Sensitive; 2D gratings handle both polarizations Largely insensitive
Alignment tolerance (1 dB penalty) About ±2.5 µm About ±0.5 µm at a bare facet; ±1–2 µm with a spot-size converter
Wafer-level test Yes, anywhere on the surface Needs an exposed facet; automated edge-coupled wafer test now exists

Sources: foundry review, coupling review, edge coupler, grating coupler.

  • Fiber attach. Fibers sit in glass V-groove arrays at 127 or 250 µm pitch, fixed with UV-cured, index-matched epoxy (coupling review). In CPO, budget about 1 dB per V-groove joint and about 1 dB more for a detachable joint (foundry quote).
  • Detachable connectors. Permanent pigtails made CPO assembly fragile and engines hard to rework, so 2025–26 brought detachable fiber-to-chip connectors: glass-waveguide edge couplers that drop into the chip's V-grooves (announcement), expanded-beam connectors with under 1.5 dB loss after re-insertion (announcement), and connectors carrying up to 50 fibers at 127 µm pitch (product).
  • Yield. In one research study, edge couplers lost about 1.5 dB per fiber and optical assembly yield was 75.5% (study). Every engine multiplies the yields of its dies and fibers, which is why test before assembly matters (see manufacturing, below).

Inside an optical engine

An engine joins four things: the photonic IC (PIC), the electronic IC (EIC), the light source and the fiber attach. The PIC carries modulators, photodiodes, couplers, heaters and monitor taps. The EIC carries modulator drivers, transimpedance amplifiers (TIAs) and the control loops that hold modulator bias, ring lock and laser power. How the EIC meets the PIC decides much of the engine's energy per bit.

  • Monolithic. Transistors and photonics share one chip. One 45 nm-class platform does this at 0.5 Tb/s per fiber (platform). There are no bond parasitics, but the electronics are tied to an older CMOS node.
  • Wire bond. EIC beside PIC, joined by bond wires. Simple and cheap, but each wire's inductance limits bandwidth and costs drive energy (packaging comparison).
  • Flip-chip or 2.5D. The EIC is flipped onto the PIC, or both sit on an interposer, joined by micro-bumps. Shorter connections cut the parasitics.
  • 3D hybrid bonding. The EIC is bonded face-to-face onto the PIC with copper-to-copper bonds at micrometer pitch, the lowest-parasitic option. The catch is that EIC heat flows straight into the photonics, which matters for rings (packaging comparison, analysis). One foundry's 3D-stacked engine platform entered volume production in 2026, and both major CPO switch families build on it (report, product).

Where the energy goes. One vendor's published model splits link energy as below (paper). It is a model from a CPO vendor, not a measurement, but its shape matches product claims: the module's DSP disappears first, then 3D stacking shrinks everything else.

Architecture Host SerDes (pJ/bit) Module or engine (pJ/bit) Laser (pJ/bit) Total (pJ/bit)
Retimed pluggable 5 16 Inside the module 21
LPO 5 8 Inside the module 13
2.5D CPO 5 4.7 2.3 12
3D-stacked CPO 2 1.2 1.1 4.3

Product claims land in the same range. One MZM-based 51.2T CPO switch claims 5.5 W per 800G (about 6.9 pJ/bit) against 14 W for pluggables, and its 102.4T successor claims 3.5 W per 800G (about 4.4 pJ/bit) (product brief, analysis). The light itself is not free: one design study puts an external laser source at about 18 W per 6.4T, about 70% of it in laser chips and their coolers at roughly 30% wall-plug efficiency (study).

  • Control loops are part of the engine. MZMs need bias control, rings need lock loops (a monitor photodiode plus a heater driven by the EIC), and lasers need power control. These loops are also where engine telemetry comes from.
  • Cooling. In CPO the engines share a package with a switch ASIC, and production systems liquid-cool both (developer blog).

Engines in 2026 products

Pluggables and CPO switches now combine the same building blocks in different ways. Two CPO families are in or entering volume: an MZM-based family from a switch-silicon vendor and a ring-based family from a GPU vendor. Their 2026 generations both use 3D-stacked engines from the same foundry; they differ mainly in the modulator (analyst note).

Product Engines Lanes Modulator Light source Claimed power Status
800G DR8 pluggable PIC 1 × 800G 8 × 100G MZM 2 lasers on the PIC — Product
1.6T DR8 pluggable PIC (silicon) 1 × 1.6T 8 × 200G MZM 2 CW lasers — Product
1.6T DR8 PIC (III-V on silicon) 1 × 1.6T 8 × 200G EAM 4 DFB lasers plus 8 optical amplifiers Under 2.7 W for the PIC Sampling since March 2025
1.6T DR8 reference design (TFLN) 1 × 1.6T 8 × 200G TFLN MZM 1 laser 20 W, fully retimed module Demonstrated March 2026
51.2T CPO switch (MZM family) 8 × 6.4T 64 × 100G per engine MZM Front-panel laser modules 5.5 W per 800G vs 14 W pluggable Deployed
102.4T CPO switch (MZM family) 16 × 6.4T, 3D-stacked 200G lanes MZM Field-replaceable ELSFPs 3.5 W per 800G Sampling since October 2025
102.4T CPO Ethernet switch (ring family) 32 × 3.2T per ASIC 16 Tx + 16 Rx × 200G per engine Micro-ring 16 laser modules of 8 lasers; 4 lanes per laser 9 W per 1.6T port vs 30 W pluggable Full production August 2026
115.2T InfiniBand CPO system (ring family) 4 ASICs, each 6 subassemblies of three 1.6T engines 8 × 200G per engine Micro-ring 18 laser modules 3.95 kW vs 7.0 kW for a standard switch Customer deliveries 2026

Sources: 800G PIC, 1.6T silicon PIC, III-V PIC, TFLN reference, 51.2T brief, 102.4T MZM switch, ring-family engines, ring-family production, customer system. Power figures are vendor claims.

  • Read the laser counts. The ring family's "4× fewer lasers" claim is made at data-center level against legacy designs with one laser per lane; per engine it means 8 lasers in each external module serving 32 transmit lanes (developer blog).
  • Socketed engines. An MSA formed in March 2026 defines a socketed 6.4T engine with 32 × 200G electrical lanes and a roadmap to 12.8T and 448G lanes (MSA). The OIF's NPO project (section 10) defines 6.4T and 12.8T engine modules with liquid cooling and laser-source definitions (OIF meeting report).
  • Volume. An analyst firm reported in July 2026 that both CPO families are starting volume ramps, with broad volume expected in 2027–28 (TrendForce).

Optical I/O chiplets for scale-up

Optical I/O puts the engine inside the accelerator's package, so GPU-to-GPU and GPU-to-memory links leave the package as light. The goal is copper-like energy and latency with fiber's reach, so a scale-up domain can grow past one rack. These engines differ from switch CPO in three ways: many slower wavelengths per fiber instead of a few fast lanes, a UCIe die-to-die interface instead of a long-reach SerDes, and little or no FEC so that latency stays in nanoseconds.

  • Ring-based dense WDM. A multi-wavelength laser feeds a bus of micro-rings, each modulating one wavelength; at the far end, drop rings each pick one wavelength onto a photodiode. One UCIe optical chiplet carries 8 Tb/s using a 16-wavelength external laser (announcement); its 2025 engineering validation reported more than 5 dB of margin across hundreds of links and no BER change from 30 to 80 °C (validation). Another vendor reports 1.6 Tb/s per fiber from 16 wavelengths of 112G PAM4 (announcement).
  • EAM-based fabric. One design uses EAMs, chosen for thermal stability, at about 2.4 pJ/bit for electronics plus 0.7 pJ/bit for the laser, and 16 Tb/s per chiplet (details). A large DSP vendor bought the company for $3.25B upfront, closing in February 2026, and expects revenue from fiscal 2028 (announcement, close).
  • Photonic interposers. A 3D active photonic interposer offers 114 Tb/s over 256 fibers with 8-wavelength WDM (announcement).
  • Standards and forecasts. The UALink consortium says optical reach extension needs only PHY-level changes (white paper). The OCI MSA, formed in March 2026, has published a 200G-per-direction bidirectional optical PHY for scale-up links, built on ring modulators and external lasers (section 27). An OCP initiative launched in August 2026 is writing open optical engine specifications aimed below 5 pJ/bit, with a base specification due in Q4 2026 (report). One analyst firm expects only 10–15% of scale-up interconnects to move to NPO or CPO by 2030–31, so copper keeps most in-rack links (LightCounting).

Product figures in this subsection are vendor claims.

Manufacturing, test and yield

Silicon photonics promises semiconductor economics, and in 2026 the constraint moved from technology to capacity. An analyst firm named optical engine yield, silicon photonics fab precision and 2.5D/3D packaging capacity as the bottlenecks for CPO (TrendForce).

  • Foundries and design kits. Commercial foundries offer process design kits (PDKs) with characterized modulators, germanium photodiodes, couplers and V-grooves on 200 and 300 mm wafers (300 mm kit). Capacity grew sharply in 2026: one foundry entered 300 mm high-volume production in March and plans to more than quadruple output by 2027 (announcement), another committed about $3B to 300 mm silicon photonics (report), and a third licensed a 300 mm research platform with ring modulators and GeSi EAMs, with risk production in 2026–27 (announcement).
  • Test before assembly. Grating couplers let a prober test every die optically before dicing, and edge-coupled wafer test is now automated at about 1.5 dB per facet and under 5 s per die (vendor). Early test matters because an engine stacks a PIC, an EIC, lasers and fibers: one bad part scraps the assembly, and in CPO it can scrap a switch package. That is the argument for known-good die, detachable fibers and external lasers.
  • Process variation. Waveguide width variation of about 5 nm and thickness variation of about 2 nm can move a ring's resonance by 2–12 nm, which heaters must then pull back, up to about 9 nm (study). MZMs are far more tolerant of the same variation.
  • Where the money goes. One analyst firm puts packaging and assembly at about 25% of a datacom pluggable's value and about 50% of a CPO engine's in 2026–27, falling to about 35% by 2031 (secondary report).
  • Market. Silicon photonics was about a third of a $4B optical chip market in 2025 and is forecast at 42% of $15B by 2031, while InP lasers fall from 58% to 46% of it (LightCounting).

Limits and next steps: 400G per lane

400G per lane roughly doubles the bandwidth a modulator must deliver, and silicon's weak electro-optic effect makes that the platform's hardest test. As of October 2026 no technology has won, and IEEE P802.3dv had not chosen a modulation format (study group status).

  • What each format asks. One IEEE contribution compared PAM4 at 212.5 GBd (106 GHz Nyquist), PAM6 at 170 GBd (85 GHz) and PAM8 at 141.7 GBd (71 GHz); PAM8 tolerated multipath interference about 7 dB worse than PAM4 (contribution). An industry panel called PAM4 feasible and the simplest, lowest-power choice (panel).
Technology Best evidence as of October 2026 Status
Silicon MZM 400G PAM4 post-deadline paper at OFC 2026; a 420G PAM4 eye on a production foundry MZM Demonstrations; the foundry says it extends silicon "another generation"
InP EML Over 110 GHz bandwidth; a 400G-per-lane DSP shown with EMLs; 1.6T DR4 prototypes (March 2026) Prototypes; one laser vendor calls it the most commercially viable for volume
