  • Rings scale by wavelength, not by baud. One foundry's roadmap takes ring engines from 200G per lane at 0.5 Tb/s per millimeter of chip edge in 2026 to 400G with several wavelengths per fiber at 4 Tb/s per millimeter by 2030 (roadmap report).
  • Energy roadmaps. Another foundry targets engines at about 5 pJ/bit in 2027 and about 2 pJ/bit by 2029 as it moves from thermo-compression to hybrid bonding (same report).

AI networks: pros and cons

Option Pros in an AI fabric Cons in an AI fabric Best fit
Silicon photonics One continuous-wave laser can feed several lanes (1 to 4 lasers for a 1.6T DR8); wafer-scale test and CMOS-scale volume; the same platform serves pluggables, LPO, NPO and CPO; almost all 1.6T DR-type optics shipping in 2026 use it Needs an attached or external InP laser; coupling loss at the fiber; silicon modulators are stretched at 400G per lane, so TFLN, BTO and EAM add-ons are candidates 1.6T DR8 pluggables and CPO or NPO engines
InP EML Over 110 GHz of bandwidth; proven at 200G per lane and shown in 400G-per-lane prototypes; strong for FR and LR One laser per lane; smaller, costlier wafers FR4 and LR4, and early 400G-per-lane modules
Multimode VCSEL Lowest cost and power; relaxed alignment Multimode reach only, about 30 m at 1.6T In-row links and active optical cables

Bottom line. Silicon photonics is the AI volume platform because one laser serves several lanes and the same engine scales into CPO and NPO; EMLs hold the longer-reach and first 400G-per-lane slots.

What it means in operations

Silicon photonic engines change fault patterns in three ways: lasers are shared, resonant modulators depend on control loops, and in CPO the field-replaceable unit shrinks to the laser module.

  • Shared lasers create correlated failures. When one laser feeds four lanes, a failing laser or a dirty laser-input connector degrades all four together. Group lane alarms by the laser that feeds them before chasing lanes one at a time. In a DR8 pluggable with two lasers, one failure takes out half the module, which in a 2 × 800G breakout is a whole port.
  • Control loops create temperature-linked faults. A ring that loses its lock drops its lane at once, and lock loss tends to follow fast thermal events such as fan, coolant or load swings. Where the engine exposes heater power, lock state and monitor-photodiode values, trend them the way section 24 trends laser bias.
  • Telemetry moves. In CPO, laser bias, temperature and output power live in the ELSFP, managed through CMIS (section 12), while the engine reports per-lane receive power and loop status. Correlating the two needs the map of which laser feeds which lanes.
  • Eye safety. ELSFP power classes reach 26 dBm, about 400 mW, per wavelength per core, and the agreement caps a fiber at 24.5 dBm under automatic power reduction to stay at IEC 60825-2 Hazard Level 1. Treat external laser ports with the care given to amplified DWDM systems (section 13).

A field guide to engine faults, using the packaging options from section 10:

Fault Typical symptom Pluggable NPO CPO
Laser aging or failure Bias climbs, then transmit power falls on every lane that laser feeds Replace the module Replace the engine module or its external laser Hot-swap the ELSFP
Dirty or damaged laser-input connector Transmit power drops on every lane fed through it while laser bias stays normal Internal; not serviceable Clean, then replace Clean, then hot-swap the ELSFP
Ring or bias lock loss One lane drops or flaps around thermal events Replace the module if it recurs Replace the engine module if it recurs Usually re-locks; a persistent fault means a board or switch repair
Fiber-attach degradation One lane's received power falls steadily at the far end while the transmitter's monitors look normal Replace the module Replace the engine module Board or switch repair; engines are not field-replaceable
Driver or TIA failure One lane is dead while its optical power is normal Replace the module Replace the engine module Board or switch repair
Section 26 · Deep dives

Long-haul coherent transmission: how it works and what limits it

6 diagrams · 15 min read
In this sectionReach classesWhat the DSP can undo, and what it cannotNoise: amplifiers, span loss and OSNRThe nonlinear ceiling: launch power and GSNRTrading capacity for reach: format, baud, shaping and FECLine systems: ROADMs, flexgrid, bands and RamanMargins and planningSubmarine systemsStandards that govern long-haul coherentWhat it means in operations

A long-haul coherent link is a noise budget. Every amplifier adds noise, every milliwatt of launch power adds nonlinear distortion in the fiber, and the receiver's DSP undoes almost everything else. Reach ends where the generalized signal-to-noise ratio (GSNR) at the receiver falls below what the chosen modulation format and FEC need. Section 8 covers the coherent transceiver and section 18 its newer features; this section follows the light through a line system hundreds to thousands of kilometers long.

Read the chain left to right. The DSP removes dispersion and polarization effects at the far end, but the noise added at each amplifier and the distortion added in each span stay in the signal, so GSNR only falls.

Reach classes

The same physics applies from 80 km to 16,000 km; what changes is how many amplified spans the noise accumulates over, and therefore which transceiver and format fit. Class boundaries are conventions that vary by operator.

Class Typical distance Amplified spans Line system Typical transceiver
Data center interconnect Up to about 120 km 0–1 Booster and pre-amplifier, or none 400ZR, 800ZR and 1600ZR pluggables (section 8)
Metro and regional Up to about 1,000 km A few to about 12 EDFAs, ROADMs ZR+ pluggables; 800G ZR+ has been shown over about 1,000–1,070 km
Long haul About 1,000–3,000 km About 12–40 EDFAs, often with Raman Embedded transponders; ZR+ at lower rates
Ultra-long haul Beyond about 3,000 km 40 or more Raman, low-loss or large-area fiber Embedded transponders with heavily shaped or QPSK-class formats
Submarine About 6,000–16,000 km About 100 or more repeaters Shore-powered repeaters every 50–100 km Submarine line terminal equipment (SLTE)

Sources: 800G ZR+ field trial, 800G ZR+ product, repeater spacing review, repeater spacing study, 16,608 km subsea result.

What the DSP can undo, and what it cannot

Coherent detection hands the DSP the full optical field, so any impairment that is linear and either fixed or slowly changing can be calculated and reversed. What the DSP cannot reverse is noise and cross-channel nonlinear distortion; those add up span by span and set the reach.

Impairment Where it comes from Typical scale What the DSP does What it costs
Chromatic dispersion (CD) Fiber; about 16.7–17 ps/nm/km at 1550 nm About 17,000 ps/nm per 1,000 km A static equalizer removes it. Embedded DSPs tolerate ±150,000–350,000 ps/nm; a 400ZR module ±2,400 ps/nm DSP power and latency grow with the dispersion to undo
Polarization-mode dispersion (DGD) Random fiber birefringence that drifts over time A few ps over 1,000 km of modern fiber An adaptive polarization equalizer tracks it. Tolerances run from about 10 ps (400ZR) to 64 ps (embedded) Small, unless the fiber moves fast
Polarization-dependent loss (PDL) Amplifiers, ROADMs and other components Fractions of a dB per element Cannot be undone, because signal and noise are lost unequally An SNR penalty; 400ZR allows 4 dB of PDL for a 2 dB penalty
Laser phase noise and frequency offset Transmit laser and local oscillator About 100 kHz linewidth lasers for 400G-class modems Carrier recovery tracks it Denser formats need quieter lasers
ROADM filtering Each wavelength-selective switch narrows the passband Penalty grows with every pass The equalizer partly restores the edges Enhanced noise; plan the number of passes
ASE noise Every optical amplifier Sets the OSNR (next subsection) Nothing Accumulates with span count
Nonlinear interference (NLI) Kerr effect in the fiber; grows with the cube of launch power Sets the launch-power ceiling The self-channel part could be back-propagated at high DSP cost; the cross-channel part acts as noise Caps useful launch power

Sources: fiber parameters, fiber PMD spec, embedded DSP tolerances, 400ZR and ZR+ tolerances, 100 kHz laser, filtering penalties.

Noise: amplifiers, span loss and OSNR

Each amplifier gives back the power its span took and adds amplified spontaneous emission (ASE) noise in proportion to its gain and noise figure. Identical spans add equal noise, so OSNR falls by 3 dB every time the number of spans doubles. For a chain of identical spans, measured in a 0.1 nm (12.5 GHz) reference bandwidth:

OSNR0.1 nm ≈ 58 + Pch − Lspan − NF − 10·log10 Nspans

Here P is the launch power per channel in dBm, L the span loss and NF the amplifier noise figure in dB. The 58 is −10·log₁₀(hν·B_ref / 1 mW) with B_ref = 12.5 GHz (0.1 nm at 1550 nm): the quantum reference in the measurement bandwidth, not any amplifier's noise floor; the amplifier's own excess noise enters through NF (derivation).

Worked example. 80 km spans at 0.2 dB/km plus 1 dB of connectors give 17 dB of span loss. With 5 dB amplifiers and 1 dBm per channel, one span delivers 58 + 1 − 17 − 5 = 37 dB OSNR. Twenty spans (1,600 km) cost 10·log₁₀ 20 = 13 dB, leaving 24 dB. For comparison, one 400G-class module datasheet asks for about 15 dB for QPSK at 60 GBd and 23.5 dB for 16QAM (datasheet), before nonlinearity takes its share.

The levers, in order of how directly they buy OSNR:

  • Span loss counts dB for dB. Stretching 80 km spans to 100 km adds 4 dB of loss per span and saves only 1 dB through fewer spans over 1,600 km, a net loss of 3 dB. Where amplifier sites can be placed, shorter spans win.
  • Amplifier noise figure counts dB for dB. EDFAs run at about 4.5–6 dB, lowest at high gain; L-band amplifiers run about 1 dB worse than C-band (GNPy amplifier models, C+L study).
  • Raman amplification spreads the gain through the fiber. Pumping the fiber itself amplifies the signal before it reaches its weakest point, for an effective noise figure of about −2 to 0 dB and about 6 dB more OSNR in a Raman-plus-EDFA hybrid, by one vendor's figures. It is unforgiving of the plant: a −21 dB reflection adds 3 dB to the equivalent noise figure, and 1 dB of connection loss costs 4 dB of Raman gain (Raman app note, Raman test guide).
  • Low-loss, large-area fiber helps twice. ITU-T G.654.E fiber (about 0.16–0.17 dB/km, 110–125 µm² effective area) lowers span loss and nonlinearity; vendors claim 2–4 dB more OSNR per span and roughly twice the reach for some formats (G.654.E white paper).
  • Launch power counts dB for dB, until it doesn't. The next subsection explains the ceiling.

The nonlinear ceiling: launch power and GSNR

Raising launch power raises OSNR dB for dB, but glass's refractive index rises slightly with light intensity (the Kerr effect). Each channel then distorts itself (self-phase modulation) and its neighbors (cross-phase modulation, four-wave mixing). In uncompensated coherent links this nonlinear interference behaves like extra Gaussian noise whose power grows with the cube of launch power, which is what the Gaussian-noise (GN) model captures. GSNR combines both noise sources:

1 / GSNR = 1 / SNRASE + 1 / SNRNLI,    PNLI = η · P3

SNR from ASE rises 1 dB per dB of launch power; SNR from NLI falls 2 dB per dB. GSNR therefore peaks at an optimum launch power, where NLI is half the ASE. At that point GSNR sits 1.76 dB below the ASE-only figure, and the curve is flat enough that a 1 dB error in the NLI estimate moves the optimum power or the reach by only about a third of a dB (GN model paper, 3 dB rule).

Below the optimum the link is noise-limited and more power helps; above it, every extra dB of launch power costs two dB of nonlinear SNR and GSNR falls. The Optics Bench lab's long-haul instrument lets you move each parameter and watch the curve shift.

  • Where the optimum lands. It depends on symbol rate, fiber, band and channel load. Published optima range from about −2 dBm per channel at 32 GBd on 75 km G.652.D spans to +2 to +8 dBm per channel at 100 GBd in a 12 THz C+L system (32 GBd study, C+L study). Line systems set per-channel power targets rather than leaving it to each transceiver.
  • Noise figure matters less than it seems. Because NLI pushes back, the optimized GSNR improves by only about two-thirds of any noise-figure gain: 3 dB lower NF buys about 2 dB of GSNR (scaling rules).
  • Large-area fiber raises the ceiling. Spreading the same power over 125 µm² instead of 80 µm² weakens the Kerr effect; one fiber vendor claims a 1.5 dB higher nonlinear limit (fiber datasheet).
  • Planning tools model it. GN-model planners such as the open-source GNPy (Telecom Infra Project) predict GSNR per channel; in a multi-operator validation they landed within 1 dB of measurement in 90% of 500 cases and placed the optimum power within 0.5 dB (validation, GNPy).

Trading capacity for reach: format, baud, shaping and FEC

At a given GSNR, the transceiver chooses how many bits each symbol carries. Fewer bits per symbol tolerate more noise and reach farther; probabilistic constellation shaping (PCS, section 2) turns that choice from a few fixed steps into a continuous dial.

  • Format costs OSNR. At the same 60 GBd, one datasheet needs about 15 dB OSNR for QPSK, 20 dB for 8QAM and 23.5 dB for 16QAM. Doubling the symbol rate at the same format costs 3 dB: QPSK needs 12 dB at 30 GBd, 15 dB at 60 GBd and 18 dB at 118 GBd (400G-class datasheet, 800G-class datasheet).
  • Shannon sets the ceiling. A dual-polarization channel can carry at most about 2 × baud × log₂(1 + SNR) bits per second. Uniform QAM gives up to 1.53 dB of that; shaping recovers about 1 dB in practice, and modern modems sit within a couple of dB of the linear Shannon limit (shaping, gap to Shannon).
  • Flex-rate turns margin into capacity. Modern embedded modems adjust shaping and baud to fit each path, from 200G to 1.6T on one 200 GBd engine, so a short, clean path carries more than a long one on the same hardware (200 GBd engine).
  • FEC sets the threshold. Stronger codes accept a worse raw BER at the cost of overhead:
FEC Used by Overhead Pre-FEC BER threshold Net coding gain
CFEC 400ZR About 15% 1.25 × 10⁻² 10.8 dB
oFEC OpenZR+, ZR+ modes About 15% 2.0 × 10⁻² 11.1–11.6 dB
Proprietary soft-decision FEC Embedded transponders Up to about 27% Up to about 3.75 × 10⁻² About 11.5–12 dB

Sources: CFEC, oFEC, embedded SD-FEC.

Sources for the plotted points: 200 GBd field results, 3 × 800G trial, 130 GBd trial, 140 GBd field result, 400G QPSK trial, 800G ZR+ trial, 800G ZR+ demo, subsea 4,300 km, subsea 16,608 km. A next generation of 2.4T- and 3.2T-capable embedded transponders was announced in March 2026, sampling mid-2027 with general availability in the second half of 2027 (announcement).

Terrestrial and subsea points are not directly comparable: submarine systems are engineered end to end for their one route, with fixed repeaters and tuned power.

Line systems: ROADMs, flexgrid, bands and Raman

The line system is everything between the transceivers: multiplexers, amplifiers, ROADMs and the fiber. It decides how many wavelengths fit, how they are routed, and how much noise and filtering each one collects.

  • ROADMs route wavelengths without converting them to electrical. Wavelength-selective switches (WSS) add, drop or pass each channel. Colorless, directionless and contentionless (CDC) add/drop lets any transceiver use any wavelength toward any direction. Every pass through a WSS narrows the channel slightly; one study kept the penalty under 1 dB through 14 filters at 32 GBd only with mitigation (filtering study), so long routes through many nodes need wider slots or fewer passes.
  • Flexgrid fits the slot to the signal. ITU-T G.694.1 places center frequencies at 193.1 THz + n × 6.25 GHz with slot widths in multiples of 12.5 GHz (RFC 7699). A 400ZR signal fits 75 GHz, 800ZR about 150 GHz, and a 200 GBd 1.6T signal a 200 GHz channel, of which 24 fill an extended C-band (200 GBd engine).
  • More band, more capacity. Conventional C-band is about 4 THz, extended C about 4.8 THz, Super C about 6 THz, and Super C plus Super L about 12 THz; Super C+L meshes and 12 THz trials were in service or trial in 2025–26 (band widths, Super C+L mesh). The S-band, below 1530 nm, needs thulium-doped or Raman amplifiers; a 15 THz S+C+L system ran 1,552 km in the lab in 2025, but no commercial S-band long-haul deployment had been reported (S+C+L loop).
  • Raman and hybrid amplification. Backward-pumped Raman gain plus an EDFA is common on long spans; in the S+C+L experiment, adding Raman raised net throughput from 88.8 to 92.8 Tb/s (same source).
  • Open line systems. When the line system and transceivers come from different vendors, each wavelength is an “alien wavelength” on the line, and the contract between them is GSNR. The Open ROADM MSA showed multi-vendor 800G pluggables with shaping across a ROADM link in 2025 (Open ROADM demo).

Band edges: Super C and Super L, S-band. Each band needs its own amplifier type, so adding a band adds a parallel amplifier chain at every site.

Margins and planning

A link planned to the exact GSNR it needs today fails as amplifiers age, fiber gets cut and spliced, and models prove optimistic. Planners therefore hold dB in reserve. The values below come from one widely cited operator study and from GNPy's examples; real allocations vary by operator.

Margin What it covers Example value
Amplifier aging Noise figure drifting up over life 0.7 dB
Transponder aging Transmitter and receiver degradation 0.5 dB
Fast variations Polarization, PDL and temperature swings 0.4 dB
Filter aging Each ROADM filter 0.05 dB per filter
Fiber repairs Extra loss from splices after cuts 1.1 dB for 600 km over 10 years (about four cuts)
Nonlinear-model uncertainty Error in the NLI estimate 1.5–3 dB
System or design margin Everything else Under 2 dB; GNPy examples use 2 dB

Sources: low-margin design study, GNPy parameters.

The same study's example network starts life with about 6 dB of margin and argues that unused margin is unsold capacity. Flex-rate transceivers and DSP-reported SNR let operators run a higher rate today and step down only when measured margin shrinks.

Submarine systems

Undersea links follow the same physics with one extra constraint: every repeater is powered over the cable's copper conductor from the shore, so total electrical power is fixed.

  • Repeaters every 50–100 km. One review gives 75–100 km; one recent cable averages 84 km (review, cable study). Power-feed equipment moved from 15 kV to 18 kV, about 20% more power (power feed).
  • Power-limited design favors more fiber pairs. Capacity rises only logarithmically with SNR but linearly with the number of fiber pairs, so space-division multiplexing (SDM) cables run more pairs at lower power each; about 24 pairs was the near-term optimum in one 2019 analysis (SDM analysis). Cables announced in 2025–26 carry 20–24 pairs, and one uses 24 pairs of two-core fiber for about 1 Pb/s over about 7,000 km (announcement).
  • Open cables are specified by GSNR. Rating the wet plant by GSNR rather than by a transponder lets any submarine line terminal light it, and spectrum sharing gives each tenant a “virtual fiber pair” with its own terminal equipment (open cable paper, spectrum sharing).
  • 2025–26 results. 800G per wavelength over 16,608 km at 18 Tb/s per fiber pair, and 20 Tb/s per pair over 10,000 km on a 20-pair trans-Pacific cable, by vendor and operator reports (16,608 km, 10,000 km).

Standards that govern long-haul coherent

No single standard defines a long-haul link. ITU-T defines the fiber, the grid and the framing; OIF and the MSAs define interoperable transceivers; Open ROADM defines how multi-vendor line systems and transponders work together. Embedded long-haul transponders themselves remain proprietary at the line side.

What it means in operations

A coherent receiver is also a line-monitoring instrument: its DSP estimates the physics it undid. Trend these values per wavelength (sections 18 and 24 list the telemetry paths) and read changes against this table.

Reading What it measures A change usually means
Chromatic dispersion estimate (ps/nm) The fiber length crossed, at about 17 ps/nm per km A step change means the path changed: a protection switch or reroute
DGD estimate (ps) Polarization-mode dispersion on the route Fast swings point to mechanically disturbed fiber, such as aerial spans
OSNR estimate ASE noise from the amplifier chain A drop points to an amplifier fault, or extra span loss from a bad splice or a bend
SNR or ESNR (electrical) Everything the receiver sees: ASE, NLI, filtering and transceiver noise ESNR falling while OSNR holds points to nonlinearity or filtering: power set too high, new neighbor channels, or more ROADM passes
Pre-FEC BER and Q Distance to the FEC threshold The margin to trend; converts to Q as below
Launch and received power per channel The power profile along the line Tilt or a dirty connector; a drop in Raman gain on Raman spans
Frequency offset Transmit laser against local oscillator A slow trend means a laser drifting with age
QdB = 20·log10( √2 · erfc−1(2 · BER) )

A pre-FEC BER of 2 × 10⁻² (the oFEC threshold) is a Q of about 6.3 dB, and 1.25 × 10⁻² (CFEC) about 7.0 dB. A wavelength reporting Q = 9 dB on oFEC therefore has about 2.7 dB of margin, and that number, trended over months, is what tells you whether a route can take a higher rate or is heading for trouble.

OCI MSA: an optical PHY for AI scale-up

The Optical Compute Interconnect (OCI) MSA, formed in March 2026 by six accelerator, switch-silicon and hyperscale companies, defines an open optical PHY for links between AI accelerators and scale-up switches (formation). It takes a different path from Ethernet's 200G-per-lane PAM4: many slower NRZ wavelengths on one fiber, built into silicon rather than into a module.

  • First specification. 200G-OCI PHY v1.0 runs 4 wavelengths × 53.125 GBd NRZ per direction (212.5 Gb/s), bidirectionally on a single fiber: forward at 1308.0–1314.9 nm, reverse at 1327.7–1334.8 nm (specification write-up).
  • Reach and build. Deployments target under 100 m with a link budget good to about 500 m. The reference design uses silicon photonics with micro-ring modulators and OIF ELSFP external lasers (section 25), managed through CMIS 5.3 with OCI extensions (same source).
  • Roadmap. A second generation doubles to 400 Gb/s per direction (up to 800 Gb/s per fiber), with 3.2 Tb/s per fiber on the longer roadmap; form factors include pluggable, on-board, co-packaged and chiplet optics (OCI MSA).
  • Protocols on top. It is a PHY: UALink can run over it, and reports describe it carrying vendor scale-up protocols as well (report).

How the pieces depend on each other

  • The lane rate is set first, jointly by IEEE (Ethernet electrical and optical PMDs) and the OIF (CEI electrical specs that SerDes vendors design to).
  • Form-factor MSAs then define cages and modules with enough lanes and cooling for that rate.
  • Optical MSAs fill reach gaps quickly, and IEEE often standardizes a similar PMD later (400G-FR4 began as an MSA).
  • CMIS ties host and module together operationally, regardless of which PMD is inside.
Section 28 · Reference

Roadmap as of October 2026

1 diagram · 4 min read

200G-per-lane PAM4 is the volume generation: 800G and 1.6T modules on 102.4 Tb/s switches. Coherent pluggables reached 1.6T on paper in September 2026, and the next two big decisions are how to signal 400G per lane and how far co-packaged optics displaces pluggables.

Optical lanes tend to lead electrical ones: 100G-per-wavelength optics (400GBASE-DR4, 100GBASE-DR) were standardized in 2017–2018, four years before 100G electrical lanes.

Supply chain EML and CW laser capacity sold out through 2027–2029 at leading suppliers; 200G EMLs over a quarter of EML revenue; AI back-end switch spending passed front-end in 2Q26 — New laser fabs take about three years; quantum-dot and comb lasers, external laser sources and silicon photonics to spread the laser count per bit

What to watch over the next 12–18 months

  • 802.3dj approval. Submission to the IEEE standards board was targeted for October 2026, for approval at the December 2026 RevCom meeting; final publication fixes the 200G-lane PMDs that early modules were built against.
  • PAM4 vs PAM6 at 400G per lane. The modulation choice in P802.3dv decides component bandwidth targets for the next decade.
  • Coherent-lite vs PAM4 at 2–10 km. If 200G-lane PAM4 LR4 holds up, coherent stays outside the building; if not, coherent moves into the campus.
  • CPO field data. Serviceability and failure rates from the first large CPO deployments will decide whether pluggables keep the switch faceplate at 400G per lane.
  • Scale-up goes optical. As GPU pods outgrow a rack, copper's ~1 m reach at 200G per lane forces optics into the scale-up domain, the largest new optics market in view.
  • XPO vs NPO vs CPO. Whether faceplate density at 3.2T and beyond is solved by bigger liquid-cooled pluggables or by moving optics next to the ASIC (section 10).
  • Laser supply. EML and pump-laser capacity at the largest suppliers is sold out into 2028–2029 and new fabs take about three years, so module lead times, not switch silicon, may pace 1.6T and CPO ramps; silicon photonics and external laser sources, which spread one laser over several lanes, are the structural answer.
  • Back-end over front-end. AI back-end switch sales passed front-end data-center switching in 2Q26, so the optics roadmap is now set by accelerator fabrics (scale-out at 200G per lane today, scale-up moving to optics) rather than by front-end refresh cycles.

Glossary

Term Meaning
ACC Active copper cable: twinax with linear redrivers
ADC / DAC Analog-to-digital / digital-to-analog converter (also: direct-attach copper cable, by context)
AEC Active electrical cable: twinax with a retiming DSP in each end
ALS / APR Automatic laser shutdown / automatic power reduction (ITU-T G.664): an amplified line system drops its output on loss of the return signal so that a cut fiber or open connector is eye-safe, then probes for restoration

APC / UPC Angled / ultra-polished physical-contact connector end faces; they do not mate
APD Avalanche photodiode: a detector with internal gain

ASE Amplified spontaneous emission: the noise optical amplifiers add
AUI Attachment unit interface: IEEE's name for the host-to-module electrical interface
Bathtub curve Two meanings: BER plotted against the sampling point across one unit interval, where the opening at a target BER is the usable eye width; and failure rate against time (infant mortality, useful life, wear-out), the curve that burn-in and GR-468 qualification are built around
Baud (GBd) Symbols per second
BER Bit error ratio; pre-FEC (raw) vs post-FEC (delivered)
BERT Bit error ratio tester: pattern generator plus error detector
BiDi Two wavelengths in opposite directions on one fiber
BTO Barium titanate: a Pockels-effect film on silicon, a 400G-per-lane modulator candidate
C2M / C2C Chip-to-module / chip-to-chip electrical links
CD Chromatic dispersion
CDB CMIS command data block, used for firmware upgrades
CDC ROADM Colorless, directionless, contentionless ROADM: any wavelength to any direction from any add/drop port, without blocking
CDR Clock and data recovery
CEI OIF Common Electrical I/O specifications
CER / FLR Codeword error ratio (codewords FEC could not correct) / frame loss ratio; FLR 6.2 × 10⁻¹¹ is treated as equivalent to a 10⁻¹³ BER
CFEC / oFEC Coherent FEC codes used by 400ZR / OpenZR+ and 800ZR
Class 1 / Class 1M IEC 60825-1 laser classes: safe to view under reasonable conditions / safe to the naked eye but not through magnifying optics; hazard level 1 in single-mode fiber is about +22 dBm at 1310 nm and +10 dBm at 1550 nm under IEC 60825-2:2021 (the 2004 table gave +12 dBm at 1310 nm)
CMIS Common Management Interface Specification for 400G+ modules
CMIS-LT OIF CMIS out-of-band link training (2026): per-lane, per-direction tuning of host and module through the management interface, for linear modules that have no electrical link training
Coherent Detection that recovers phase and polarization using a local laser
CPC Co-packaged copper: twinax that plugs into a socket on or beside the ASIC package, bypassing board traces
CPO / NPO Co-packaged / near-packaged optics
COBO On-board optics on the main board near the chip; a precursor to NPO
COM Channel operating margin: IEEE's simulated pass/fail margin for an electrical channel, in dB
Comb laser A source that emits many evenly spaced wavelengths at once, for dense WDM
CTLE / FFE / DFE Linear, feed-forward and decision-feedback equalizers
Cutoff wavelength Wavelength above which a fiber carries a single mode; at most 1260 nm for cabled G.652, which is why the O-band starts there
CW-WDM MSA Defines 8-, 16- and 32-wavelength O-band laser grids for dense-WDM optical I/O
CWDM / LAN-WDM / DWDM Coarse (20 nm: CWDM4 at 1271/1291/1311/1331 nm), LAN (800 GHz: 1295.56/1300.05/1304.58/1309.14 nm) and dense (≤ 100 GHz) wavelength grids
DCO / ACO Digital / analog coherent optics (DSP inside / outside the module)
DGD / PDL Differential group delay (PMD at one instant) / polarization-dependent loss; the DSP tracks DGD, while PDL costs SNR
DML / EML Directly modulated laser / electro-absorption modulated laser
DOM / DDM Digital optical monitoring: temperature, voltage, bias, Tx and Rx power
EAM Electro-absorption modulator: an electric field shifts the absorption edge (GeSi or III-V)
EDFA Erbium-doped fiber amplifier (C-band; L-band variants use longer erbium fiber)
Edge / grating coupler Fiber coupler at the chip's edge (lower loss, broadband) or on its surface (testable on the wafer)
EIC / PIC Electronic IC (drivers, TIAs, control loops) / photonic IC (modulators, detectors, couplers)
ELSFP External laser small form-factor pluggable, for CPO
Engineered link A pairing outside any spec, qualified as a specific combination of hosts and modules; LPO facing a retimed module is one today
ER (extinction ratio) Ratio of the highest to the lowest optical level, P3/P0 for PAM4 or P1/P0 for NRZ, in dB; IEEE minimum 3.5 dB for PAM4; a low ER wastes average power through OMA
ERL Effective return loss: reflections weighted by how much they hurt after equalization
ESNR Electrical SNR the coherent DSP measures after equalization; unlike OSNR it includes nonlinear, filtering and transceiver penalties
Fast and narrow / slow and wide Few lanes at the highest rate with DSP and FEC, or many lanes at modest NRZ rates via WDM, parallel fibers or wide packaging
FAU Fiber array unit: a V-groove fiber array bonded to a photonic chip
FIT / MTTF Failures per billion device-hours / mean time to failure (10⁹ ÷ FIT hours)
Flexgrid ITU-T G.694.1 DWDM grid: channel centers at 193.1 THz + n × 6.25 GHz, slot widths in 12.5 GHz steps
Flyover cable Twinax routed above the board from the ASIC package to a port or engine, bypassing lossy board traces
FRO Fully retimed optics: the conventional module, with a DSP on transmit and on receive
G.654.E ITU-T terrestrial fiber with a large effective area (about 125 µm²) and low loss, for longer coherent spans
G.657 ITU-T bend-insensitive single-mode fiber (A1, A2, B2, B3)
Ge photodiode Germanium-on-silicon detector: about 1 A/W at 1310 nm, 50–70 GHz in foundry kits
Gearbox Changes lane count and rate between host and media sides
GN model / NLI Gaussian-noise model: treats fiber nonlinear interference (NLI) as extra Gaussian noise that grows with the cube of launch power
gNMI gRPC Network Management Interface: streams OpenConfig telemetry (SAMPLE or ON_CHANGE)
GR-468 Telcordia reliability qualification for optoelectronic devices
Grey optics Fixed-wavelength, non-DWDM optics
GSNR Generalized SNR: amplifier noise and nonlinear noise combined into one figure that predicts coherent performance
Hazard level IEC 60825-2 rating of a location in a fiber system (1, 1M, 2, 2M, 3R, 3B, 4) by the power accessible there, rather than of a product; decides labeling and whether ALS is required
HCF Hollow-core fiber: light guided in an air core by antiresonant glass membranes (NANF, DNANF)
Heterogeneous / hybrid integration III-V bonded onto the silicon wafer, then processed / a finished laser die attached to the chip
Hybrid bonding Direct copper-to-copper bonding at micrometer pitch, used to stack an EIC on a PIC
IM-DD Intensity modulation, direct detection
Imaging fiber A fiber with thousands of cores that carries a picture; micro-emitter cables send hundreds of slow light channels through one
IPoDWDM IP over DWDM: coherent pluggables in router or switch ports in place of transponders, driving the line system directly
IQ modulator Modulates in-phase and quadrature field components
ITLA Integrable tunable laser assembly
Kerr effects (SPM / XPM / FWM) Intensity-dependent refractive index: self- and cross-phase modulation and four-wave mixing, the nonlinear noise the GN model sums; grows with launch power × effective length ÷ effective area
KGD Known-good die: tested before assembly, so one bad part does not scrap an engine
KP4 / KR4 RS(544,514) / RS(528,514) Reed-Solomon FEC; KP4 corrects up to 15 symbol errors per 5,440-bit codeword, KR4 up to 7
LACC Linear active copper cable: another name for ACC
Launch power Optical power per channel entering a span: too low and amplifier noise dominates, too high and nonlinear noise does
LPO / LRO / RTLR Linear pluggable optics / linear receive optics / retimed transmitter, linear receiver
MACsec / MKA IEEE 802.1AE hop-by-hop Ethernet encryption / its key agreement protocol
MCF Multi-core fiber: several cores in one cladding, uncoupled or coupled
MFD / Aeff Mode field diameter (about 9.2 µm at 1310 nm and 10.4 µm at 1550 nm in G.652) / effective area (about 80 µm² in G.652, 110–130 µm² in terrestrial G.654.E, up to 150 µm² in submarine G.654.D); sets coupling loss and the nonlinear threshold
MicroLED A micrometer-scale LED; arrays of them carry slow-and-wide optical links without lasers
MLSE Maximum-likelihood sequence estimation
MMC VSFF multi-fiber connector on a TMT ferrule: 12, 16 or 24 fibers, up to 3× MPO density
MMF / SMF Multimode / single-mode fiber
MPI Multipath interference from reflections
MPO Multi-fiber push-on connector (12 or 16 fibers common)
MRM / MZM Micro-ring modulator (resonant, one wavelength) / Mach-Zehnder modulator (interferometric, broadband)
MSA Multi-source agreement
Noise figure (NF) An amplifier’s SNR degradation in dB, about 4–6 dB for an EDFA; enters the OSNR rule 58 + P − L − NF − 10·log N
NRZ / PAM4 / PAM6 2-, 4- and 6-level pulse amplitude modulation
OCI MSA Optical Compute Interconnect MSA: an open optical PHY for AI scale-up links, starting at 200G per direction on one fiber
OCS Optical circuit switch: steers light between fibers with mirrors or liquid crystals
OLTS Optical loss test set: a light source and a power meter, the tier-1 certification instrument; the OTDR is tier 2
OM3 / OM4 / OM5 (EMB) Laser-optimized 50 µm multimode grades by effective modal bandwidth at 850 nm: 2,000 / 4,700 / 4,700 MHz·km; OM5 adds 2,470 MHz·km at 953 nm for SWDM
OMA Optical modulation amplitude: P1 − P0 for NRZ or P3 − P0 for PAM4, the swing the receiver sees; OMA = 2 · P avg · (ER − 1) / (ER + 1), so a low ER wastes average power
Open CPX MSA Socketed optical engine for NPO and CPO: 6.4T and 7.2T sockets at 200G per lane (specification published September 2026), with a roadmap to 12.8T and 448G lanes
OpenConfig Vendor-neutral YANG models for configuration and telemetry
Optical I/O Optical engines inside an accelerator package for scale-up links, often ring-based dense WDM
ORL / return loss Optical return loss: total power reflected back toward the transmitter; APC connectors give 60 dB and more, UPC about 50 dB; poor ORL destabilizes lasers and causes MPI
OS2 / G.652.D Low-water-peak single-mode fiber, the default data-center and campus fiber, usable from the O-band to the L-band
OSNR Optical signal-to-noise ratio
OTDR Optical time-domain reflectometer: maps loss and reflections along a fiber
OTN / OTUCn / FlexO ITU-T G.709 optical transport framing (OTU4 = 100G, OTUCn = n × 100G) and its flexible, pluggable-friendly variant FlexO; the framing inside 400ZR and ZR+
P2MP coherent Point-to-multipoint coherent: one hub split into routable digital subcarriers
PCS Probabilistic constellation shaping (also: physical coding sublayer, by context)
PDK Process design kit: a foundry's characterized device library and design rules
PID (Cisco) Product ID, the orderable part number: form factor, speed, PMD and suffix for grey optics (QDD-400G-DR4-S); checked per platform in Cisco's TMG compatibility matrix
PM fiber Polarization-maintaining fiber: carries external laser light to polarization-sensitive silicon modulators
PMD Physical medium dependent sublayer, the optical spec (e.g. DR4); also polarization mode dispersion
PMD coefficient Growth of polarization mode dispersion with length, in ps/√km (0.2 link design value for G.652.D, 0.1 or better in modern cable); DGD is its value at one instant
Pockels effect Linear electro-optic effect: absent in silicon, present in lithium niobate and BTO
PRBS Pseudo-random bit sequence, a test pattern
Precoding (1/(1+D)) PAM4 coding option that turns a typical DFE error burst into two errored symbols, at the cost of doubling each random error
PTP / SyncE IEEE 1588 time synchronization / synchronous Ethernet frequency distribution
Q-factor Pre-FEC BER expressed in dB, Q = 20·log₁₀(√2·erfc⁻¹(2·BER)); operators track Q margin above the FEC threshold
QAM / QPSK Quadrature amplitude modulation / quadrature phase-shift keying
QKD Quantum key distribution: keys sent with single photons so eavesdropping is detectable
Quantum limit Fewest photons per bit at which an ideal detector reaches a target BER, about 10 per bit at 10⁻⁹ for on-off keying; real IM-DD receivers sit 25–35 dB above it
Raman amplification Gain created in the transmission fiber itself by a strong pump about 13 THz above the signal; lowers the span's effective noise figure
Redriver A linear amplifier and equalizer that boosts a signal without recovering its clock
Responsivity Photodiode current per watt of light (A/W): about 0.8–1.0 for InGaAs and germanium at 1310–1550 nm, 0.5 for GaAs at 850 nm; the theoretical maximum is 1.06 A/W at 1310 nm
Retimer Recovers and re-launches lanes at the same rate
RF over waveguide A cable that carries a millimeter-wave or terahertz radio carrier through plastic (dielectric) cores instead of light or baseband copper
RIN Relative intensity noise: a laser’s power fluctuation per hertz of bandwidth, in dB/Hz; it scales with signal power, so it sets an error floor that more receive power cannot fix
RJ / DJ / TJ Random, deterministic and total jitter; TJ at a target BER is what the timing bathtub measures
ROADM / WSS Reconfigurable optical add-drop multiplexer / wavelength-selective switch
SBS / SRS Stimulated Brillouin scattering (reflects a narrow-linewidth launch above roughly +5 to +10 dBm on a long span; raised by dithering the laser) / stimulated Raman scattering (moves power toward longer wavelengths, tilting the band)
SDM Space-division multiplexing: more cores or modes rather than more wavelengths
SECQ Stressed eye closure quaternary: the eye closure of the deliberately impaired signal used in a stressed receiver sensitivity test, set equal to the TDECQ limit
Sensitivity Lowest OMA (or average power) at which a receiver meets the target BER; stressed sensitivity is measured with a worst-case transmitter signal
SER Symbol error ratio; with Gray-coded PAM4, BER is about half the SER
SerDes Serializer/deserializer: high-speed I/O on an ASIC
Shoreline density Bandwidth per millimeter of chip edge (Tb/s/mm); also called beachfront density
Shot noise / thermal noise Noise from the photon arrival statistics (grows as √P) / from the TIA’s resistance (independent of P); PIN receivers are thermal-limited, APD and coherent receivers approach the shot limit
SLTE Submarine line terminal equipment: the transponders and line gear at each cable landing station
SMSR Side-mode suppression ratio: how single-wavelength a DFB or EML is, at least 30 dB; poor SMSR shows up as dispersion penalty and MPI
SN-MT 8-, 16- or 32-fiber MT-style ferrule in the SN duplex footprint; roughly 2.7–3× MPO-16 density depending on panel layout
SOA Semiconductor optical amplifier: compact and O-band capable; a receiver preamplifier in ER4 and ER8 optics and a booster in some ZR modules; its gain is pattern-dependent
SOI Silicon-on-insulator: the silicon photonics wafer, typically 220 nm of silicon on buried oxide
SRMO Short-Reach Micro-Emitter Optics: an OCP workstream, started October 2026, to standardize micro-emitter (microLED) links
SSPRQ / PRBS31Q PAM4 test patterns for transmitter (TDECQ) and BER testing
Super C / Super L Extended C and L bands of about 6 THz each; together they roughly double the spectrum per fiber
TDECQ Transmitter and dispersion eye closure quaternary: PAM4 transmitter quality
TDP Transmitter and dispersion penalty: the NRZ-era sensitivity penalty of a real transmitter over the target fiber; TDECQ is its PAM4 successor
TEC Thermoelectric cooler: holds a LAN-WDM or DWDM laser within about ±1 nm; why LR4 and coherent modules draw more power than CWDM4
TFLN Thin-film lithium niobate modulators
Thermo-optic tuning Heaters that shift a waveguide's index slowly, to bias MZMs, lock rings and trim filters
TIA Transimpedance amplifier after the photodiode
TOSA / ROSA / BOSA Transmit / receive / bidirectional optical sub-assembly: the packaged laser with its driver, or photodiode with its TIA, inside a module
TP (test points) IEEE compliance points: TP1a (host output at the connector), TP2 (optical output), TP3 (optical input), TP4 (module electrical output), TP4a (host input); each a contract boundary between host and module
Transponder / muxponder Line-system cards that map one / several client signals onto a coherent wavelength; what IPoDWDM removes
TRO Transmit-retimed optics: another name for LRO, with a DSP on transmit only
Twinax Shielded twin-axial copper pairs: the medium inside DAC, ACC and AEC cables
UCIe Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express: the die-to-die interface optical I/O chiplets use
UI Unit interval: one symbol period, 18.8 ps at 53.125 GBd and 9.4 ps at 106.25 GBd; jitter and eye width are quoted in UI
VCSEL Vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser (850 nm for SR, 880–940 nm for SWDM, 1060 nm for some slow-and-wide links; multimode)
VDM CMIS versatile diagnostics monitoring: per-lane SNR, BER and more
VOA Variable optical attenuator; fixed attenuators pad ER and ZR optics on short links, VOAs level power in line systems
VSFF Very-small-form-factor connectors (SN, MDC, CS)
Water peak Hydroxyl absorption near 1383 nm that split the historical windows; suppressed in G.652.D, which opened the E-band
XPN 64-bit MACsec packet numbering (802.1AEbw) so the counter does not wrap within minutes at 40G and above; needs the GCM-AES-XPN cipher suites
XPO eXtra-dense Pluggable Optics: a liquid-cooled 64 × 200G (12.8T) pluggable MSA announced in 2026
XSR / XSR+ OIF extra-short-reach electrical classes used for CPO and NPO links
Zero-dispersion wavelength (λ₀) / slope (S₀) Where chromatic dispersion crosses zero (1300–1324 nm for G.652) and how fast it grows away from there (at most 0.092 ps/(nm²·km)); D(λ) = S₀/4 · (λ − λ₀⁴/λ³)
ZR / ZR+ / OpenZR+ / Bright ZR+ 400G coherent pluggable classes: OIF 400ZR (16QAM, CFEC, about 120 km amplified), OpenZR+ (oFEC, multi-rate, metro reach) and high-output Bright variants for ROADM networks
Section 30 · Reference

Mastery checks

22 min read

If you can answer these without looking back, you have the mental models this guide is built around. Answers follow the questions.

57 questions
  1. 01A 100G lane runs at 53.125 GBd. Why that number, and why not 50 GBd?
    100 Gb/s of payload grows with 256b/257b transcoding and RS(544,514) overhead to 106.25 Gb/s, and PAM4 carries 2 bits per symbol, so 53.125 GBd. The extra rate is the price of FEC.
  2. 02Why does PAM4 cost about 9.5 dB of SNR versus NRZ, and what did the industry buy with that loss?
    The same swing is split into three eyes, each one-third the height: 20·log₁₀ 3 ≈ 9.5 dB. It halved the symbol rate, and therefore the bandwidth that lasers, drivers and copper channels must deliver.
  3. 03A 400G QSFP-DD DR4 and a 400G QSFP112 DR4 carry the same optical signal. What differs inside them, and why does it matter?
    The QSFP-DD module has 8 × 50G host lanes and needs a gearbox; the QSFP112 has 4 × 100G host lanes and a simpler 1:1 retimer. The gearbox adds power and latency, and the module must match the host's lane rate.
  4. 04Your host shows steadily rising corrected FEC codewords on one port, but the module's DOM looks perfect. Name three places the problem could be.
    The near-end host channel, the optical segment (including dirty connectors that DOM average power will not reveal), and the far-end host channel. Compare module VDM SNR and pre-FEC BER with host counters, then swap one element at a time.
  5. 05Can a 400G DR4 break out to four 100G CWDM4 ports? Explain with the lane-matching rule.
    No. DR4 lanes are 100G PAM4 each; CWDM4 is four 25G NRZ lanes multiplexed onto one fiber pair. A DR4 lane can only meet a single-lane 100G PAM4 port (100G-DR or FR1).
  6. 06Why do almost all IM-DD single-mode optics sit near 1310 nm, while coherent sits near 1550 nm?
    Standard fiber has near-zero chromatic dispersion around 1310 nm, so IM-DD pulses stay sharp. At 1550 nm, loss is lowest and EDFAs work, and the coherent DSP removes the large dispersion electronically.
  7. 07What does a coherent receiver's local laser actually do?
    It mixes with the incoming light so that phase and polarization differences become intensity differences a photodiode can measure. Without it, phase is invisible to a square-law detector.
  8. 08Why do 2 km 200G-per-lane optics run at 113.4375 GBd while 500 m ones run at 106.25 GBd?
    Longer 200G links add an inner Hamming(128,120) FEC inside the module to tolerate a worse raw BER. Its overhead raises the line rate; 500 m links meet the standard BER without it.
  9. 09What does an LPO module give up in exchange for halving its power?
    Its DSP. The host SerDes must equalize the whole end-to-end channel, interoperability must be validated per host-and-module pairing, reach is limited, and per-segment diagnostics are weaker.
  10. 10A 10 km LR4 module on a 3 m patch shows errors. Is receiver overload the likely cause, and what do you check?
    Probably not. IEEE 10 km PMDs are specified for a 0 dB channel: 100GBASE-LR4 allows at most +4.5 dBm average launch per lane and the receiver tolerates +4.5 dBm, so a back-to-back link sits at the receiver's rated maximum, not above it. Read DOM Rx power against the module's rated maximum first. If it is within limits, the usual causes are a dirty or damaged end face, a wavelength-plan mismatch at the far end (LR4 vs CWDM4 vs 4WDM-10 vs 100G-LR1), a FEC-mode mismatch on the host, or a non-compliant module launching above the far receiver's maximum. Only in that last case, or with ER- and ZR-class optics whose launch exceeds the receiver maximum, do you add a fixed attenuator sized from the data sheet.
  11. 11Why does the symbol-error histogram tell you more than the uncorrectable-codeword counter?
    Uncorrectable counts only move once margin is already gone. The histogram shows how many bad symbols codewords carry, so a tail creeping toward 15 warns you while the link still looks clean.
  12. 12A 400ZR channel fits a 75 GHz slot; 800ZR needs about 150 GHz. What does that say about capacity per fiber?
    Doubling the rate per wavelength roughly doubles the spectrum each channel occupies, so capacity per fiber rises far less than per-wavelength rate. Spectral efficiency, not baud, sets fiber capacity.
  13. 13Why do CPO designs keep the laser in a front-panel pluggable?
    Lasers are the least reliable and most heat-sensitive component. Keeping them in pluggable external laser sources makes them replaceable and away from the hot ASIC.
  14. 14What happens to passive copper reach when lane rate doubles, and what replaced it in the rack?
    It roughly halves, to about 1 m at 200G per lane. Active electrical cables with retiming DSPs took over most in-rack links beyond that.
  15. 15Two modules both say "100G, duplex LC, single-mode" and will not link. Give two reasons.
    Different wavelength plans or modulation: LR4 (LAN-WDM, 4 × 25G NRZ), CWDM4 (CWDM, 4 × 25G NRZ) and FR1/LR1 (one 100G PAM4 wavelength) do not interoperate. FEC mode mismatch is another candidate.
  16. 16Why does moving optics from a pluggable to NPO or CPO cut power, and what does it cost?
    It shortens the electrical channel from 10–30 cm to a few cm or millimeters, so the SerDes needs far less equalization and the module DSP disappears. The cost is serviceability (engines cannot be swapped at the faceplate), tighter coupling to one switch vendor, and younger fault-isolation tooling.
  17. 17A 1.6T OSFP must serve two 800G ports. Which variants allow that, and why can't a 1.6T DR8 split into 100G ports?
    2×DR4, 2×FR4, or a DR8 broken out as 2 × 800G-DR4. Its lanes are 200G PAM4, and a 100G port cannot receive a 200G lane, so the lane-matching rule (section 6) rules out 100G breakout.
  18. 18How does XPO differ from CPO in where the optics live and how they are replaced?
    XPO keeps the optics at the faceplate as a large, liquid-cooled, hot-swappable module carrying 12.8T; CPO puts optical engines on the ASIC package, runs fiber to the panel, and only the external lasers are swappable.
  19. 19A new DR4 link shows every lane dark at both ends, with normal Tx power. What polarity problem is likely?
    The channel never crosses transmit to receive: a Type A trunk without a flip elsewhere sends Tx 1–4 into the far module's Tx 1–4. A Type B trunk, or the correct patch cords for the polarity method in use, fixes it (section 16).
  20. 20Why would an AI operator pay for hollow-core fiber between data centers?
    Latency: hollow-core cuts delay per km by about 30%, so sites can sit roughly 45% farther apart for the same latency budget and still behave as one cluster. Lower loss and nonlinearity are a bonus.
  21. 21A PTP clock is off by about 10 ns after a fiber repair. What do you suspect?
    New asymmetry: one fiber of the pair is now about 4 m longer than the other (about 2.5 ns of error per meter), or a swapped BiDi or module changed the transmit and receive delays. Measure the asymmetry and compensate.
  22. 22Telemetry shows a lane's laser bias climbing for weeks while Tx power stays flat. What is happening, and what do you do?
    The laser is aging: its control loop drives more current to hold the same output. Schedule a replacement before it reaches its bias limit instead of waiting for it to fail (section 24).
  23. 23Why does every silicon photonic engine need indium phosphide, and what are the four ways to add it?
    Silicon's indirect bandgap means it cannot lase, so the light comes from InP: an external laser source over fiber, a hybrid laser die attached to the chip, III-V material bonded onto the wafer (heterogeneous), or, still in research, laser material grown directly on silicon (section 25).
  24. 24A ring-based CPO link flaps whenever the coolant loop changes temperature; an MZM-based link beside it does not. Why?
    A ring is resonant. Its dip moves about 0.1 nm per kelvin, and a drift of about 1 K can break the link unless the heater and lock loop keep up. An MZM is broadband and barely notices the same change.
  25. 25Four lanes of a DR8 pluggable fail together while the other four are clean. What do you suspect first?
    A shared laser. Silicon DR8 designs often split one laser across four lanes, so a failing laser or its coupling takes out exactly that group. Check the lasers before chasing individual lanes.
  26. 26Why does stacking the EIC on the PIC with hybrid bonds cut energy per bit, and what new problem does it create?
    Copper-to-copper bonds at micrometer pitch replace bond wires and bumps, removing most of the parasitic load the drivers must charge, so drive energy falls. In exchange, the EIC's heat flows straight into the photonics, which matters most for temperature-sensitive rings.
  27. 27When would you choose a grating coupler over an edge coupler?
    When you need to test every die on the wafer before dicing, or attach fiber to the chip's surface. Choose an edge coupler when you need the lowest loss and a wide optical band, and can hold alignment to about ±1 µm (sub-micron at a bare facet, ±1–2 µm with a spot-size converter) instead of the ±2.5 µm a grating coupler allows; the spot-size converter is what makes passive-alignment fiber-array attach possible.
  28. 28A long-haul design doubles from 10 to 20 identical spans. Why does OSNR fall by about 3 dB, and what else falls with it?
    Each amplifier adds about the same noise while the launch power stays fixed, so 20 spans carry twice the noise of 10: 10·log₁₀ 2 ≈ 3 dB, the 10·log₁₀ N term in the OSNR rule. Nonlinear noise also accumulates with distance, so GSNR, the figure that predicts errors, falls by a little more (section 26).
  29. 29Raising one channel's launch power by 2 dB improved its pre-FEC BER, but its neighbors got worse. What happened?
    The channel was below its own optimum, so more power helped it. But nonlinear interference grows with the cube of power, and cross-phase modulation from the louder channel lands on its neighbors. Set launch power for the whole band, not channel by channel.
  30. 30A coherent receiver's dispersion estimate jumped from about 17,000 to 27,000 ps/nm overnight while traffic stayed up. What do you suspect?
    The light is on a longer path: a protection switch or ROADM reroute added roughly 600 km of fiber at about 17 ps/nm per km. The DSP absorbed the dispersion, but latency rose and OSNR margin fell. Check restoration events before suspecting the module.
  31. 31Receiver OSNR is unchanged, but the module's ESNR has dropped 1.5 dB. Where do you look?
    At what OSNR does not see: nonlinear noise after a launch-power change, a narrowed or misaligned ROADM filter, PDL, or transceiver aging. If neighbors on the same path dropped too, the line is the cause; if only this channel did, look at its transceiver or its filter slot.
  32. 32All 64 lanes of one NPO engine go dark while the engines beside it stay clean. What do you check first, and what do you replace?
    Check the light first: the external laser modules that feed that engine and their fibers, which swap from the front panel. If the light arrives, the engine has failed; unplug it from its socket and fit a spare while the ASIC stays in place. With CPO the engine sits on the ASIC package, so only the lasers are serviceable (section 10).
  33. 33Why might an NPO engine build its lasers in when nearly every CPO design keeps them external?
    Because the NPO engine is socketed: a dead built-in laser costs an engine swap rather than a switch, and an engine a few centimeters from the ASIC can be cooled on its own. Built-in lasers then win back the coupling loss, PM fiber and front-panel laser slots that external lasers cost. The price is a maintenance window for the engine's whole 6.4–12.8T instead of a front-panel hot-swap (section 10).
  34. 34Your AI cluster team wants LPO on every link to save power. Where would you push back?
    On links over about 500 m, on hosts whose SerDes are not qualified for linear modules, in mixed-vendor fabrics, and wherever fast fault isolation matters. LPO saves over 10 W per 1.6T module, but each host-and-module pair needs qualification, margins are tight at 200G per lane, and without a module DSP you lose the telemetry that separates a dirty connector from an aging laser (section 4).
  35. 35On one NPO switch the inner engines run linear but the second-row engines need help. Why, and what are the options?
    Distance: the second row's longer traces exceed the roughly 13 dB XSR+ budget, and at 224G the same budget covers about half the trace length it did at 112G. The options are cutting the loss (flyover cable, better laminate) to stay linear, or adding conditioning: a half-retimed engine, a fully retimed engine, or a bigger host SerDes. Each costs power, about 100 W per pJ/bit on a 102.4T switch (section 10).
  36. 36Why does scale-up optical I/O lean slow and wide while scale-out stays fast and narrow?
    Scale-up links are short, so energy per bit, latency and shoreline density dominate, and many NRZ lanes over dense WDM with no FEC win. Scale-out needs reach, standard PMDs and multi-vendor pluggables, which favor 200G and 400G PAM4 lanes with DSP and FEC (section 10).
  37. 37How many fibers does a 102.4T switch with DR-type optics terminate, and what actually reduces that number?
    512 lanes × 2 fibers = 1,024, or 64 sixteen-fiber connectors, plus laser-feed fibers with external lasers. VSFF connectors such as MMC and SN-MT shrink the panel about 3× but not the fiber count; 4 wavelengths per fiber cut it to 256, bidirectional 4 each way to 128, 16 wavelengths to 64, and 4-core fiber cuts strands to 256 (section 16).
  38. 38What problem does co-packaged copper solve, and when does a scale-up link switch to an OCI-style optical PHY?
    At 224G the board trace is the worst part of the channel. CPC plugs twinax in at the package, so long-reach SerDes copper reaches about 1–2.5 m with no lasers (one demonstration ran 2.5 m over a 48 dB channel at about 4 pJ/bit). Once a link leaves the rack, or copper reach halves again at 448G, an optical PHY such as OCI takes over: 4 NRZ wavelengths each way on one fiber, under 100 m (section 10).
  39. 39Your switch runs LPO and the accelerator runs FRO. Which direction of that link is harder, and what does each end's telemetry tell you?
    Neither is linear end to end. Switch to accelerator, the FRO's DSP equalizes the switch's linear transmit path, and its media-side SNR measures that whole linear segment. Accelerator to switch, the switch SerDes recovers clean FRO light through the LPO's TIA, the LRO case. The pairing is still an engineered link outside the LPO MSA, so qualify the switch, LPO and FRO together (section 4).
  40. 40In a two-tier fabric, how much of the all-linear power saving survives if the accelerator end stays FRO?
    Three-quarters at any module power, because three of the four modules per accelerator port go linear. With 1.6T figures of about 23 W FRO and 9 W LPO: 92 W all-FRO, 36 W all-linear and 50 W mixed, so 42 of 56 W saved. At 1.6T, where LPO is not yet MSA-specified, LRO on the switch ports keeps about half (30 of 56 W).
  41. 41Which Cisco 800G parts break out to eight 100G links at 2 km, and to two 400G DR4 links at 500 m?
    For 2 km, QDD-8X100G-FR (800G-DR8-2, a QSFP-DD800 part) to eight QSFP-100G-FR-S. For 500 m, OSFP-800G-DR8 or DR8P to two QDD-400G-DR4-S or QSFP-400G-DR4, or eight 100G-DR; QDD-8X100G-FR can also run as two 400G DR4s. The switch's port split must match either way (section 6).
  42. 42A link reports a pre-FEC BER of 10⁻⁶. Roughly how much optical margin is that, and what would make the estimate wrong?
    About 1.4 dB. It is 2.8 dB of electrical SNR above the 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ limit, halved for a thermal-noise-limited receiver (section 5). It overstates the margin if reflections or laser noise create an error floor, if bursts load the codewords, or if the host channels already use part of the FEC budget.
  43. 43How long must a BERT run with no errors to claim 10⁻¹² at 95% confidence on a 106.25 Gb/s lane, and why are links not qualified to 10⁻¹⁵?
    3.0/BER bits, so 3 × 10¹² bits, about 28 s. 10⁻¹⁵ would need 3 × 10¹⁵ bits, about 7.8 hours per lane, so links are qualified on pre-FEC BER, which takes milliseconds, and post-FEC performance is inferred from the FEC cliff.
  44. 44A 1.6T link must span 4 m between adjacent racks at 200G per lane. Which cable types reach it today, and what does each cost?
    Passive DAC is out at about 1 m, and linear ACCs list 1–2.5 m in catalogs. First-generation AECs list 1–3 m, so 4 m needs a second-generation AEC (claims of 6 m and more, sampling in October 2026) or optics. Optics means two 1.6T modules and fiber today, since no shipping 1.6T AOC was found. Either way the link pays near optics-class power: 22 W typical per first-generation AEC end in one catalog, against 33.5 W for a twin-port 1.6T module in the same catalog. RF waveguide and micro-emitter cables target exactly this gap, but they are evaluation kits or 2027 products, so qualify them before planning on them (section 9).
  45. 45Why does a slow-and-wide microLED cable need a gearbox, and what limits its reach?
    The host still speaks 100G or 200G PAM4 lanes, but a microLED switches at only a few Gb/s. The gearbox splits each fast lane across many slow channels and the far end reassembles them; the modeled 800G research design uses 400 data channels plus 60 for a cross-channel code. Reach is limited mainly by chromatic dispersion: an LED's spectrum is over 10 nm wide and visible light disperses strongly in silica, so links stop at tens of meters (20 m measured, 50 m modeled). Bundle stiffness and new connectors limit how far the idea scales (section 9).
  46. 46How much slicer SNR does a 100G PAM4 lane need to sit at the KP4 threshold, and how does that compare with NRZ at 10⁻¹² without FEC?
    With Gray coding, PAM4's BER ≈ (3/4)·erfc(√(SNR/10)) for levels ±1 and ±3 (mean power 5). For 2.4 × 10⁻⁴, erfc(x) = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ gives x ≈ 2.55, so SNR ≈ 65, or 18.1 dB. NRZ needs BER = ½·erfc(√(SNR/2)); for 10⁻¹² that is x ≈ 4.97, SNR ≈ 49, or 16.9 dB. NRZ at 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ would need only 10.9 dB, so FEC is worth about 6 dB of slicer SNR and PAM4 costs about 7.3 dB in average-power terms: net, the industry paid about 1.2 dB of SNR and 6.25% of baud for half the symbol rate.
  47. 47A lane shows a pre-FEC BER of 10⁻⁵. Estimate the uncorrectable-codeword rate, and explain why that figure is healthy.
    RS(544,514) works on 10-bit symbols, so with random errors a symbol is bad with probability about 10 × 10⁻⁵ = 10⁻⁴, and a 544-symbol codeword holds 0.054 bad symbols on average. Sixteen or more are needed to defeat it: the Poisson tail gives about 0.054¹⁶ ÷ 16! ≈ 3 × 10⁻³⁴ per codeword, and at the 1.95 × 10⁷ codewords per second of a 106.25 Gb/s lane that is 6 × 10⁻²⁷ per second: never. At the 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ threshold the mean rises to 1.3 bad symbols and the tail to about 10⁻¹² per codeword, which is where the delivered BER reaches 10⁻¹³. The assumption that breaks this is independence: a DFE burst or a periodic interferer stacks errors into one codeword, which is why the symbol-error histogram matters more than the mean BER.
  48. 48Why does a 100G LR4 module carry a thermoelectric cooler while a CWDM4 module does not? Use numbers.
    A DFB drifts about 0.1 nm per °C, so an uncooled laser moves about 7 nm over a 0–70 °C case range. LAN-WDM lanes sit 4.5 nm apart (1295.56, 1300.05, 1304.58, 1309.14 nm) with about ±1 nm of tolerance, so an uncooled laser would walk into its neighbor's filter; the TEC holds it near a setpoint. CWDM4 lanes sit 20 nm apart with ±6.5 nm of tolerance, so 7 nm of drift fits uncooled. The price is roughly 0.5–1 W and a control loop, which is why CWDM4 and FR4 are the cheap 2 km parts. LAN-WDM's other reward is that all four lanes sit within 15 nm of λ₀ and tolerate 10 km, while CWDM's 1271 nm lane sees about −4 ps/(nm·km) and is held to 2 km, or 6 km in IEEE's 400GBASE-LR4-6.
  49. 4910 Gb/s NRZ at 1550 nm reaches 80 km without dispersion compensation. Why did 1550 nm IM-DD never scale to 25G or 100G lanes?
    Dispersion-limited reach scales as 1/B² for the same source, and 80 km × 17 ps/(nm·km) ≈ 1,360 ps/nm is about what a 10G transmitter tolerates. At 25.78 GBd that reach becomes 80 × (10.3/25.78)² ≈ 13 km, and at 53.125 GBd about 3 km; the dispersion-induced power-fading null for 1,360 ps/nm sits at 6.8 GHz, inside the signal band of anything faster than 10G. So 25G-lane ER4 and 100G-lane ER8 stayed at LAN-WDM near 1310 nm with SOA preamplifiers, and anything at 1550 nm beyond a few kilometers went coherent, where the DSP absorbs tens of thousands of ps/nm.
  50. 50What is the quantum-limited sensitivity of a 100G PAM4 lane at 1310 nm, and where do the roughly 33 dB between it and a real receiver go?
    Ideal on-off keying needs about 10 photons per bit for 10⁻⁹. At 106.25 Gb/s that is 1.06 × 10¹² photons per second; a 1310 nm photon carries 1.52 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so the power is 1.6 × 10⁻⁷ W, or −38 dBm. A real 100G-per-lane receiver is specified at about −4.4 dBm OMA outer for a clean signal and −1.9 dBm stressed (400GBASE-DR4). The gap: the TIA's thermal noise, which dominates a PIN receiver (about 22 dB net of the 2.5 dB the FEC-era BER target gives back); PAM4's 4.8 dB of optical power; finite ER, bandwidth-limited ISI and reflections (3–4 dB); and the 2–2.5 dB the receiver gives back for a transmitter at the TDECQ limit. An APD or SOA preamplifier recovers 5–10 dB, and coherent detection with a strong local oscillator reaches the shot-noise regime, which is a large part of why coherent wins beyond tens of kilometers.
  51. 51Does an 800ZR link close over a single 80 km span? Over 120 km?
    OSNR in 0.1 nm ≈ 58 + P_launch − L_span − NF − 10·log₁₀ N. With 0 dBm per channel, 0.25 dB/km including splices (20 dB at 80 km), a 5.5 dB preamplifier noise figure and one span: 58 − 20 − 5.5 = 32.5 dB against the roughly 27 dB an 800ZR receiver requires, 5.5 dB of margin. At 120 km the span is 30 dB and the OSNR 22.5 dB, 4.5 dB short, so launch power is raised to +4 or +5 dBm per channel (watching the nonlinear ceiling) or Raman gain is added. That arithmetic is what "80–120 km, amplified" means.
  52. 52Convert a 51.2T switch's optics power into pJ/bit for retimed, linear and co-packaged optics.
    64 × 800G retimed modules at 16 W are 1,024 W; divided by 51.2 Tb/s that is 20 pJ/bit. Linear modules at 8 W give 512 W and 10 pJ/bit; co-packaged optics at about 5 pJ/bit give 256 W. A 51.2T switch ASIC at about 500 W is itself near 10 pJ/bit, so with retimed modules the optics burn twice what the ASIC does; on a 102.4T switch every pJ/bit is about 100 W.
  53. 53A 100,000-module fleet must see fewer than one optics failure per month. What module FIT does that require, and what follows for the laser?
    Failures per year = FIT × 10⁻⁹ × 8,760 × 100,000 = FIT × 0.876. For 12 a year, FIT must be 13.7 or lower. A typical pluggable is quoted at 100–500 FIT, which gives 90–440 failures a year, 7–37 a month, so the target cannot be met by component quality alone; it is met by predictive replacement from telemetry and by keeping the laser, the dominant FIT contributor, replaceable, which is one argument for external laser sources in CPO.
  54. 54An 800G DR8 launches +1 dBm on each of eight fibers in an MPO-16. What is the total power, and is the port still Class 1?
    dBm do not add: 8 × 1.26 mW = 10 mW, or +1 + 10·log₁₀ 8 = +10 dBm. At the IEEE lane maximum of about +4 dBm it would be 20 mW, +13 dBm. Under IEC 60825-2 Ed. 4.0 (2021) hazard level 1 at 1310 nm in single-mode fiber is about +22 dBm (the 2004 table said +12 dBm, a figure many datasheets still quote), so even +13 dBm is well inside; IEEE still assesses the worst-case combination of lanes on through a 7 mm aperture at 100 mm, and at 850 nm, where the limit is +5.9 dBm, multi-lane SR ports have been classified 1M rather than 1, which is why 802.3 carries an eye-safety analysis for every MPO PMD. The practical rule does not change: never view an open port, cap it, measure it. An EDFA booster at +20 dBm (100 mW) or a Raman pump near 1 W is far beyond Class 1 and relies on automatic laser shutdown.
  55. 55A 2 km FR4 link runs through two patch cords, two panels and a trunk: six mated connector pairs. Does it close, and what if a seventh is added?
    Fiber: 2 km × 0.5 dB/km = 1.0 dB. Six standard-grade pairs at TIA-568.3's 0.75 dB are 4.5 dB, 5.5 dB in all against the 4.0 dB maximum channel loss: it does not close on paper. With low-loss hardware at 0.35 dB per pair the connectors cost 2.1 dB and the total is 3.1 dB, 0.9 dB of margin; a seventh low-loss pair takes it to 3.45 dB, which still closes, while a seventh standard pair would not. A measured loss from an OLTS replaces the planning figures. FR4's 2 km is also a dispersion allocation for the 1271 and 1331 nm lanes, so a 3 km link that fits the loss is still out of specification.
  56. 56Why does 400G at 16QAM reach about 120 km while 100G QPSK on the same fiber reached thousands of kilometers? Quantify in OSNR.
    At the same symbol rate 16QAM needs about 7 dB more SNR than QPSK for the same BER: its constellation points are √5 closer at equal mean power and it carries twice the bits. 400ZR also runs about 60 GBd against 100G QPSK's 32 GBd, and required OSNR scales with baud: +10·log₁₀(60/32) ≈ +2.7 dB. About 10 dB more OSNR in all, which at 3 dB per doubling of span count is roughly one-tenth the spans, before counting the pluggable's lower launch power and the nonlinear ceiling. That is why 400ZR is a DCI part and why metro and long-haul 400G use QPSK or 8QAM at higher baud (section 26).
  57. 57At 100G per lane, 802.3db keeps 100 m on OM4 only for its SR class with tighter transmitter specifications and adds a relaxed VR class at 50 m, and 802.3ds targets 30–50 m at 200G per lane. Why does multimode reach shrink with each step, and what does OM5 change?
    Halving the unit interval (37.6 ps at 26.5625 GBd, 18.8 ps at 53.125 GBd, 9.4 ps at 106.25 GBd) doubles the fraction of a symbol that the same delay spread consumes. Two spreads grow with length: modal dispersion, bounded by OM4's 4,700 MHz·km effective modal bandwidth, and chromatic spread from the VCSEL's roughly 0.5 nm spectral width at about −100 ps/(nm·km) at 850 nm. Holding the ISI penalty constant means halving the length at each step, or tightening the transmitter (narrower spectral width, lower TDECQ), which is what the SR class does to keep 100 m. OM5 guarantees bandwidth to 953 nm (2,470 MHz·km) so that SWDM can carry four wavelengths per fiber pair; it reduces fiber count and does not extend 850 nm reach. This is why multimode is leaving the AI fabric at 200G per lane and why the enterprise plant question is how many OM4 runs are under 50 m.
Vendor-neutral and standards-first. Fast-moving figures carry their sources; vendor numbers are labeled as claims. The editable doc version holds the same content.
